title: Classical causal AI
audience: Undergraduates in statistics, computer science, data science, or physics who know basic probability and linear algebra
intro: Define the effect of an action with structural causal models and the do-operator. Read independences off causal graphs, choose what to adjust for, and prove when an effect can be computed from observational data. Then meet potential outcomes, causal discovery, counterfactuals, and the extra assumptions behind causal machine learning, transport, and fairness, before Level 5 turns to quantum systems.

lessons.title: Structural causal models
lessons.objective: Write a structural causal model, compute an intervention by replacing one structural equation, and compare the interventional distribution with the observational one.
lessons.big_idea: A causal model is a set of mechanisms; an intervention replaces one mechanism and keeps the others, so seeing $X = x$ and setting $X = x$ can give different answers from the same model.
outcomes: Write the structural equations, background distribution and induced graph of a small structural causal model, and derive its observational distribution by substitution in topological order.
Build the submodel $M_x$ for $do(X = x)$ and compute $P(Y \mid do(X = x))$ by hand and by simulation.
Prove the truncated factorization for a Markovian model and use it to explain why $P(y \mid x)$ and $P(y \mid do(x))$ differ when $X$ and $Y$ share a cause.

key_terms.meaning: Background variables with a joint distribution, plus one assignment $V_i := f_i(\mathrm{PA}_i, U_i)$ per modeled variable.
Endogenous variables are explained inside the model; exogenous (background) variables $U$ are inputs whose distribution is given.
The rule $:=$ that computes a variable from its direct causes. It is directional: it is not an equation you may solve for either side.
Replace the assignment of $X$ by the constant $x$ and keep every other assignment and the background distribution.
The model produced by that replacement; $P(V \mid do(X = x))$ is its distribution.
An acyclic SCM whose background terms $U_1, \dots, U_n$ are jointly independent.

motivation: Here is a model in three lines: a fair coin $U$, then $X := U$, then $Y := 2X + U$. Fit a line to data from it and you get $Y = 3X$ exactly, with no error. A forecaster is delighted. A policy maker who reads the fitted line and decides to push $X$ from 0 to 1 expects $Y$ to rise by 3, but it rises by 2. Nothing was wrong with the data or the fit. The forecaster answered a question about *seeing* $X = 1$; the policy maker asked about *making* $X = 1$.

The extra 1 came from the background coin $U$, which raises both $X$ and $Y$. Records with $X = 1$ are records where the coin landed heads, so they carry the coin's direct contribution to $Y$ with them. Setting $X$ by hand breaks that link. A structural causal model makes the difference precise: it writes one mechanism per variable, and an intervention replaces exactly one mechanism. With that one idea, [L2-08](#lesson-l2-08)'s slogan that setting is not selecting becomes a calculation, and the rest of Level 4 (adjustment, frontdoor, counterfactuals) is built on it [@pearlcausality; @peters].

blocks.md: A structural causal model describes how each modeled variable is produced. Every variable gets its own rule, and the rule names the variable's direct causes. We write the rule with $:=$ rather than $=$ because it only runs one way: $Y := 2X + U$ says that $Y$ is computed from $X$ and $U$, not that $X$ is computed from $Y$.

blocks.title: Structural causal model
blocks.label: def-l4-01-scm
blocks.md: A structural causal model $M = \langle U, V, F, P(U)\rangle$ consists of background (exogenous) variables $U$ with a joint distribution $P(U)$; modeled (endogenous) variables $V = \{V_1, \dots, V_n\}$; and, for each $V_i$, an assignment $V_i := f_i(\mathrm{PA}_i, U_i)$ with parents $\mathrm{PA}_i \subseteq V \setminus \{V_i\}$ and $U_i \subseteq U$. The **induced graph** $G(M)$ has an arrow $V_j \to V_i$ whenever $V_j \in \mathrm{PA}_i$. The model is **recursive** if $G(M)$ has no directed cycle, and **Markovian** if it is recursive and $U_1, \dots, U_n$ are jointly independent [@pearlcausality; @peters].

blocks.title: A recursive model fixes one joint distribution
blocks.label: prop-l4-01-unique
blocks.md: In a recursive SCM, each value $u$ of the background variables determines exactly one value $v = (v_1, \dots, v_n)$ of the modeled variables. Hence $P(U)$ induces a unique joint distribution $P_M(V)$, the **observational distribution**.

An acyclic graph has a topological order: relabel so that every parent of $V_i$ has a smaller index. Fix $u$. Then $V_1$ has no modeled parents, so $v_1 = f_1(u_1)$ is determined. If $v_1, \dots, v_{i-1}$ are determined, the parents of $V_i$ are among them, so $v_i = f_i(\mathrm{pa}_i, u_i)$ is determined. By induction $v = s(u)$ for a function $s$, and $P_M(V = v) = P(U \in s^{-1}(v))$. Without acyclicity this fails: $X := Y$, $Y := 1 - X$ has no solution at all.

blocks.latex: U \sim \mathrm{Bernoulli}(1/2), \qquad X := U, \qquad Y := 2X + U
blocks.label: eq-l4-01-toy

blocks.md: Run the model [](#eq-l4-01-toy) on both values of the coin. If $U = 0$ then $X = 0$ and $Y = 0$; if $U = 1$ then $X = 1$ and $Y = 3$. Only those two rows ever occur, so $\mathbb{E}[Y \mid X = 1] - \mathbb{E}[Y \mid X = 0] = 3 - 0 = 3$. This is the observed contrast. The model $X := U$, $Y := 2X + U$ is recursive but not Markovian, because one background coin feeds both assignments.

blocks.alt: A three-node graph U, X, Y with the equations U ~ Bernoulli(1/2), X := U, Y := 2X + U. Values flow along the arrows for U = 0 and U = 1. Then the arrow from U to X is cut and X := U becomes X := x.
blocks.caption: The same three lines answer two questions. Running the machine gives the observed contrast 3; cutting the arrow into $X$ and replacing $X := U$ by $X := x$ gives $\mathbb{E}[Y \mid do(X = x)] = 2x + \tfrac{1}{2}$, a contrast of 2.
blocks.describe: The graph has a background node $U$ with arrows to $X$ and to $Y$, and an arrow from $X$ to $Y$. Under it are the assignments $U \sim \mathrm{Bernoulli}(1/2)$, $X := U$ and $Y := 2X + U$. The machine runs twice: with $U = 0$ a pulse travels along the arrows and gives $X = 0$, $Y = 0$; with $U = 1$ it gives $X = 1$, $Y = 3$. The observed contrast is written as $3 - 0 = 3$. Then a red cross cuts the arrow from $U$ to $X$, the arrow disappears, and the assignment $X := U$ turns into $X := x$. Under $do(X = 1)$ the outcome is 2 or 3 with mean 2.5; under $do(X = 0)$ it is 0 or 1 with mean 0.5. The boxed result is $\mathbb{E}[Y \mid do(X = x)] = 2x + \tfrac{1}{2}$: causal contrast 2, not the observed 3.

blocks.title: Intervention and submodel
blocks.label: def-l4-01-do
blocks.md: Let $X \subseteq V$ and let $x$ be a value of $X$. The **submodel** $M_x$ is $M$ with the assignment of every $V_i \in X$ replaced by the constant $V_i := x_i$; all other assignments and $P(U)$ stay as they were. The **interventional distribution** is $P(V \mid do(X = x)) := P_{M_x}(V)$. In the graph, $M_x$ deletes every arrow that points into $X$ and keeps all other arrows [@pearlcausality].

Apply the definition to [](#eq-l4-01-toy). In $M_x$ the assignment $X := U$ becomes $X := x$, while $Y := 2X + U$ and the coin are untouched. So $Y = 2x + U$, and linearity of expectation from [L3-07](#lesson-l3-07) gives

blocks.latex: \mathbb{E}[Y \mid do(X = x)] = \mathbb{E}[2x + U] = 2x + \tfrac{1}{2}
blocks.label: eq-l4-01-toy-do

blocks.md: The interventional means are $2.5$ and $0.5$, so the causal contrast is 2, while the observed contrast was 3. The gap of 1 is the coin's direct contribution, which rides along with $X$ in the records because $X$ copies the coin.

blocks.title: Conditioning filters; intervening rebuilds
blocks.md: $P(Y \mid X = x)$ keeps the model $M$ and looks only at the rows where $X$ happened to equal $x$. $P(Y \mid do(X = x))$ runs a different model, $M_x$, on every row. The two agree when nothing else links $X$ to $Y$; [L4-02](#lesson-l4-02) and [L4-04](#lesson-l4-04) make that condition exact.

blocks.alt: A graph with Z pointing to X and Y and X pointing to Y. Blue bars show P(Y=1 | X=x) of 0.20 and 0.70. The arrow from Z to X is cut, and orange bars show P(Y=1 | do(X=x)) of 0.35 and 0.55.
blocks.caption: Cut the arrow into $X$, replace its assignment, keep the rest. Seeing gives risks $0.20$ and $0.70$; doing gives $0.35$ and $0.55$. The interventional risk equals $0.5 \cdot 0.8 + 0.5 \cdot 0.3$, an average over $Z$ with the weights $Z$ has in the whole population.
blocks.describe: On the left is the graph $Z \to X$, $Z \to Y$, $X \to Y$, with assignments $Z := U_Z$, $X := f_X(Z, U_X)$ and $Y := f_Y(X, Z, U_Y)$. On the right, blue bars rise to the observational risks $P(Y = 1 \mid X = 0) = 0.20$ and $P(Y = 1 \mid X = 1) = 0.70$. Then the arrow from $Z$ to $X$ flashes red, is crossed out and disappears, and the assignment of $X$ changes to $X := x$. Orange bars rise to the interventional risks $P(Y = 1 \mid do(X = 0)) = 0.35$ and $P(Y = 1 \mid do(X = 1)) = 0.55$. Two lines compare the contrasts: seeing $0.70 - 0.20 = 0.50$, doing $0.55 - 0.35 = 0.20$. The last formula shows why: $P(Y = 1 \mid do(X = 1)) = \sum_z P(Y = 1 \mid X = 1, z) P(z) = 0.5 \cdot 0.8 + 0.5 \cdot 0.3 = 0.55$.

blocks.md: The binary model in the animation is the course engine's model, `qcai.science.causal`: $Z \sim \mathrm{Bernoulli}(0.5)$; $P(X = 1 \mid Z = 1) = 0.8$ and $P(X = 1 \mid Z = 0) = 0.2$; and $P(Y = 1 \mid X, Z) = 0.1 + 0.2X + cZ$ with confounding strength $c = 0.5$. Each variable has its own independent background noise, so the model is Markovian. For Markovian models the observational distribution has a famous product form.

blocks.title: Markov factorization
blocks.label: thm-l4-01-markov
blocks.md: If $M$ is Markovian, its observational distribution factorizes over the induced graph:

blocks.latex: P(v_1, \dots, v_n) = \prod_{i=1}^{n} P(v_i \mid \mathrm{pa}_i)
blocks.label: eq-l4-01-markov

blocks.md: Order the variables topologically. By the chain rule $P(v) = \prod_i P(v_i \mid v_1, \dots, v_{i-1})$. The earlier variables $V_1, \dots, V_{i-1}$ are functions of $U_1, \dots, U_{i-1}$ only (Proposition [](#prop-l4-01-unique)), and $U_i$ is independent of those. Given $V_1, \dots, V_{i-1}$, the value $V_i = f_i(\mathrm{pa}_i, U_i)$ therefore depends on the past only through $\mathrm{pa}_i$, and $P(v_i \mid v_1, \dots, v_{i-1}) = P(f_i(\mathrm{pa}_i, U_i) = v_i) = P(v_i \mid \mathrm{pa}_i)$.

blocks.title: Truncated factorization
blocks.label: thm-l4-01-truncated
blocks.md: Let $M$ be Markovian and $X \subseteq V$. For every $v$ that agrees with $x$ on $X$, $\; P(v \mid do(X = x)) = \prod_{i:\, V_i \notin X} P(v_i \mid \mathrm{pa}_i)$, and $P(v \mid do(X = x)) = 0$ for every other $v$. The factors are the observational conditionals of $M$, wherever $P(\mathrm{pa}_i) > 0$ [@pearlcausality; @peters].

The submodel $M_x$ is again Markovian: its graph is $G(M)$ minus the arrows into $X$, and its background terms are the same independent $U_i$. Apply the Markov factorization to $M_x$. A variable in $X$ is the constant $x_i$, so its factor is $1$ if $v_i = x_i$ and $0$ otherwise. A variable outside $X$ keeps its assignment $f_i$ and its noise $U_i$, so its factor is $P_{M_x}(v_i \mid \mathrm{pa}_i) = P(f_i(\mathrm{pa}_i, U_i) = v_i) = P_M(v_i \mid \mathrm{pa}_i)$. This step is **modularity**: changing one mechanism leaves the others intact.

blocks.title: Adjusting for the parents of the treatment
blocks.label: cor-l4-01-parents
blocks.md: In a Markovian model, let $Y \ne X$ be a variable that is not a parent of $X$, and suppose $P(x \mid \mathrm{pa}_X) > 0$ for every $\mathrm{pa}_X$. Then $P(y \mid do(x)) = \sum_{\mathrm{pa}_X} P(y \mid x, \mathrm{pa}_X)\, P(\mathrm{pa}_X)$.

Comparing the two factorizations, $P(v \mid do(x)) = P(v) / P(x \mid \mathrm{pa}_X)$ for every $v$ that agrees with $x$. Sum over all variables except $Y$ and $\mathrm{PA}_X$. The denominator does not depend on the summed variables, so $P(y, \mathrm{pa}_X \mid do(x)) = P(y, x, \mathrm{pa}_X) / P(x \mid \mathrm{pa}_X) = P(y \mid x, \mathrm{pa}_X) P(\mathrm{pa}_X)$. Summing over $\mathrm{pa}_X$ gives the claim.

Compare with seeing: $P(Y = 1 \mid X = 1) = \sum_z P(Y = 1 \mid X = 1, z) P(z \mid X = 1) = 0.8 \cdot 0.8 + 0.2 \cdot 0.3 = 0.70$. The only difference is the weight on $Z$: $P(z \mid X = 1)$ instead of $P(z)$. Among treated records, $Z = 1$ is over-represented (0.8 instead of 0.5), and $Z = 1$ raises the risk of $Y$ on its own. In the same way $P(Y = 1 \mid X = 0) = 0.20$ but $P(Y = 1 \mid do(X = 0)) = 0.35$.

blocks.title: The toy model is not covered, and that is instructive
blocks.md: The theorem needs independent background terms. In $X := U$, $Y := 2X + U$ the shared coin breaks this. Making the coin a modeled node $U \to X$, $U \to Y$ restores the Markov property, but the corollary still cannot be applied: $P(X = 1 \mid U = 0) = 0$, so the positivity condition fails and $P(Y \mid X = 1, U = 0)$ is undefined. The model still answers $do(X = 1)$, because it states the mechanism of $Y$. Data alone could not.

Now vary the confounding strength $c$, the amount by which $Z = 1$ raises the risk of $Y$. Bayes' rule gives $P(Z = 1 \mid X = 1) = 0.5 \cdot 0.8 / 0.5 = 0.8$ and $P(Z = 1 \mid X = 0) = 0.2$, whatever $c$ is. Therefore

while the truncated factorization gives the causal risk difference $P(Y = 1 \mid do(X = 1)) - P(Y = 1 \mid do(X = 0)) = 0.2$ for every $c$. At $c = 0.5$ the observed contrast is $0.50$, a bias of $0.30$. At $c = 0$ the two agree, because then $Z$ no longer affects $Y$ and the path through $Z$ carries nothing.

blocks.alt: A derivation that simplifies the observed contrast to 0.2 + 0.6c, then a graph where a blue point traces the rising line 0.2 + 0.6c while an orange dashed line stays at 0.2.
blocks.caption: The observed contrast $0.2 + 0.6c$ climbs with the confounding strength while the causal effect stays at $0.2$. At $c = 0.5$ the bias is $0.30$.
blocks.describe: The top of the frame derives the observed contrast. $P(Y = 1 \mid X = 1) - P(Y = 1 \mid X = 0)$ equals $0.2 + c\,[P(Z = 1 \mid X = 1) - P(Z = 1 \mid X = 0)]$; the bracket becomes $(0.8 - 0.2)$ and then the line simplifies to $0.2 + 0.6c$. Beside it, the interventional contrast is $0.2$ for every $c$. Below, axes show confounding strength $c$ from 0 to 0.6 and risk difference from 0 to 0.6. An orange dashed line sits at 0.2. A blue point starts at $(0, 0.2)$ and traces a straight rising line while a readout shows $c$ and the observed contrast. At $c = 0.5$ it stops at $0.50$, and a red segment marks the bias $0.30$ between the two lines. The point then continues to $c = 0.6$, where the observed contrast is $0.56$.

blocks.caption: Move the slider to change the confounding strength $c$. The blue bars are what you see in data; the orange bars are what an intervention would produce. The right panel tracks the two contrasts.
blocks.describe: The first panel has grouped bars for $X = 0$ and $X = 1$: blue for $P(Y = 1 \mid X = x)$ and orange for $P(Y = 1 \mid do(X = x))$. At $c = 0.5$ these are 0.20 and 0.70 (blue) and 0.35 and 0.55 (orange). The second panel plots the observed contrast $0.2 + 0.6c$ as a rising blue line and the causal effect 0.2 as a flat orange line for $c$ from 0 to 0.6, with a marker at the chosen $c$. At $c = 0$ every blue bar equals its orange partner.

blocks.caption: The same story with continuous variables. In $Z \sim N(0,1)$, $X := Z + N_X$, $Y := X + 2Z + N_Y$ the regression slope of $Y$ on $X$ is $\mathrm{Cov}(X, Y)/\mathrm{Var}(X) = (2 + 2)/2 = 2$, but setting $X$ moves the mean of $Y$ with slope 1. The purple ticks on the right are the interventional means $\mathbb{E}[Y \mid do(X = x)] = x$.

blocks.explain: Simulate the binary model twice: once as written (seeing), once with the assignment of $X$ replaced (doing). The course engine `qcai.science.causal` gives the exact values. The last lines adjust for $Z$ using only the observational sample.
blocks.source:
import numpy as np
from qcai import science

# The binary SCM  Z -> X -> Y <- Z  with the course engine's default numbers.
rng = np.random.default_rng(2024)
n = 400_000
c = 0.5                                   # confounding strength: how much Z raises the risk of Y

def run(n, do_x=None):
    z = rng.random(n) < 0.5                                   # Z := U_Z
    if do_x is None:
        x = rng.random(n) < np.where(z, 0.8, 0.2)              # X := f_X(Z, U_X)
    else:
        x = np.full(n, bool(do_x))                             # X := x   (graph surgery)
    y = rng.random(n) < 0.1 + 0.2 * x + c * z                  # Y := f_Y(X, Z, U_Y), unchanged
    return z, x, y

z, x, y = run(n)
see1, see0 = y[x].mean(), y[~x].mean()
do1 = run(n, do_x=1)[2].mean()
do0 = run(n, do_x=0)[2].mean()
exact = science.causal(0.5, 0.2, 0.8, 0.1, 0.2, c)
print(f"seeing  P(Y=1|X=1) = {see1:.3f}  (exact {exact['treated']:.2f})")
print(f"seeing  P(Y=1|X=0) = {see0:.3f}  (exact {exact['untreated']:.2f})")
print(f"doing   P(Y=1|do(X=1)) = {do1:.3f}  (exact {exact['do1']:.2f})")
print(f"doing   P(Y=1|do(X=0)) = {do0:.3f}  (exact {exact['do0']:.2f})")

# Adjustment for the parent Z uses only observational data and recovers the interventional risk.
adj1 = sum(y[x & (z == v)].mean() * (z == v).mean() for v in (0, 1))
print(f"adjusted sum_z P(Y=1|X=1,z)P(z) = {adj1:.3f}")

blocks.explain: The continuous model and the toy model. Regression recovers the observational slope 2; the interventional slope is 1. In the toy model the observed contrast is 3 and the causal contrast is 2.
blocks.source:
# Linear-Gaussian SCM:  Z ~ N(0,1),  X := Z + N_X,  Y := X + 2Z + N_Y
rng = np.random.default_rng(7)
n = 200_000
zl = rng.normal(size=n)
xl = zl + rng.normal(size=n)
yl = xl + 2 * zl + rng.normal(size=n)
slope_obs = np.cov(xl, yl)[0, 1] / np.var(xl, ddof=1)

# do(X = x) for two values of x: replace X's equation, keep Y's equation and the noise law
def mean_y_do(xv):
    zz = rng.normal(size=n)
    return np.mean(xv + 2 * zz + rng.normal(size=n))

slope_do = (mean_y_do(1.0) - mean_y_do(-1.0)) / 2
print(f"regression slope of Y on X: {slope_obs:.3f}   (population value 2)")
print(f"interventional slope d E[Y|do(x)]/dx: {slope_do:.3f}   (population value 1)")

# The toy model with a shared background input: X := U, Y := 2X + U
u = rng.random(n) < 0.5
xt, yt = u.astype(int), 2 * u + u
print("toy model, seeing:", yt[xt == 1].mean() - yt[xt == 0].mean())
print("toy model, doing: ", np.mean(2 * 1 + u) - np.mean(2 * 0 + u))

blocks.title: Three kinds of question
blocks.md: Pearl's ladder sorts questions by what they need [@pearlcausality; @bareinboim]. **Association** ($P(y \mid x)$) needs only the observational distribution. **Intervention** ($P(y \mid do(x))$) needs the mechanisms, or assumptions that let you identify them from data ([L4-04](#lesson-l4-04) to [L4-07](#lesson-l4-07)). **Counterfactuals** (what would $Y$ have been for this unit, had $X$ been different) need the full SCM including the background distribution; they are the subject of [L4-09](#lesson-l4-09).

worked_example.title: Seeing and doing in the binary model, by hand
worked_example.problem: In the engine's model ($P(Z = 1) = 0.5$; $P(X = 1 \mid Z) = 0.8$ or $0.2$; $P(Y = 1 \mid X, Z) = 0.1 + 0.2X + 0.5Z$) compute $P(Y = 1 \mid X = 1)$ and $P(Y = 1 \mid do(X = 1))$.
steps: Marginal of the treatment: $P(X = 1) = 0.5 \cdot 0.8 + 0.5 \cdot 0.2 = 0.5$.
Bayes' rule for the confounder among the treated: $P(Z = 1 \mid X = 1) = 0.5 \cdot 0.8 / 0.5 = 0.8$.
Outcome risks within strata of the treated: $P(Y = 1 \mid X = 1, Z = 1) = 0.8$ and $P(Y = 1 \mid X = 1, Z = 0) = 0.3$.
Seeing averages them with the treated weights: $0.8 \cdot 0.8 + 0.2 \cdot 0.3 = 0.64 + 0.06 = 0.70$.
Doing averages them with the population weights (Corollary [](#cor-l4-01-parents)): $0.5 \cdot 0.8 + 0.5 \cdot 0.3 = 0.55$.
worked_example.result: $P(Y = 1 \mid X = 1) = 0.70$ but $P(Y = 1 \mid do(X = 1)) = 0.55$. The difference comes entirely from the weight on $Z$.

exercises.prompt: Change the toy model to $X := U$, $Y := 3X + 2U$ with the same fair coin $U$. Find the observed contrast and the intervention contrast.
exercises.solution: Observed: $U = 1$ gives $X = 1$, $Y = 5$; $U = 0$ gives $X = 0$, $Y = 0$. The observed contrast is $5 - 0 = 5$. Under $do(X = x)$, $Y = 3x + 2U$ with $\mathbb{E}[Y \mid do(X = x)] = 3x + 1$, so the means are 4 and 1 and the causal contrast is 3.

exercises.prompt: In the binary model with $c = 0.5$, compute $P(Y = 1 \mid X = 0)$ and $P(Y = 1 \mid do(X = 0))$.

Let $Z \sim N(0,1)$, $X := aZ + N_X$, $Y := bX + gZ + N_Y$ with independent standard normal noises. Show that the regression slope of $Y$ on $X$ is $b + ag/(a^2 + 1)$ while $\frac{d}{dx}\mathbb{E}[Y \mid do(X = x)] = b$. Check $a = 1$, $b = 1$, $g = 2$.
exercises.solution: $\mathrm{Var}(X) = a^2 + 1$ and $\mathrm{Cov}(X, Z) = a$. $\mathrm{Cov}(X, Y) = b\,\mathrm{Var}(X) + g\,\mathrm{Cov}(X, Z) = b(a^2 + 1) + ag$, so the slope is $b + ag/(a^2 + 1)$. Under $do(X = x)$, $Y = bx + gZ + N_Y$ and $\mathbb{E}[Y \mid do(X = x)] = bx$, slope $b$. With $a = 1, b = 1, g = 2$: $1 + 2/2 = 2$ versus 1, as in the figure.

exercises.prompt: Use the truncated factorization to prove: in a Markovian model, if $X$ has no parents, then $P(y \mid do(x)) = P(y \mid x)$ whenever $P(x) > 0$.
exercises.solution: With $\mathrm{PA}_X = \emptyset$ the factor of $X$ is $P(x)$, so for $v$ agreeing with $x$, $P(v \mid do(x)) = P(v)/P(x)$. Summing over all variables except $Y$ (with $X$ fixed at $x$) gives $P(y \mid do(x)) = P(y, x)/P(x) = P(y \mid x)$. This is why randomizing $X$ (which makes it parentless) lets the observed contrast estimate the causal one, as in [L2-08](#lesson-l2-08).

exercises.prompt: Model A: $X := U_X$, $Y := X$. Model B: $Y := U_Y$, $X := Y$. Both $U$'s are fair coins. Show that the two models have the same observational distribution but different $P(Y = 1 \mid do(X = 1))$. What does this say about learning interventions from $P(V)$ alone?
exercises.solution: In both models $X = Y$ always and each is a fair coin, so $P(X = Y = 0) = P(X = Y = 1) = 1/2$ in both. In Model A, $do(X = 1)$ keeps $Y := X$, so $P(Y = 1 \mid do(X = 1)) = 1$. In Model B, $do(X = 1)$ replaces $X := Y$ and leaves $Y := U_Y$, so $P(Y = 1 \mid do(X = 1)) = 1/2$. The observational distribution does not determine the interventional one; extra assumptions (a graph, an experiment) are needed. [L4-07](#lesson-l4-07) develops this as identification.

check.question: What does the ideal intervention $do(X = x)$ change in a structural causal model?
options: It replaces every assignment in the model
It keeps only the records in which $X = x$
It replaces the assignment of $X$ by the constant $x$ and keeps the other assignments and $P(U)$
check.explanation: An ideal intervention is modular: exactly the mechanism of $X$ is replaced. Keeping only the records with $X = x$ is conditioning, which is a different operation.

check.question: In $U \sim \mathrm{Bernoulli}(1/2)$, $X := U$, $Y := 2X + U$, what is $\mathbb{E}[Y \mid do(X = 1)]$?
check.explanation: Under $do(X = 1)$, $Y = 2 + U$ with $\mathbb{E}[U] = 1/2$, so the mean is 2.5. The value 3 is $\mathbb{E}[Y \mid X = 1]$, which conditions on $U = 1$.

check.question: In the binary model, $P(Y = 1 \mid X = 1) = 0.70$ but $P(Y = 1 \mid do(X = 1)) = 0.55$. Why?
options: The intervention changes the mechanism of $Y$
Treated records contain more $Z = 1$ units than the population, and $Z$ raises the risk of $Y$ directly
check.explanation: Both quantities average the same stratum risks 0.8 and 0.3. Seeing uses $P(Z = 1 \mid X = 1) = 0.8$, doing uses $P(Z = 1) = 0.5$. The values are exact, so sample size plays no role, and $X$ does have an effect of 0.2.

check.question: $U$ is a fair coin coded 0 or 1, and $x$ is a fixed number. What is $\mathbb{E}[2x + U]$?
check.explanation: Expectation is linear: $\mathbb{E}[2x + U] = 2x + \mathbb{E}[U] = 2x + 1/2$. This one line is the whole interventional calculation in the toy model.

misconceptions.claim: "A structural equation is just a regression equation."
misconceptions.correction: A regression describes $\mathbb{E}[Y \mid X]$ in the observed population. A structural assignment states how $Y$ would respond if its inputs were changed. In the toy model the regression is $Y = 3X$ but the assignment is $Y := 2X + U$.

misconceptions.claim: "$P(Y \mid do(X = x))$ is $P(Y \mid X = x)$ in a cleaner dataset."
misconceptions.correction: They are different quantities defined by different models ($M_x$ versus $M$). They coincide only under conditions on the graph, for example when $X$ has no parents or when no noncausal path links $X$ and $Y$.

misconceptions.claim: "If a model predicts well, its interventional answers are right."
misconceptions.correction: Models A and B in the challenge exercise predict identically and disagree about every intervention. Predictive accuracy constrains $P(V)$, not the mechanisms.

lessons.connect: The do-operator and the truncated factorization are the foundation for the rest of Level 4. [L4-02](#lesson-l4-02) reads conditional independences off the induced graph, [L4-03](#lesson-l4-03) sorts variables into confounders, mediators and colliders, and [L4-04](#lesson-l4-04) generalizes the parent adjustment of Corollary [](#cor-l4-01-parents) to the backdoor criterion. In Level 6 the same idea, replacing one mechanism while keeping the others, reappears for quantum causal models.
lessons.caution: An ideal intervention is a modeling idealization: it changes exactly one mechanism and nothing else. A real action (a policy, a drug, a nudge) may change several mechanisms, or change the mechanism only for some units, and should then be modeled explicitly. The truncated factorization assumes a Markovian model (independent background terms, no cycles) and positivity where conditionals are used. Everything here is computed from fully specified models and simulations; deciding whether a real system is described by a given SCM is a separate, empirical question.

instructor.why: Students arrive with regression and with the slogan that correlation is not causation. The SCM turns that slogan into a definition: an intervention is a specific modification of a model, and its consequences can be computed and compared with conditioning [@pearlcausality; @peters; @hernan].
teaching_notes: Start with the three-line toy model and ask the class to predict the effect of pushing $X$ from 0 to 1 before anyone fits a line. Most will say 3.
Insist on $:=$ for assignments for the first week; ask students to rewrite $Y := 2X + U$ as an assignment for $X$ and discuss why that changes the model.

Use the interactive to show that the bias $0.6c$ vanishes exactly when $c = 0$, then ask what other change to the model would remove it (making $X$ independent of $Z$, that is, $P(X = 1 \mid Z)$ the same for both values of $Z$).
The proof of the Markov factorization is short and worth doing on the board: it explains where independent background terms are used.
instructor.assessment: The second core exercise and the worked example test the computation; the stretch exercise on the linear model tests whether students can derive omitted-variable bias from the structure; the challenge exercise tests the conceptual point that $P(V)$ does not fix interventions.
instructor.extend: Have students add a mediator $M$ between $X$ and $Y$ and verify by simulation that the truncated factorization still holds. Brady Neal's notes give a gentle parallel treatment [@bradyneal], and Peters, Janzing and Schölkopf discuss SCMs with noise terms and their identifiability [@peters].

further.note: Chapters on SCMs and the do-operator, with many small worked graphs.
The Mixtape's chapter on directed acyclic graphs gives applied examples of seeing versus doing.

lessons.title: DAGs and d-separation
lessons.objective: Use the chain, fork and collider rules to decide which conditional independences a causal graph implies, and justify the rules with the soundness theorem.
lessons.big_idea: A causal graph is a compact list of conditional independences: two sets are independent given $Z$ whenever every path between them is blocked by $Z$, and conditioning closes chains and forks but opens colliders.
outcomes: Classify each interior node of a path as a chain, fork or collider node and decide whether the path is blocked by a given set $Z$.
Decide d-separation in a graph with six or more nodes by enumerating paths and, independently, by the moralization test.
State the soundness theorem precisely (which distributions, which direction) and verify it numerically with exact partial correlations.

key_terms.meaning: Nodes joined by arrows with no directed cycle; in a causal DAG an arrow means direct cause relative to the modeled variables.
A sequence of distinct nodes in which each consecutive pair is joined by an arrow in either direction.
A node on a path where both neighboring arrows point in, as $C$ in $A \to C \leftarrow B$. Being a collider is a property of the node on that path.
A path that contains a noncollider in $Z$, or a collider that is not in $Z$ and has no descendant in $Z$.
$X \perp_d Y \mid Z$: every path between $X$ and $Y$ is blocked by $Z$.
The undirected graph obtained by joining every pair of parents of a common child and then dropping directions.

motivation: A graph with six variables can make $\binom{6}{2} \cdot 2^4 = 240$ statements of the form "these two are independent given that set". A causal model commits to some of them and not others, and data can test them. Checking 240 statements by integrating a joint distribution would be hopeless. The graph does it by reading paths.

Three tiny graphs carry all the logic. In a chain and a fork, the middle node passes dependence along until you condition on it. In a collider, the middle node stops dependence until you condition on it, and then it creates dependence that was not there. That second fact surprises almost everyone; it is behind selection bias, Berkson's paradox and many published errors. This lesson turns the three rules into one test, d-separation, proves that it never claims a false independence, and checks it numerically on a six-node graph [@pearlcausality; @spirtes; @peters].

blocks.md: In [L4-01](#lesson-l4-01) a Markovian model gave the factorization $P(v) = \prod_i P(v_i \mid \mathrm{pa}_i)$ over its graph. We now forget the equations and keep only the graph, and ask which independences every such distribution must satisfy. Some vocabulary first, for a DAG $G$: the **parents** of $V$ have arrows into $V$; its **descendants** are the nodes reachable from $V$ along directed paths, including $V$ itself in this lesson; its **ancestors** are the nodes from which $V$ is reachable, again including $V$ itself, so the ancestors of a set always contain the set.

blocks.title: Markov to a graph
blocks.label: def-l4-02-markov
blocks.md: A distribution $P$ over $V$ is **Markov to** (factorizes over) a DAG $G$ if $P(v) = \prod_{i} P(v_i \mid \mathrm{pa}_i)$ for all $v$. Every Markovian SCM produces such a distribution (Theorem [](#thm-l4-01-markov)).

blocks.caption: The running six-node graph. There are two paths between $A$ and $E$: $A \to C \leftarrow B \to E$ and $A \to C \to D \to F \leftarrow E$. Each contains a collider ($C$ on the first, $F$ on the second).

blocks.md: A **path** may follow arrows in either direction. The same node can be a collider on one path and not on another: $C$ is a collider on $A \to C \leftarrow B \to E$ but a chain node on $A \to C \to D \to F \leftarrow E$.

blocks.alt: Chain, fork and collider side by side; a token passes through the chain and fork but stops at the collider; after conditioning on the middle node the results reverse.
blocks.caption: Conditioning on the middle node closes chains and forks, and opens colliders.
blocks.describe: Three small graphs stand side by side: a chain $X \to M \to Y$, a fork $X \leftarrow M \to Y$ and a collider $X \to M \leftarrow Y$. With nothing conditioned on, an orange token travels from $X$ toward $Y$ in each graph. It passes through the chain and the fork, which are marked open, and stops at the middle of the collider, which is crossed out and marked blocked. Then the three middle nodes turn grey, meaning we condition on $M$. Now the token stops at $M$ in the chain and the fork (blocked) and passes through the collider (open). Under each graph the rule is written: $X \perp\!\!\!\perp Y \mid M$ for the chain and the fork, and for the collider $X$ and $Y$ are independent but not given $M$. The final line says: conditioning on the middle closes chains and forks, and opens colliders.

blocks.title: The three junctions
blocks.label: prop-l4-02-junctions
blocks.md: Let $P$ be Markov to a three-node graph. (a) Chain $X \to M \to Y$ and (b) fork $X \leftarrow M \to Y$: $X \perp\!\!\!\perp Y \mid M$. (c) Collider $X \to M \leftarrow Y$: $X \perp\!\!\!\perp Y$, and there are distributions Markov to the collider in which $X$ and $Y$ are dependent given $M$.

(a) $P(x, m, y) = P(x) P(m \mid x) P(y \mid m)$, so $P(y \mid x, m) = P(x, m, y)/P(x, m) = P(y \mid m)$, which does not depend on $x$. (b) $P(x, m, y) = P(m) P(x \mid m) P(y \mid m)$; divide by $P(m)$ to get $P(x, y \mid m) = P(x \mid m) P(y \mid m)$. (c) $P(x, m, y) = P(x) P(y) P(m \mid x, y)$; summing over $m$ gives $P(x, y) = P(x)P(y)$. For dependence given $M$, let $X$ and $Y$ be fair coins and $M = X \oplus Y$ (exclusive or). Given $M = 0$, $Y = X$ with certainty, so $P(Y = 1 \mid X = 1, M = 0) = 1 \ne 1/2 = P(Y = 1 \mid M = 0)$.

blocks.caption: Linear-Gaussian versions of the three junctions, 4000 samples each. Overall, $X$ and $Y$ are correlated in the chain and the fork and uncorrelated in the collider. Inside a thin slice of $M$ (purple), the correlation vanishes for the chain and the fork and appears (negative) for the collider. The population values are $1/\sqrt3 \approx 0.58$, $0.5$ and $0$ overall, and $0$, $0$ and $-0.5$ given $M$.

blocks.title: Descendants of a collider count too
blocks.md: Conditioning on a descendant of a collider also opens the collider. If $D$ is a noisy copy of $C$ in $A \to C \leftarrow B$, then learning $D$ tells you something about $C$, and that is enough to couple $A$ and $B$. This is why the definition below mentions descendants.

blocks.title: Blocked paths and d-separation
blocks.label: def-l4-02-dsep
blocks.md: Let $Z$ be a set of nodes. A path $p$ is **blocked** by $Z$ if it has an interior node $W$ such that either (i) $W$ is a noncollider on $p$ and $W \in Z$, or (ii) $W$ is a collider on $p$ and neither $W$ nor any descendant of $W$ is in $Z$. For pairwise disjoint sets $X$, $Y$ and $Z$, the sets $X$ and $Y$ are **d-separated** by $Z$, written $X \perp_d Y \mid Z$, if every path between a node of $X$ and a node of $Y$ is blocked by $Z$. Otherwise they are **d-connected** [@pearlcausality; @spirtes]. Later lessons also write $X \perp_d Y \mid Z$ as $(X \perp\!\!\!\perp Y \mid Z)_G$, with the graph as a subscript.

Apply it to the running graph with $X = \{A\}$ and $Y = \{E\}$. With $Z = \emptyset$, path 1 is blocked at the collider $C$ and path 2 at the collider $F$, so $A \perp_d E$. With $Z = \{D\}$, the collider $C$ on path 1 has the descendant $D$ in $Z$, so it no longer blocks, and $B$ is an unconditioned noncollider; path 1 is open, so $A \not\perp_d E \mid \{D\}$. With $Z = \{B, D\}$, path 1 is blocked at $B$ and path 2 at $D$, so $A \perp_d E \mid \{B, D\}$.

blocks.alt: The six-node graph with two paths between A and E walked by a token for three conditioning sets; blocking nodes are crossed out and three verdicts are written.
blocks.caption: Walk every path node by node. Adding $D$ opens a collider through its descendant; adding $B$ as well closes the path again.
blocks.describe: The six-node graph has arrows $A \to C$, $B \to C$, $C \to D$, $B \to E$, $D \to F$ and $E \to F$. The question is whether $A$ and $E$ are d-separated by a set $Z$. Two paths connect them: path 1, $A \to C \leftarrow B \to E$, and path 2, $A \to C \to D \to F \leftarrow E$. Round one, $Z$ empty: a token walks path 1 and stops at the collider $C$; it walks path 2 and stops at the collider $F$. The verdict $A \perp_d E$ is written. Round two, $Z = \{D\}$ (D turns grey): on path 1 the collider $C$ now has a conditioned descendant $D$, so the token passes $C$ and the unconditioned noncollider $B$ and reaches $E$; the path is marked open. Path 2 is blocked at $D$, a noncollider in $Z$. The verdict is $A \not\perp_d E \mid \{D\}$. Round three, $Z = \{B, D\}$: path 1 is blocked at $B$ and path 2 at $D$, so $A \perp_d E \mid \{B, D\}$. The three verdicts stay on screen in a box.

blocks.caption: Choose a conditioning set with the buttons. Grey nodes are conditioned on; open paths between $A$ and $E$ are highlighted in orange, and the title gives the verdict and the first blocking node of each path.
blocks.describe: The six-node graph is drawn with arrows. Buttons choose $Z$ from $\emptyset$, $\{C\}$, $\{D\}$, $\{F\}$, $\{B\}$, $\{B, D\}$ and $\{B, C\}$. For $\emptyset$, $\{B\}$, $\{B, D\}$ and $\{B, C\}$ no path is highlighted and the title says d-separated. For $\{C\}$ and $\{D\}$ path $A - C - B - E$ is highlighted and the title says d-connected. For $\{F\}$ both paths are highlighted, because $F$ is a collider on path 2 and a descendant of the collider $C$ on path 1.

blocks.title: Deciding $X \perp_d Y \mid Z$ without listing paths
blocks.label: alg-l4-02-moral
blocks.md:
1. Keep only the ancestors of $X \cup Y \cup Z$ (including those sets).
2. Moralize: join every pair of parents that share a child, then drop all directions.
3. Delete the nodes of $Z$ and their edges.
4. Answer **d-separated** if no node of $X$ can reach a node of $Y$ in what is left.

The number of paths can grow exponentially with the size of the graph; this test needs only graph search, so it runs in time linear in the number of edges after moralization.

blocks.title: Soundness of d-separation (global Markov property)
blocks.label: thm-l4-02-soundness
blocks.md: Let $G$ be a DAG and $X, Y, Z$ disjoint sets of its nodes. If $X \perp_d Y \mid Z$ in $G$, then $X \perp\!\!\!\perp Y \mid Z$ in **every** distribution $P$ that is Markov to $G$ [@geiger1990; @lauritzen1990; @pearlcausality; @spirtes; @peters].

blocks.title: Moralization criterion
blocks.label: lem-l4-02-moral
blocks.md: $X \perp_d Y \mid Z$ in $G$ if and only if $Z$ separates $X$ from $Y$ in the moral graph of the subgraph of $G$ induced by the ancestors of $X \cup Y \cup Z$. This equivalence, used by the algorithm above, is due to Lauritzen, Dawid, Larsen and Leimer (1990) [@lauritzen1990]; its proof is a careful but elementary argument about paths.

*Proof sketch of the theorem, assuming the lemma.* Let $\mathcal A$ be the ancestors of $X \cup Y \cup Z$.

**Step 1 (marginalize to an ancestral set).** Summing $\prod_i P(v_i \mid \mathrm{pa}_i)$ over a node with no children removes exactly its own factor, because that factor sums to 1 and no other factor mentions the node. Nodes outside $\mathcal A$ can be removed one at a time this way, childless first, so $P(v_{\mathcal A}) = \prod_{i \in \mathcal A} P(v_i \mid \mathrm{pa}_i)$.

**Step 2 (factors live on cliques of the moral graph).** Each factor depends on a node and its parents. In the moral graph these are pairwise joined, so $P(v_{\mathcal A}) = \prod_c \psi_c(v_c)$ with every $c$ a clique of the moral ancestral graph $H$.

**Step 3 (separation gives independence).** By the lemma, $Z$ separates $X$ from $Y$ in $H$. Let $R$ be the nodes that $X$ can reach in $H$ after deleting $Z$, and $W$ the remaining nodes outside $R \cup Z$, so $Y \subseteq W$. No clique meets both $R$ and $W$ (its nodes would be adjacent, and $W$ would be reachable). Grouping the factors gives $P(v_{\mathcal A}) = f(v_R, v_Z)\, g(v_W, v_Z)$, and a joint density of this form satisfies $R \perp\!\!\!\perp W \mid Z$. Since $X \subseteq R$ and $Y \subseteq W$, $X \perp\!\!\!\perp Y \mid Z$.

blocks.alt: The six-node graph is reduced step by step: F is removed, A and B are joined, arrows become lines, D is deleted, and the surviving path A - B - E is highlighted; then B is deleted too.
blocks.caption: The moralization test on the running graph. It gives the same verdicts as walking paths, and it is the bridge from the graph to the factorization in the soundness proof.
blocks.describe: The same six-node graph is used to answer whether $A$ and $E$ are d-separated by $\{D\}$, with the moralization test. Step 1 keeps only the ancestors of $A$, $E$ and $D$: node $F$ and its two incoming arrows fade away. Step 2 marries the parents of a common child: a red dashed line joins $A$ and $B$, the two parents of $C$. Step 3 drops all directions, so every arrow becomes a plain line. Step 4 deletes the conditioning set: $D$ and its line disappear. Step 5 asks whether $A$ can still reach $E$: the path $A - B - E$ lights up, so the verdict is $A \not\perp_d E \mid \{D\}$. Then $B$ is deleted as well, which leaves $A$ joined only to $C$ and $E$ isolated, so $A \perp_d E \mid \{B, D\}$. The closing line states the criterion: d-separated in $G$ if and only if separated in the moral ancestral graph.

blocks.title: Completeness and faithfulness are separate statements
blocks.md: Soundness goes one way: d-separation implies independence. The converse fails for particular distributions: a distribution can have extra independences that the graph does not imply (exercise 5 builds one by cancelling two paths). What is true is **completeness** [@geiger1990]: if $X \not\perp_d Y \mid Z$, then *some* distribution Markov to $G$ has $X$ and $Y$ dependent given $Z$; for linear-Gaussian models with coefficients drawn from a density, the cancelling choices have probability zero [@spirtes; @pearlcausality]. Assuming that the true distribution has no extra independences is the **faithfulness** assumption, which causal discovery in [L4-08](#lesson-l4-08) relies on.

blocks.explain: Implement the moralization test and compare it with networkx on all 240 statements the six-node graph can make about pairs of nodes.
blocks.source:
import itertools
import networkx as nx
import numpy as np

nodes = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]
edges = [("A", "C"), ("B", "C"), ("C", "D"), ("B", "E"), ("D", "F"), ("E", "F")]
G = nx.DiGraph(edges)

def d_separated(G, xs, ys, zs):
    # moralization criterion: ancestral subgraph -> marry parents -> drop directions -> delete zs -> reachability
    keep = set().union(*(nx.ancestors(G, v) | {v} for v in set(xs) | set(ys) | set(zs)))
    H = G.subgraph(keep)
    M = nx.Graph(H.to_undirected())
    for v in H:
        M.add_edges_from(itertools.combinations(list(H.predecessors(v)), 2))
    M.remove_nodes_from(zs)
    reach = set().union(*(nx.node_connected_component(M, x) for x in xs))
    return not (reach & set(ys))

statements = []
for x, y in itertools.combinations(nodes, 2):
    rest = [v for v in nodes if v not in (x, y)]
    for k in range(len(rest) + 1):
        for zs in itertools.combinations(rest, k):
            statements.append((x, y, set(zs)))

ours = [d_separated(G, {x}, {y}, zs) for x, y, zs in statements]
theirs = [nx.is_d_separator(G, {x}, {y}, zs) for x, y, zs in statements]
print("statements checked:", len(statements), " agree with networkx:", ours == theirs)
print("d-separations that hold:", sum(ours))
for zs in [set(), {"D"}, {"B", "D"}, {"F"}]:
    print("A, E given", sorted(zs) or "{}", "->", "d-separated" if d_separated(G, {"A"}, {"E"}, zs) else "d-connected")

blocks.explain: Soundness checked exactly. In a linear-Gaussian model, conditional independence is a zero partial correlation, and the covariance matrix follows from the coefficients. With generic coefficients the zeros appear exactly at the d-separations, and a large sample gives the same verdicts up to sampling noise.
blocks.source:
# Soundness, checked exactly: a linear-Gaussian SCM on G with generic coefficients.
# V = B V + N with independent unit-variance noise, so Cov(V) = (I - B)^-1 (I - B)^-T.
rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
idx = {v: i for i, v in enumerate(nodes)}
B = np.zeros((6, 6))
for a, b in edges:
    B[idx[b], idx[a]] = rng.uniform(0.5, 1.5) * rng.choice([-1, 1])
A_ = np.linalg.inv(np.eye(6) - B)
Sigma = A_ @ A_.T

def pcorr(S, i, j, cond):
    sub = [i, j] + list(cond)
    K = np.linalg.inv(S[np.ix_(sub, sub)])
    return -K[0, 1] / np.sqrt(K[0, 0] * K[1, 1])

rho = np.array([abs(pcorr(Sigma, idx[x], idx[y], [idx[z] for z in zs])) for x, y, zs in statements])
sep = np.array(ours)
print("largest |partial corr| among d-separated pairs:", f"{rho[sep].max():.1e}")
print("smallest |partial corr| among d-connected pairs:", f"{rho[~sep].min():.3f}")

# The same verdicts from 200 000 samples
n = 200_000
V = rng.normal(size=(n, 6)) @ A_.T
Ssamp = np.cov(V, rowvar=False)
for zs in [set(), {"D"}, {"B", "D"}]:
    r = pcorr(Ssamp, idx["A"], idx["E"], [idx[z] for z in zs])
    print("sample partial corr of A, E given", sorted(zs) or "{}", "=", round(r, 4))

worked_example.title: Conditioning on a common descendant
worked_example.problem: In the running graph, are $A$ and $E$ d-separated by $Z = \{F\}$?
steps: List the paths: $A \to C \leftarrow B \to E$ and $A \to C \to D \to F \leftarrow E$.
Path 1: the collider $C$ is not in $Z$, but its descendant $F$ is, so $C$ does not block. $B$ is a noncollider not in $Z$, so it does not block. Path 1 is open.
Path 2: $C$ and $D$ are noncolliders not in $Z$; $F$ is a collider in $Z$. Nothing blocks, so path 2 is open too.

Check with the moralization test: the ancestors of $\{A, E, F\}$ are all six nodes; marrying the parents of $C$ and of $F$ adds $A - B$ and $D - E$; deleting $F$ leaves $A - B - E$ and $A - C - D - E$, so $A$ reaches $E$.
worked_example.result: $A \not\perp_d E \mid \{F\}$, through two open paths. Conditioning on a common descendant of colliders can open several paths at once.

exercises.prompt: In the graph $A \leftarrow Z \to B$ with no other edges, are $A$ and $B$ d-separated with no conditioning? What changes when you condition on $Z$?
exercises.solution: The only path $A \leftarrow Z \to B$ has the fork node $Z$, a noncollider. With $Z$ not conditioned on, nothing blocks it, so $A$ and $B$ are d-connected. Conditioning on $Z$ blocks the only path, so $A \perp_d B \mid Z$.

exercises.prompt: In the running graph, decide whether $B \perp_d D \mid \{C\}$, and whether $B \perp_d D \mid \{C, F\}$.
exercises.solution: Paths between $B$ and $D$: $B \to C \to D$ and $B \to E \to F \leftarrow D$. Given $\{C\}$: the first is blocked at the noncollider $C$; the second at the collider $F$ (not conditioned, no descendants). So $B \perp_d D \mid \{C\}$. Given $\{C, F\}$: the first is still blocked at $C$, but $F$ is now a conditioned collider and $E$ an unconditioned noncollider, so the second path is open: $B \not\perp_d D \mid \{C, F\}$.

exercises.prompt: Prove the local Markov property from d-separation: in any DAG, a node $V$ is d-separated from each non-descendant $W$ (not a parent) by its parents $\mathrm{PA}_V$.
exercises.solution: Take a path from $V$ to $W$. If its first edge is $V \leftarrow P$, then $P$ is a parent, and on the path the edge at $P$ has its tail at $P$, so $P$ is a noncollider in $Z = \mathrm{PA}_V$: blocked. If its first edge is $V \to C$, follow the path. It cannot be directed all the way, or $W$ would be a descendant of $V$. So there is a first node where two arrowheads meet, a collider $K$, reached from $V$ by a directed path; $K$ and all its descendants are descendants of $V$. None of them is a parent of $V$, since that would create a directed cycle. So $K$ blocks the path. Every path is blocked.

exercises.prompt: Let $X$ and $Y$ be independent fair coins and $M = X \oplus Y$. Show that $X \perp\!\!\!\perp Y$, that $X$ and $Y$ are dependent given $M$, and that $X \perp\!\!\!\perp M$ even though the graph has the arrow $X \to M$. Which assumption does the last fact violate?
exercises.solution: $X$ and $Y$ are independent by construction. Given $M = 0$, $Y = X$; given $M = 1$, $Y = 1 - X$; so each determines the other given $M$. For $X$ and $M$: $P(M = 1 \mid X = x) = P(Y \ne x) = 1/2$ for both $x$, so $X \perp\!\!\!\perp M$. The graph has $X \to M$, so $X$ and $M$ are d-connected; an independence the graph does not imply violates faithfulness. Soundness is not violated: it only promises independences, never dependences.

exercises.prompt: In the linear model $M := aX + N_M$, $Y := bX + gM + N_Y$ with independent noises, find a choice of coefficients with $a, b, g$ all nonzero that makes $X \perp\!\!\!\perp Y$. Explain why this does not contradict the soundness theorem, and what it says about inferring the graph from independences.
exercises.solution: $Y = (b + ga)X + gN_M + N_Y$, so $\mathrm{Cov}(X, Y) = (b + ga)\mathrm{Var}(X)$. Choosing $b = -ga$ (for example $a = 1$, $g = 2$, $b = -2$) gives zero covariance, hence independence in the Gaussian case. Soundness only says that d-separations imply independences; here an independence holds without d-separation, which is allowed. It shows that a single distribution can hide arrows that exist, so learning a graph from independences needs faithfulness, which rules out exact cancellations like $b = -ga$.

exercises.prompt: In the running graph, how many of the 16 subsets $Z$ of $\{B, C, D, F\}$ d-separate $A$ from $E$? Characterize them.
exercises.solution: Eight. If $Z$ contains $B$, path 1 is blocked at $B$, and path 2 is blocked at $C$ or $D$ if either is in $Z$, or else at the collider $F$ if $F \notin Z$; the only failure would be $Z = \{B, F\}$, and indeed $\{B, F\}$ leaves path 2 open. So the seven sets containing $B$ other than $\{B, F\}$ work: $\{B\}$, $\{B, C\}$, $\{B, D\}$, $\{B, C, D\}$, $\{B, C, F\}$, $\{B, D, F\}$, $\{B, C, D, F\}$. If $Z$ omits $B$, path 1 is blocked only if the collider $C$ has no descendant in $Z$, that is $Z \cap \{C, D, F\} = \emptyset$, so $Z = \emptyset$, which also blocks path 2 at $F$. Total $7 + 1 = 8$, as the code confirms.

check.question: In the collider $X \to M \leftarrow Y$ with no other edges, what does conditioning on $M$ do to the path between $X$ and $Y$?
options: It has no effect because the path was already open
It opens the path, so $X$ and $Y$ can become dependent
check.explanation: A collider blocks a path unless it, or one of its descendants, is conditioned on. Conditioning on $M$ opens the path.

check.question: In the running graph, why are $A$ and $E$ d-connected given $\{D\}$?
options: $D$ is a descendant of the collider $C$, which opens $A \to C \leftarrow B \to E$
check.explanation: $D$ does block path 2, but a single open path is enough for d-connection, and path 1 opens because the collider $C$ has the conditioned descendant $D$ while $B$ is unconditioned.

check.question: What does the soundness theorem guarantee?
options: The graph can be recovered uniquely from data
If $X \perp_d Y \mid Z$, then $X \perp\!\!\!\perp Y \mid Z$ in every distribution Markov to $G$
Every d-connected pair has a nonzero causal effect
If $X$ and $Y$ are independent given $Z$ in the data, then $X \perp_d Y \mid Z$
check.explanation: Soundness runs from the graph to the distribution. The reverse direction needs faithfulness, and d-connection does not imply a causal effect (a fork creates dependence without one).

check.question: Which junction is $X \leftarrow M \to Y$?
check.explanation: Both arrows leave $M$, so $M$ is a common cause of $X$ and $Y$: a fork. Conditioning on $M$ blocks it.

misconceptions.claim: "Conditioning on more variables can only remove spurious association."
misconceptions.correction: Conditioning on a collider, or on a descendant of one, creates association. In the running graph $A \perp_d E$ holds with nothing conditioned on, and fails once $D$ is added.

misconceptions.claim: "If two variables are d-connected they must be dependent in the data."
misconceptions.correction: Soundness only guarantees independences. Exact cancellations (exercise 5) or functions like exclusive or (exercise 4) can make d-connected variables independent; ruling this out is the faithfulness assumption.

misconceptions.claim: "A collider is a type of variable."
misconceptions.correction: Being a collider is a property of a node on a particular path. $C$ is a collider on $A \to C \leftarrow B \to E$ and a chain node on $A \to C \to D \to F \leftarrow E$.

lessons.connect: d-separation is the engine of the next three lessons. [L4-03](#lesson-l4-03) uses it to sort variables into confounders, mediators and colliders; [L4-04](#lesson-l4-04) states the backdoor criterion as a d-separation in a modified graph; [L4-08](#lesson-l4-08) runs it backwards, from tested independences to graphs. In Level 6, quantum causal models keep a version of d-separation even though they give up classical hidden variables.
lessons.caution: d-separation is a statement about a stated graph. If the graph omits a common cause, a selection mechanism, or a feedback loop, the implied independences can be wrong. The theorem gives independences for every distribution that factorizes over the graph; it never guarantees dependences, and detecting an independence in finite data is a statistical test with its own error rates. The numerical checks in this lesson use exact covariances of linear-Gaussian models, where independence is the same as zero partial correlation; for other distributions zero correlation does not imply independence.

instructor.why: Students can memorize the three junctions and still fail on graphs with several paths and descendants of colliders. Walking paths node by node, then confirming with the moralization test, gives two independent procedures that must agree, and the soundness proof shows why the rules are not arbitrary [@pearlcausality; @spirtes; @peters].
teaching_notes: Start with the junction figure: ask students to predict the slice correlation for each panel before revealing it. The collider panel is the one they get wrong.
Make students write "blocked at ... because ..." for each path; most errors come from forgetting the descendant clause or treating a node as a collider on every path.
Use the interactive to collect the separating sets for $A$ and $E$ and conjecture the pattern before the last challenge exercise.
The proof sketch has three steps that can be done on the board in ten minutes; leave the lemma's path argument as reading.
instructor.assessment: The second core exercise and the worked example test path reading with colliders and descendants; the stretch proof of the local Markov property tests whether students can reason about arbitrary paths; the challenge exercise on cancellation tests the difference between soundness and faithfulness.
instructor.extend: Have students implement the reachability (Bayes-ball) version of d-separation, which follows active trails instead of moralizing, and compare it with networkx on random DAGs. Peters, Janzing and Schölkopf discuss the Markov properties and their equivalence in detail [@peters].

further.note: The chapter on graphical models gives the junctions and d-separation with many small examples.
A Python library whose independence tests and discovery algorithms build on these rules.

lessons.title: Confounders, mediators, and colliders
lessons.objective: Choose adjustment variables by their role in the causal graph relative to a treatment and an outcome, and compute what adjusting for a confounder, a mediator or a collider does to an estimate.
lessons.big_idea: The same act, adding a variable to a regression or stratifying on it, removes bias when the variable is a confounder, removes part of the effect when it is a mediator, and creates bias when it is a collider; the graph, not the data, tells you which.
outcomes: Label each variable of a causal graph as a confounder, mediator or collider relative to a stated treatment, outcome and path.
Derive the omitted-variable formula $\beta + \gamma\,\mathrm{Cov}(X, Z)/\mathrm{Var}(X)$ and use it to explain a reversed slope.
Compute the total and direct effects in a linear mediation model and show what regression on a mediator estimates.
Prove that selecting on a sum of independent variables induces a negative correlation and compute it.

key_terms.meaning: A variable on an open noncausal (backdoor) path between treatment and outcome, typically a common cause of both.
A variable on a directed path from treatment to outcome, through which part of the effect flows.
A node with two arrowheads on a path; conditioning on it, or on its descendant, opens the path.
The change in $\mathbb{E}[Y \mid do(X = x)]$ per unit change in $x$, through all directed paths.
The effect of $X$ on $Y$ with the mediator held fixed by intervention; in a linear model, the coefficient on the direct arrow.
Bias from analyzing only units that pass a selection rule which depends on the variables being studied; often a collider at the selection node.

motivation: "Control for everything you can measure" sounds like caution. It is not. Take a study of a treatment $X$ and an outcome $Y$ with three extra variables: $Z$ measured before treatment, $M$ measured between treatment and outcome, and $C$ measured afterward. In the linear model of this lesson the true total effect is 4. Regressing $Y$ on $X$ alone gives 5. Adding $Z$ gives 4, correct. Adding $Z$ and $M$ gives 1. Adding all three gives 0. Every one of these numbers is an exact population value; none is noise.

The three extra variables play three different roles. $Z$ is a confounder: adjusting for it removes bias. $M$ is a mediator: adjusting for it removes part of the very effect you want. $C$ is a collider: adjusting for it creates bias out of nothing. [L4-02](#lesson-l4-02) gave the path rules; this lesson applies them to the practical question of what to adjust for, with formulas for how much each mistake costs [@hernan; @pearlcausality].

sections.heading: Roles are relative to a question

blocks.md: Fix a treatment $X$ and an outcome $Y$. Every other variable gets a role from the paths it sits on between $X$ and $Y$. A path that starts with an arrow into $X$, as in $X \leftarrow Z \to Y$, is a **backdoor path**: it carries association but not effect. A path whose arrows all point from $X$ toward $Y$ is **causal**.

blocks.title: Confounder, mediator, collider
blocks.label: def-l4-03-roles
blocks.md: Relative to $X$, $Y$ and a path $p$ between them: a node $W$ on $p$ is a **mediator** if $p$ is a directed path $X \to \cdots \to W \to \cdots \to Y$; a **collider** if both edges of $p$ at $W$ point into $W$; and a **confounding** node if $p$ is a backdoor path and $W$ is a noncollider on it, so that conditioning on $W$ blocks $p$. A variable is called a confounder of the effect of $X$ on $Y$ when it lies, as a noncollider, on an open backdoor path [@hernan; @pearlcausality].

blocks.caption: The lesson's combined graph. Relative to the effect of $X$ on $Y$: $Z$ is a confounder (on the backdoor path $X \leftarrow Z \to Y$), $M$ is a mediator (on $X \to M \to Y$), and $C$ is a collider (on $X \to C \leftarrow Y$). The linear coefficients are $Z \to X$: 1, $X \to M$: 1.5, $M \to Y$: 2, $X \to Y$: 1, $Z \to Y$: 2, and 1 for both arrows into $C$.

blocks.title: A practical rule, made precise in L4-04
blocks.md: To estimate a total effect, adjust for variables that block every backdoor path, and never adjust for a descendant of the treatment (mediators, colliders such as $C$, and their descendants). [L4-04](#lesson-l4-04) proves that this backdoor criterion is sufficient. Being measured before treatment is not enough on its own: a pre-treatment collider exists (see the remark on M-bias below).

Let $Z$ be a fair coin, $X := 2Z + N_X$ and $Y := 3Z - 0.5X + 0.5N_Y$ with standard normal noises. The causal effect of $X$ on $Y$ is $-0.5$. But $Z$ raises both $X$ and $Y$, so in pooled data high $X$ comes with high $Y$.

blocks.title: Omitted-variable formula
blocks.label: prop-l4-03-ovb
blocks.md: Suppose $Y = \beta X + \gamma Z + N_Y$ with $\mathbb{E}[N_Y] = 0$ and $N_Y$ uncorrelated with $(X, Z)$. Then the population slope of the regression of $Y$ on $X$ alone is

blocks.latex: \beta_{\text{pooled}} = \frac{\mathrm{Cov}(X, Y)}{\mathrm{Var}(X)} = \beta + \gamma\,\frac{\mathrm{Cov}(X, Z)}{\mathrm{Var}(X)}
blocks.label: eq-l4-03-ovb

blocks.md: $\mathrm{Cov}(X, Y) = \beta\,\mathrm{Var}(X) + \gamma\,\mathrm{Cov}(X, Z) + \mathrm{Cov}(X, N_Y)$, and the last term is zero. Divide by $\mathrm{Var}(X)$. Regressing on both $X$ and $Z$ instead returns $(\beta, \gamma)$, because the normal equations are solved by the true coefficients when $N_Y$ is uncorrelated with the regressors.

Here $\mathrm{Var}(Z) = 1/4$, $\mathrm{Cov}(X, Z) = 2 \cdot 1/4 = 0.5$ and $\mathrm{Var}(X) = 4 \cdot 1/4 + 1 = 2$, so [](#eq-l4-03-ovb) gives $\beta_{\text{pooled}} = -0.5 + 3 \cdot 0.5/2 = 0.25$. The pooled slope has the wrong sign. Within each stratum of $Z$ the slope is $-0.5$, the causal effect. This is the reversal of [L2-06](#lesson-l2-06), now with a formula for its size.

blocks.alt: A scatter plot whose pooled regression line rises with slope 0.25; when points are colored by Z, each group shows a falling line with slope -0.5.
blocks.caption: Pooled, the slope is $0.25$; within each stratum of the confounder, it is $-0.5$. The omitted-variable formula accounts for the whole gap.
blocks.describe: A scatter plot shows 160 sampled points from the model $Z \in \{0, 1\}$ with probability one half each, $X := 2Z + N_X$, $Y := 3Z - 0.5X + 0.5N_Y$; a small graph beside it has arrows $Z \to X$ (coefficient 2), $Z \to Y$ (coefficient 3) and $X \to Y$ (coefficient $-0.5$). First all points are grey and the population regression line of $Y$ on $X$ is drawn: pooled slope $0.25$, rising. Then the points are colored by $Z$: blue for $Z = 0$ (lower left) and orange for $Z = 1$ (upper right). Inside each color a line with slope $-0.5$ is drawn, falling, and the pooled line fades. A derivation on the right explains the gap: $\beta_{\text{pooled}} = \beta + \gamma\,\mathrm{Cov}(X, Z)/\mathrm{Var}(X)$, which becomes $-0.5 + 3 \cdot 0.5/2$ and then $0.25$. The last line says that adjusting for $Z$ recovers $-0.5$.

sections.heading: Mediators: adjusting removes part of the effect

blocks.md: Now let $M := 1.5X + N_M$ and $Y := X + 2M + N_Y$, with $X$, $N_M$, $N_Y$ independent. Substituting the first assignment into the second gives $Y = X + 2(1.5X + N_M) + N_Y = 4X + 2N_M + N_Y$, so $\mathbb{E}[Y \mid do(X = x)] = 4x$: the **total effect** is 4, of which 1 travels along $X \to Y$ and $1.5 \times 2 = 3$ along $X \to M \to Y$.

blocks.title: What regression on a mediator estimates
blocks.label: prop-l4-03-mediator
blocks.md: In the linear model $M := bX + N_M$, $Y := dX + eM + N_Y$ with $X$, $N_M$, $N_Y$ independent, the total effect of $X$ on $Y$ is $d + be$, and the population regression of $Y$ on $(X, M)$ has coefficient $d$ on $X$: the controlled direct effect, not the total effect.

Substitution gives $Y = (d + be)X + eN_M + N_Y$, and under $do(X = x)$ the same substitution holds with $X = x$, so $\mathbb{E}[Y \mid do(x)] = (d + be)x$. For the regression, $Y = dX + eM + N_Y$ with $N_Y$ independent of $(X, M)$ (because $M$ is a function of $X$ and $N_M$), so $\mathbb{E}[Y \mid X, M] = dX + eM$ and the coefficients are $(d, e)$.

blocks.alt: A graph X to M to Y with a direct arrow X to Y; a stacked bar of height 4 split into direct 1 and indirect 3; adjusting for M drains the indirect part.
blocks.caption: The total effect $4X + 2N_M + N_Y$ splits into a direct part 1 and an indirect part 3. Holding $M$ fixed in the regression leaves only the direct part.
blocks.describe: A graph has $X \to M$ with coefficient 1.5, $M \to Y$ with coefficient 2, and $X \to Y$ with coefficient 1. The assignments $M := 1.5X + N_M$ and $Y := X + 2M + N_Y$ are written, and substitution turns $Y = X + 2(1.5X + N_M) + N_Y$ into $Y = 4X + 2N_M + N_Y$: the total effect of $X$ on $Y$ is 4. A stacked bar shows this 4 as a purple direct part of height 1 and an orange indirect part of height $1.5 \times 2 = 3$, labeled regress $Y$ on $X$. Then $M$ turns grey (adjusted for), the arrows through $M$ fade, and the orange part drains away, leaving the purple bar of height 1, labeled regress $Y$ on $X$ and $M$. The formula $\mathbb{E}[Y \mid X, M] = 1 \cdot X + 2M$ appears with the notes: coefficient of $X$ is 1, the direct effect; valid only if nothing else links $M$ and $Y$.

blocks.title: The direct effect needs its own assumptions
blocks.md: The proof used that nothing else links $M$ and $Y$. If an unmeasured $U$ affects both ($M \leftarrow U \to Y$), then $M$ is a collider on $X \to M \leftarrow U \to Y$, and conditioning on $M$ opens that path: the coefficient on $X$ is then biased even for the direct effect (the last challenge exercise computes how much). Mediation analysis is a subject of its own [@hernan; @pearlcausality].

Let $A$ and $B$ be independent fair coins, and keep a record only when $C = \max(A, B) = 1$. The kept pairs are $01$, $10$ and $11$, equally likely. Then $P(A = 1 \mid C = 1) = 2/3$ for each coin, but $P(A = 1, B = 1 \mid C = 1) = 1/3 \ne (2/3)^2 = 4/9$. Within the kept records the coins are dependent: learning that one is 0 forces the other to be 1. This is **Berkson's paradox**; the selection node $C$ is a collider on $A \to C \leftarrow B$.

blocks.title: Selection on a sum
blocks.label: prop-l4-03-sum
blocks.md: Let $A, B$ be independent $N(0, 1)$ and keep only units with $S = A + B > t$. Then, among kept units, $\operatorname{corr}(A, B) = \frac{v - 2}{v + 2}$ where $v = \mathrm{Var}(S \mid S > t)$. Since $v < 2$, the correlation is negative for every $t$; at $t = 0$ it equals $-1/(\pi - 1) \approx -0.467$.

Let $D = A - B$. The pair $(S, D)$ is jointly normal with $\mathrm{Cov}(S, D) = \mathrm{Var}(A) - \mathrm{Var}(B) = 0$, so $S$ and $D$ are independent, each $N(0, 2)$. Selection depends only on $S$, so after selection $D$ is still $N(0, 2)$ and independent of $S$. Write $A = (S + D)/2$ and $B = (S - D)/2$. Then $\mathrm{Cov}(A, B \mid S > t) = (v - 2)/4$ and $\mathrm{Var}(A \mid S > t) = \mathrm{Var}(B \mid S > t) = (v + 2)/4$, which gives the ratio. Truncating a normal distribution strictly reduces its variance, so $v < 2$. At $t = 0$, $S \mid S > 0$ is half-normal with $v = 2(1 - 2/\pi)$, and $(v - 2)/(v + 2) = (-4/\pi)/(4 - 4/\pi) = -1/(\pi - 1)$.

blocks.alt: Independent points A, B; a line A + B = t sweeps across and points below it turn grey; a live graph shows the correlation among kept points falling below zero.
blocks.caption: Keep only $A + B > t$. The stricter the selection, the more negative the correlation among the kept units, although $A$ and $B$ are independent in the population.
blocks.describe: A scatter of 300 points $(A, B)$ drawn independently from standard normals, all red at first. A line $A + B = t$ sweeps from the lower left to the upper right as $t$ goes from $-3.5$ to $1.5$; points below the line turn grey (not kept) and points above stay red (kept). On the right, a graph of the population correlation $\operatorname{corr}(A, B \mid A + B > t)$ against $t$ is traced live, starting near 0 and falling steadily, with a readout of $t$ and the correlation (about $-0.30$ at $t = -1$ and $-0.62$ at $t = 1$). The threshold then returns to $t = 0$, where the value $-1/(\pi - 1) \approx -0.467$ is marked and boxed. The formula $\operatorname{corr} = \frac{v - 2}{v + 2}$ with $v = \mathrm{Var}(A + B \mid A + B > t)$ is shown at the bottom.

blocks.caption: Left: 3000 independent pairs, with the kept ones ($A + B > 0$) in red; the sample correlation among kept pairs is close to the population value $-1/(\pi - 1)$. Right: the population correlation among kept pairs as a function of the threshold $t$, from Proposition [](#prop-l4-03-sum).

blocks.title: M-bias: a collider measured before treatment
blocks.md: In $X \leftarrow U_1 \to W \leftarrow U_2 \to Y$ with $U_1, U_2$ unmeasured, the pre-treatment variable $W$ is a collider. The backdoor path is blocked as long as $W$ is left alone; adjusting for $W$ opens it. If $W$ also affects $X$ or $Y$ directly, it can be both a collider and a confounder on different paths, and no adjustment by observed variables may suffice. Roles belong to paths, not to variables [@hernan; @pearlcausality].

blocks.caption: Choose an adjustment set for the combined model with the buttons (none, $\{Z\}$, $\{Z, M\}$, $\{Z, C\}$, $\{Z, M, C\}$); the bars for $\{M\}$ and $\{C\}$ are shown for comparison. Each bar shows the exact population coefficient of $X$ when $Y$ is regressed on $X$ and the chosen variables; the dashed lines mark the total effect 4 and the direct effect 1.
blocks.describe: The first panel shows the combined graph with the adjusted variables in grey. Five buttons choose the adjustment set: none, $\{Z\}$, $\{Z, M\}$, $\{Z, C\}$ and $\{Z, M, C\}$. The second panel shows one labeled bar for each of seven adjustment sets, with the chosen one highlighted. The exact coefficients are: none 5, $\{Z\}$ 4, $\{Z, M\}$ 1, $\{Z, C\}$ $-0.17$, $\{M\}$ 2, $\{C\}$ $-0.25$, and $\{Z, M, C\}$ 0. Only $\{Z\}$ hits the total effect, and only $\{Z, M\}$ hits the direct effect.

blocks.explain: Simulate the combined model and run the seven regressions. With 200 000 samples the coefficients match the exact values in the interactive to about two decimals.
blocks.source:
import itertools
import numpy as np

# Combined linear SCM: Z confounder, M mediator, C collider (independent standard normal noises)
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
n = 200_000
Z = rng.normal(size=n)
X = Z + rng.normal(size=n)
M = 1.5 * X + rng.normal(size=n)
Y = X + 2 * M + 2 * Z + rng.normal(size=n)
C = X + Y + rng.normal(size=n)
data = {"Z": Z, "M": M, "C": C}

def coef_of_x(adjust):
    cols = [np.ones(n), X] + [data[v] for v in adjust]
    beta, *_ = np.linalg.lstsq(np.column_stack(cols), Y, rcond=None)
    return beta[1]

print("true total effect 4, direct effect 1")
for k in range(4):
    for adj in itertools.combinations(["Z", "M", "C"], k):
        name = ", ".join(adj) or "nothing"
        print(f"adjust for {name:8s}  coefficient of X = {coef_of_x(adj):6.3f}")

blocks.explain: The two collider examples: exact fractions for the coins, and a Monte Carlo check of Proposition [](#prop-l4-03-sum) at $t = 0$.
blocks.source:
from fractions import Fraction
import math

# Berkson with coins: A, B fair and independent, keep a record when C = max(A, B) = 1
kept = [(a, b) for a in (0, 1) for b in (0, 1) if max(a, b) == 1]
pA = Fraction(sum(a for a, b in kept), len(kept))
pAB = Fraction(sum(a * b for a, b in kept), len(kept))
print("P(A=1 | C=1) =", pA, "  P(A=1, B=1 | C=1) =", pAB, "  product of marginals =", pA * pA)

# Selection on a sum: A, B ~ N(0,1) independent, keep A + B > 0
A_, B_ = rng.normal(size=(2, 400_000))
keep = A_ + B_ > 0
print("sample corr among kept:", round(np.corrcoef(A_[keep], B_[keep])[0, 1], 4))
v = 2 * (1 - 2 / math.pi)                       # Var(A + B | A + B > 0): half-normal with variance 2
print("formula (v - 2)/(v + 2) =", round((v - 2) / (v + 2), 4), "  -1/(pi - 1) =", round(-1 / (math.pi - 1), 4))

worked_example.title: Reading roles and predicting estimates in the combined model
worked_example.problem: In the combined graph ($Z \to X$, $Z \to Y$, $X \to M \to Y$, $X \to Y$, $X \to C \leftarrow Y$) with the stated coefficients, which adjustment set estimates the total effect of $X$ on $Y$, and what does regressing on $X$ alone give?
steps: List the paths from $X$ to $Y$: causal $X \to Y$ and $X \to M \to Y$; backdoor $X \leftarrow Z \to Y$; and $X \to C \leftarrow Y$, which is blocked at the collider $C$ unless $C$ is conditioned on.

The total effect is the sum over causal paths: $1 + 1.5 \cdot 2 = 4$. To estimate it, block the backdoor path with $Z$, leave $M$ (a mediator) and $C$ (a collider and descendant of $X$) alone: adjustment set $\{Z\}$.

Regressing on $X$ alone leaves the backdoor open. With $Y = 4X + 2Z + (\text{noise uncorrelated with } X)$ after substituting $M$, formula [](#eq-l4-03-ovb) gives $4 + 2\,\mathrm{Cov}(X, Z)/\mathrm{Var}(X) = 4 + 2 \cdot 1/2 = 5$.
Adding $M$ to $\{Z\}$ blocks the indirect path and leaves the direct coefficient 1 (Proposition [](#prop-l4-03-mediator)); adding $C$ opens $X \to C \leftarrow Y$ and drives the estimate below zero.
worked_example.result: $\{Z\}$ gives the total effect 4; no adjustment gives 5; $\{Z, M\}$ gives the direct effect 1; sets containing $C$ give values unrelated to either effect.

exercises.prompt: With independent fair coins $A$, $B$ and the inclusion rule $C = \max(A, B) = 1$, calculate $P(B = 1 \mid A = 0, C = 1)$ and $P(B = 1 \mid A = 1, C = 1)$.
exercises.solution: If $A = 0$ and the record is kept, $B$ must be 1, so the first probability is 1. If $A = 1$, the record is kept whatever $B$ is, and both values stay equally likely, so the second probability is $1/2$. Since these differ, $A$ and $B$ are dependent given $C = 1$.

exercises.prompt: In the combined graph, give the role of $Z$, $M$ and $C$ relative to the effect of $X$ on $Y$, and say which of them should be adjusted for to estimate the total effect.
exercises.solution: $Z$ is a confounder (noncollider on the backdoor path $X \leftarrow Z \to Y$); $M$ is a mediator (on the causal path $X \to M \to Y$); $C$ is a collider on $X \to C \leftarrow Y$ and a descendant of $X$. Adjust for $Z$ only.

exercises.prompt: In the mediation model take $b = 0.5$, $e = -2$, $d = 1$. Compute the total effect and the coefficient of $X$ when $Y$ is regressed on $X$ and $M$. What would an analyst conclude from each number?
exercises.solution: Total effect $d + be = 1 + 0.5 \cdot (-2) = 0$. The regression on $(X, M)$ gives $d = 1$. An analyst who adjusts for $M$ would report a positive effect of $X$, while setting $X$ actually leaves the mean of $Y$ unchanged: the direct and indirect paths cancel. Both numbers are correct answers to different questions.

exercises.prompt: Let $Z \sim N(0, 1)$, $X := Z + N_X$, $Y := \beta X + 2Z + N_Y$ with independent standard normal noises. Find the slope of the regression of $Y$ on $X$ alone.
exercises.solution: $\mathrm{Cov}(X, Z) = 1$ and $\mathrm{Var}(X) = 2$, so formula [](#eq-l4-03-ovb) gives $\beta + 2 \cdot 1/2 = \beta + 1$. The bias is $+1$ whatever $\beta$ is.

exercises.prompt: Use Proposition [](#prop-l4-03-sum) and the half-normal variance to show that $\operatorname{corr}(A, B \mid A + B > 0) = -1/(\pi - 1)$, and explain why the correlation tends to 0 as $t \to -\infty$.
exercises.solution: For $S \sim N(0, \sigma^2)$, $\mathbb{E}[S \mid S > 0] = \sigma\sqrt{2/\pi}$ and $\mathbb{E}[S^2 \mid S > 0] = \sigma^2$, so $\mathrm{Var}(S \mid S > 0) = \sigma^2(1 - 2/\pi)$. With $\sigma^2 = 2$, $v = 2 - 4/\pi$, and $(v - 2)/(v + 2) = (-4/\pi)/(4 - 4/\pi) = -1/(\pi - 1) \approx -0.467$. As $t \to -\infty$ almost every unit is kept, so $v \to 2$ and the correlation $(v - 2)/(v + 2) \to 0$: no selection, no induced correlation.

exercises.prompt: Mediator-outcome confounding. Let $X, U, N_M, N_Y$ be independent standard normals, $M := X + U + N_M$ and $Y := X + M + U + N_Y$. The direct effect of $X$ is 1. Find the population coefficient of $X$ when $Y$ is regressed on $X$ and $M$, and explain the bias with a path.
exercises.solution: Given $X$ and $M$, the only unknown in $Y$ is $U + N_Y$. Since $M - X = U + N_M$ with $\mathrm{Var}(U) = \mathrm{Var}(N_M) = 1$, the best linear predictor is $\mathbb{E}[U \mid X, M] = (M - X)/2$, and $N_Y$ predicts to 0. So $\mathbb{E}[Y \mid X, M] = X + M + (M - X)/2 = 0.5X + 1.5M$, and the coefficient on $X$ is $0.5$, not 1. Conditioning on $M$ opens $X \to M \leftarrow U \to Y$, where $M$ is a collider.

check.question: Which adjustment can create a new noncausal association between treatment and outcome?
options: Conditioning on a collider such as $C$ in $X \to C \leftarrow Y$
Conditioning on a common cause of $X$ and $Y$
check.explanation: A collider blocks its path until it, or a descendant, is conditioned on. Conditioning opens the path and creates association even when its causes were independent.

check.question: In $M := 1.5X + N_M$, $Y := X + 2M + N_Y$, what is the coefficient of $X$ when $Y$ is regressed on both $X$ and $M$?
check.explanation: Holding $M$ fixed removes the indirect path, leaving the direct coefficient 1. The total effect is 4, and 3 is the indirect part.

check.question: Pooled data show slope $0.25$; within each level of the only confounder $Z$ the slope is $-0.5$. Which number estimates the causal effect of $X$ on $Y$?
check.explanation: Stratifying on the confounder blocks the backdoor path $X \leftarrow Z \to Y$. The pooled slope adds the bias $\gamma\,\mathrm{Cov}(X, Z)/\mathrm{Var}(X) = 0.75$.

check.question: In the graph $A \to C \to D$ with $B \to C$, are $A$ and $B$ d-separated given $\{D\}$?
options: Yes, because $D$ is not on the path
No, because $D$ is a descendant of the collider $C$
check.explanation: The only path is $A \to C \leftarrow B$ with collider $C$. Conditioning on its descendant $D$ opens it, so $A$ and $B$ are d-connected given $\{D\}$.

misconceptions.claim: "Adjusting for more variables is always safer."
misconceptions.correction: In the combined model, adding $M$ to the correct set $\{Z\}$ moves the estimate from 4 to 1, and adding $C$ moves it to 0. Each added variable must earn its place by its role in the graph.

misconceptions.claim: "Any variable measured before treatment is safe to adjust for."
misconceptions.correction: Timing rules out mediators and descendants of treatment, but not colliders: in the M-bias graph a pre-treatment variable is a collider and adjusting for it creates bias.

misconceptions.claim: "A correlation found among selected cases must reflect a real link."
misconceptions.correction: Selecting on a common effect induces correlation between independent causes: $-1/(\pi - 1) \approx -0.467$ for selection on $A + B > 0$, with no link between $A$ and $B$ at all.

lessons.connect: The roles defined here become a criterion in [L4-04](#lesson-l4-04): a set satisfies the backdoor criterion if it blocks every backdoor path and contains no descendant of the treatment. [L4-05](#lesson-l4-05) shows that a mediator can rescue identification when the confounder is unmeasured, and [L4-10](#lesson-l4-10) returns to selection when data are transported between populations. Collider bias reappears in Level 6, where post-selection in quantum experiments raises the same question of what conditioning creates.
lessons.caution: All numbers here come from fully specified linear-Gaussian or binary models, so regression coefficients equal the causal quantities exactly when the assumptions hold. With nonlinear models, effect heterogeneity or measurement error, adjusting for the right set still removes confounding but the regression coefficient may no longer equal the average effect; [L4-04](#lesson-l4-04) uses standardization instead. Roles are assigned relative to an assumed graph; if the graph omits an unmeasured common cause, a variable can be a confounder and a collider at once, and no adjustment set from the observed variables may exist.

instructor.why: Students and many practitioners adjust for every available covariate. Showing four exact numbers (5, 4, 1, 0) from one model, each produced by a defensible-looking regression, makes the case that the graph must come before the regression [@hernan; @pearlcausality; @seeing].
teaching_notes: Open with the four regression results of the combined model and ask the class to rank them before revealing which equals the total effect.
