Link the confounder animation to the reversal lesson [L2-06](#lesson-l2-06): the omitted-variable formula is the quantitative version of that story.
Run the Berkson coin example physically: students flip two coins, discard the trials with two tails, and tabulate the rest. The dependence is visible after about 40 trials.
Stress that the mediator result answers a different question (direct effect) and needs an extra assumption (no mediator-outcome confounding).
instructor.assessment: The core exercises test role labeling and Berkson's rule; the stretch exercise on cancelling paths tests the difference between total and direct effects; the last challenge exercise tests whether students can see a collider hidden inside a mediation analysis.
instructor.extend: Have students write a function that, given a DAG, a treatment and an outcome, lists every adjustment set of observed variables that blocks all backdoor paths without descendants of the treatment, and test it on the M-bias and butterfly graphs. Hernán and Robins discuss selection bias as collider stratification in detail [@hernan], and DoWhy implements this kind of check [@dowhy].

further.note: The chapters on confounding and on selection bias treat both in the language of graphs.
A library that identifies valid adjustment sets from a stated graph before estimating.

lessons.title: Backdoor adjustment
lessons.objective: Decide whether a set of measured variables satisfies the backdoor criterion and use it to compute an intervention effect by standardization or by inverse probability weighting.
lessons.big_idea: If a measured set blocks every noncausal path into the treatment without touching its descendants, then reweighting stratum risks to one common covariate mix turns an observed contrast into a causal effect.
outcomes: Check the backdoor criterion for a candidate set by listing every backdoor path, applying the d-separation blocking rule to each, and excluding descendants of the treatment.
Derive the adjustment formula $P(y \mid do(x)) = \sum_z P(y \mid x, z)P(z)$ from the truncated factorization and compute standardized risks and their difference.
Compute an inverse probability weighted estimate, prove that it equals standardization in the population, and state the positivity condition both need.
Simulate a confounded model and compare the naive, standardized, and weighted estimates with the true effect.

key_terms.meaning: Setting $X$ to $x$ by an outside action, which replaces the mechanism that normally produces $X$ and leaves every other mechanism unchanged.
A path between treatment $X$ and outcome $Y$ whose first edge points into $X$, such as $X \leftarrow Z \rightarrow Y$.
A set $Z$ satisfies it when no member of $Z$ is a descendant of $X$ and $Z$ blocks every backdoor path from $X$ to $Y$.
Averaging stratum risks $P(y \mid x, z)$ over one common distribution $P(z)$ for every treatment value.
The treatment probability $e(z) = P(X = 1 \mid Z = z)$ in the stratum $Z = z$.
Weighting each unit by $1/P(X = x \mid Z = z)$ for the treatment it received, which builds a pseudo-population where $X$ is independent of $Z$.
Every stratum that occurs in the target population has a nonzero probability of each treatment value being compared.

motivation: Here is a puzzle. In a model population, a treatment raises the risk of an outcome by $0.1$ among people with $Z = 0$ and by $0.2$ among people with $Z = 1$. Yet the treated group's risk is $0.68$ and the untreated group's risk is $0.20$, a difference of $0.48$. How can the overall difference be more than twice as large as the effect in either group? The answer is that $Z$ does two jobs at once: it makes treatment more likely and it raises the risk. Comparing treated and untreated people mixes the effect of $X$ with the effect of being the kind of person who gets $X$.

This lesson answers two questions that every observational study faces. When can the effect of an intervention, $P(y \mid do(x))$, be computed from data where nobody was assigned anything? And how? The backdoor criterion gives a purely graphical test for the first question [@pearl]. Standardization and inverse probability weighting give two computations of the same answer [@hernan]. Both are only as good as the causal graph, which is why the test comes before the arithmetic.

blocks.md: Take the smallest confounded model. A binary covariate $Z$ has $P(Z = 1) = 0.5$. It raises the chance of treatment, $P(X = 1 \mid Z = 0) = 0.2$ and $P(X = 1 \mid Z = 1) = 0.8$, and it raises the risk of the outcome. The stratum risks $P(Y = 1 \mid X = x, Z = z)$ are $0.2$ and $0.8$ for treated people with $Z = 0$ and $Z = 1$, and $0.1$ and $0.6$ for untreated people. This is not the course engine's additive model of [L4-01](#lesson-l4-01): here the treatment adds $0.1$ to the risk when $Z = 0$ and $0.2$ when $Z = 1$. The graph is below; $X$, $Y$ and $Z$ are all measured.

blocks.mermaid:
graph LR
  Z[Z covariate] --> X[X treatment]
  Z --> Y[Y outcome]
  X --> Y
blocks.caption: The running example. $Z$ opens the backdoor path $X \leftarrow Z \rightarrow Y$, so the observed association between $X$ and $Y$ mixes the causal arrow with the common cause.

blocks.title: Intervention and the truncated factorization
blocks.label: def-l4-04-truncated
blocks.md: Let a causal DAG on variables $V_1, \dots, V_k$ have the Markov factorization $P(v) = \prod_i P(v_i \mid pa_i)$, where $pa_i$ are the values of the parents of $V_i$ (see [L4-01](#lesson-l4-01) and [L4-02](#lesson-l4-02)). The intervention $do(X = x)$ removes the mechanism of $X$ and holds $X$ at $x$; every other mechanism is unchanged. The interventional distribution is the product of the remaining factors, [](#eq-l4-04-truncated), for every $v$ that agrees with $X = x$, and $0$ otherwise. [L4-07](#lesson-l4-07) studies this rule and its limits in detail.

blocks.latex: P(v \mid do(X = x)) = \prod_{i:\, V_i \neq X} P(v_i \mid pa_i)\,\Big|_{X = x}
blocks.label: eq-l4-04-truncated

blocks.title: Adjustment for the parents of the treatment
blocks.label: thm-l4-04-parents
blocks.md: In a causal DAG whose variables are all measured, let $T$ be the set of parents of $X$. For every $t$ with $P(t) > 0$ assume $P(x \mid t) > 0$. Then $P(y \mid do(x)) = \sum_t P(y \mid x, t)\, P(t)$. This restates Corollary [](#cor-l4-01-parents) of [L4-01](#lesson-l4-01); the proof below reaches it by a slightly different route.

Write $W$ for all variables other than $X$, $T$ and $Y$. Compare the observational factorization with [](#eq-l4-04-truncated): the only difference is the missing factor $P(x \mid t)$, so for every $(t, y, w)$, $P(t, y, w \mid do(x)) = P(x, t, y, w)/P(x \mid t)$. By the chain rule, $P(x, t, y, w) = P(t)\,P(x \mid t)\,P(y, w \mid x, t)$. Dividing, $P(t, y, w \mid do(x)) = P(t)\,P(y, w \mid x, t)$. Summing over $w$ and $t$ gives $P(y \mid do(x)) = \sum_t P(t)\, P(y \mid x, t)$. Positivity makes every conditional probability in the formula well defined.

In the running example $Z$ is the only parent of $X$, so $P(Y = 1 \mid do(X = 1)) = 0.5(0.2) + 0.5(0.8) = 0.50$ and $P(Y = 1 \mid do(X = 0)) = 0.5(0.1) + 0.5(0.6) = 0.35$. The causal risk difference is $0.50 - 0.35 = 0.15$, the average of the two stratum effects $0.1$ and $0.2$. The naive contrast of $0.48$ overstates it more than threefold.

The parents of $X$ are often unmeasured, or there are better sets to use. We need a test that says which sets of measured variables do the same job. The idea: the association between $X$ and $Y$ travels along every path between them. Directed paths out of $X$ carry the effect we want. Paths that enter $X$ through an incoming arrow, the **backdoor paths**, carry spurious association. A good adjustment set closes all backdoor paths and leaves the directed paths alone.

blocks.title: Backdoor criterion
blocks.label: def-l4-04-backdoor
blocks.md: A set $Z$ of variables satisfies the **backdoor criterion** relative to an ordered pair $(X, Y)$ in a DAG if (i) no node in $Z$ is a descendant of $X$, and (ii) $Z$ blocks every path between $X$ and $Y$ that contains an arrow into $X$. A path is **blocked** by $Z$ when it contains a noncollider that is in $Z$, or a collider such that neither it nor any of its descendants is in $Z$ (the d-separation rule of [L4-02](#lesson-l4-02)) [@pearlcausality].

blocks.alt: A six-node causal graph. The directed path from X through W to Y is highlighted in blue, the four backdoor paths are highlighted one at a time and listed, then three candidate sets are tested and each path is marked open or blocked.
blocks.caption: The backdoor criterion is checked path by path. Conditioning on $Z_3$ alone closes three paths but opens the fourth through the collider $Z_3$; the set $\{Z_1, Z_3\}$ closes all four.
blocks.describe: The graph has arrows $Z_1 \to X$, $Z_1 \to Z_3$, $Z_2 \to Z_3$, $Z_2 \to Y$, $Z_3 \to X$, $Z_3 \to Y$, $X \to W$ and $W \to Y$. The directed path $X \to W \to Y$ is highlighted in blue as the path to keep open. The four backdoor paths are highlighted and listed: $X \leftarrow Z_3 \rightarrow Y$, $X \leftarrow Z_1 \rightarrow Z_3 \rightarrow Y$, $X \leftarrow Z_3 \leftarrow Z_2 \rightarrow Y$ and $X \leftarrow Z_1 \rightarrow Z_3 \leftarrow Z_2 \rightarrow Y$. With the empty set the first three are open and the fourth is blocked by the collider $Z_3$. With $\{Z_3\}$ the first three become blocked, but the fourth is opened because its collider is now conditioned on. With $\{Z_1, Z_3\}$ all four are blocked, so the set is valid. Finally $W$ is flagged: it is a descendant of $X$ and must never be in an adjustment set for the total effect.

graph TD
  Z1 --> X
  Z1 --> Z3
  Z2 --> Z3
  Z2 --> Y
  Z3 --> X
  Z3 --> Y
  X --> W
  W --> Y
blocks.caption: The same six-node graph as a static reference. $Z_3$ is a confounder on some paths and a collider on the path through $Z_1$ and $Z_2$.

blocks.md: Work through the graph by hand. There are exactly four backdoor paths: $X \leftarrow Z_3 \rightarrow Y$, $X \leftarrow Z_1 \rightarrow Z_3 \rightarrow Y$, $X \leftarrow Z_3 \leftarrow Z_2 \rightarrow Y$, and $X \leftarrow Z_1 \rightarrow Z_3 \leftarrow Z_2 \rightarrow Y$. On the last one $Z_3$ is a collider. The empty set leaves three paths open. The set $\{Z_3\}$ blocks the first three, because $Z_3$ is a noncollider on each, but it opens the fourth. Adding either $Z_1$ or $Z_2$ closes that path again, so $\{Z_1, Z_3\}$, $\{Z_2, Z_3\}$ and $\{Z_1, Z_2, Z_3\}$ are valid. Any set that contains $W$ fails condition (i).

blocks.title: Backdoor adjustment
blocks.label: thm-l4-04-backdoor
blocks.md: If $Z$ satisfies the backdoor criterion relative to $(X, Y)$, and $P(x, z) > 0$ for every $z$ with $P(z) > 0$, then the causal effect of $X$ on $Y$ is identified and [](#eq-l4-04-adjust) holds [@pearlcausality; @pearl].

blocks.latex: P(y \mid do(x)) = \sum_z P(y \mid x, z)\, P(z)
blocks.label: eq-l4-04-adjust

blocks.md:
*Proof sketch.* Condition on $Z$ inside the interventional distribution: $P(y \mid do(x)) = \sum_z P(y \mid do(x), z)\, P(z \mid do(x))$. Two facts finish the argument.

(a) $P(z \mid do(x)) = P(z)$. The non-descendants of $X$ form a set that contains the parents of each of its members (a parent of a non-descendant cannot be $X$ or a descendant of $X$). In [](#eq-l4-04-truncated), sum out the descendants of $X$ from the last one in a topological order back to the first: each factor sums to 1, leaving the product of the factors of the non-descendants. Summing $X$ and its descendants out of the observational factorization leaves the same product. So the joint distribution of the non-descendants, and of $Z$ by condition (i), is the same with and without the intervention.

(b) $P(y \mid do(x), z) = P(y \mid x, z)$. Delete the arrows out of $X$. By condition (ii), $Z$ d-separates $X$ from $Y$ in that graph, so given $Z$ the only association left between $X$ and $Y$ in the original graph flows along directed paths out of $X$, which the intervention leaves intact. Turning this sentence into a formal proof is exactly rule 2 of the do-calculus, which [L4-07](#lesson-l4-07) introduces; see [@pearlcausality], Section 3.3.

Substituting (a) and (b) gives [](#eq-l4-04-adjust). When $Z$ is the parent set of $X$, [](#thm-l4-04-parents) proves the same result without the do-calculus.

blocks.explain: Enumerate the backdoor paths of the six-node graph, test every candidate set with the blocking rule, and cross-check against `networkx`: the criterion is equivalent to 'no descendants of $X$, and $Z$ d-separates $X$ and $Y$ once the arrows out of $X$ are deleted'.

blocks.title: More adjustment is not always better
blocks.md: $\{Z_3\}$ is a natural guess, since $Z_3$ is a common cause of $X$ and $Y$, and it is wrong: it opens the collider path. Adjusting for the mediator $W$ is also wrong: it blocks the effect we are trying to measure. Adjustment sets are chosen from the graph, never by including every measured variable.

sections.heading: Standardization: one covariate mix for both arms

blocks.md: Why does the naive contrast fail, and what exactly does adjustment change? By the law of total probability ([L3-07](#lesson-l3-07)), the observed risk in arm $x$ is a weighted average of stratum risks with the arm's own covariate mix $P(z \mid x)$. The adjusted risk uses the same stratum risks with the population mix $P(z)$. Equation [](#eq-l4-04-two-averages) shows the two side by side: the only change is the weights.

blocks.latex: P(Y = 1 \mid X = x) = \sum_z P(Y = 1 \mid x, z)\, P(z \mid x) \qquad\text{versus}\qquad P(Y = 1 \mid do(X = x)) = \sum_z P(Y = 1 \mid x, z)\, P(z)
blocks.label: eq-l4-04-two-averages

blocks.alt: Two panels of rectangles, one for the treated and one for the untreated arm. Each rectangle's width is a stratum weight and its height a stratum risk; the widths slide to equal halves and the total areas change from 0.68 and 0.20 to 0.50 and 0.35.
blocks.caption: Width is the stratum weight, height the stratum risk, area the average risk. Moving both arms to the population mix $P(Z) = (0.5, 0.5)$ turns the observed contrast $0.48$ into the causal $0.15$.
blocks.describe: Each arm is drawn as two adjacent rectangles, one per stratum of $Z$. The heights are the stratum risks: $0.2$ and $0.8$ for the treated arm, $0.1$ and $0.6$ for the untreated arm. At first the widths are the arms' own covariate mixes: the treated arm is $0.20$ of $Z = 0$ and $0.80$ of $Z = 1$, the untreated arm $0.80$ and $0.20$. The total areas, shown live, are the observed risks $0.68$ and $0.20$, a contrast of $0.48$. The widths then slide to the population mix $0.50$ and $0.50$ for both arms. The heights never change. The areas become $0.50$ and $0.35$, and the contrast becomes $0.50 - 0.35 = 0.15$.

blocks.md: Bayes' rule gives the arm mixes: $P(Z = 1 \mid X = 1) = 0.8 \cdot 0.5/0.5 = 0.8$ and $P(Z = 1 \mid X = 0) = 0.2$. So the observed risks are $0.2(0.2) + 0.8(0.8) = 0.68$ and $0.8(0.1) + 0.2(0.6) = 0.20$, while the standardized risks are $0.50$ and $0.35$. The treated arm is crowded into the high-risk stratum, and the naive comparison credits the treatment with that crowding. Treatment-specific weights would keep the crowding; one common weight removes it.

blocks.caption: Change the confounding strength $c$, where $P(X = 1 \mid Z = 0) = 0.5 - c$ and $P(X = 1 \mid Z = 1) = 0.5 + c$. (This $c$ moves the treatment probabilities; it is a different parameter from the $c$ of [L4-01](#lesson-l4-01), which moved the outcome risk.) Observed risks move; standardized risks do not.
blocks.describe: The first panel shows the observed and standardized risks of $Y = 1$ for each arm. The second panel plots the naive contrast against $c$, a straight line from $0.15$ at $c = 0$ to about $0.64$ at $c = 0.45$, and the adjusted contrast, a flat line at the true $0.15$. At $c = 0$ treatment does not depend on $Z$ and the two agree. At $c = 0.3$, the lesson's value, the observed risks are $0.68$ and $0.20$ and the standardized ones $0.50$ and $0.35$.

blocks.md: Standardization fixes the weights of the strata. Inverse probability weighting fixes the people instead: it up-weights units whose treatment was unusual for their stratum, so that every stratum ends up with the same treatment mix.

blocks.title: IPW equals standardization
blocks.label: prop-l4-04-ipw
blocks.md: Assume positivity, $0 < P(X = x \mid Z = z)$ whenever $P(z) > 0$. Then $\mathbb{E}\left[\dfrac{\mathbf{1}\{X = x\}\, Y}{P(X = x \mid Z)}\right] = \sum_z \mathbb{E}[Y \mid X = x, Z = z]\, P(z)$. If $Z$ satisfies the backdoor criterion, the left side is therefore $\mathbb{E}[Y \mid do(X = x)]$.

Condition on $Z$ and then on $X$: $\mathbb{E}\big[\mathbf{1}\{X = x\} Y / P(X = x \mid Z)\big] = \sum_z P(z) \cdot \dfrac{P(X = x \mid z)\, \mathbb{E}[Y \mid x, z]}{P(X = x \mid z)} = \sum_z P(z)\, \mathbb{E}[Y \mid x, z]$. The indicator keeps only units with $X = x$, which occur with probability $P(X = x \mid z)$ in stratum $z$; the weight cancels that probability. The last statement is [](#thm-l4-04-backdoor).

blocks.alt: A two by two grid of squares, rows X equal 1 and 0, columns Z equal 0 and 1, with counts 100, 400, 400, 100. Weights 5, 1.25, 1.25, 5 grow every square to 500.
blocks.caption: In a population of 1000, weighting by $1/P(X = x \mid Z = z)$ grows every cell to 500. In the pseudo-population treatment no longer depends on $Z$, and the plain contrast is $0.15$.
blocks.describe: A grid shows the 1000 people of the running example by treatment and covariate: 100 treated and 400 untreated with $Z = 0$, 400 treated and 100 untreated with $Z = 1$. Each square is shaded red in proportion to its risk of $Y = 1$. The weights are $1/P(X = x \mid Z = z)$: $100 \times 5 = 500$, $400 \times 1.25 = 500$, $400 \times 1.25 = 500$ and $100 \times 5 = 500$. The squares grow until every cell holds 500, so $X$ is independent of $Z$ in the pseudo-population. The treated risk is $(500 \cdot 0.2 + 500 \cdot 0.8)/1000 = 0.50$, the untreated risk is $(500 \cdot 0.1 + 500 \cdot 0.6)/1000 = 0.35$, and the difference is $0.15$.

blocks.caption: A continuous confounder $Z \sim N(0, 1)$ with propensity $P(X = 1 \mid Z) = 1/(1 + e^{-1.5 Z})$, 40,000 simulated units. Left: the treated arm sits to the right of the untreated arm. Right: after weighting by $1/P(X = x \mid Z)$, both arms have the population distribution of $Z$, and their means are both close to 0.

blocks.title: Positivity
blocks.md: If some stratum has $P(X = 1 \mid Z = z) = 0$, nobody there is treated, the stratum risk $P(y \mid X = 1, z)$ is undefined, and the IPW weight $1/0$ does not exist. No amount of data repairs this; only extra modeling assumptions that extrapolate from other strata can fill the gap. Propensities close to 0 or 1 cause the finite-sample version of the same problem: a few units get huge weights and the estimate becomes very noisy.

blocks.explain: Simulate 200,000 units from the running model, compute the naive contrast, standardization and IPW from the observed data, and compare them with the effect of a simulated intervention. The last lines check the course engine `qcai.science.causal`, whose additive model has true effect 0.2.
blocks.source:
import numpy as np
from qcai import science

rng = np.random.default_rng(2024)
n = 200_000
RISK = {(1, 0): 0.2, (1, 1): 0.8, (0, 0): 0.1, (0, 1): 0.6}     # P(Y=1 | X=x, Z=z)

def draw_y(x, z):
    p = np.select([(x == 1) & (z == 0), (x == 1) & (z == 1), (x == 0) & (z == 0)], [0.2, 0.8, 0.1], 0.6)
    return (rng.random(len(x)) < p).astype(int)

z = (rng.random(n) < 0.5).astype(int)                     # P(Z=1) = 0.5
x = (rng.random(n) < np.where(z == 1, 0.8, 0.2)).astype(int)   # P(X=1|Z) = 0.2, 0.8
y = draw_y(x, z)

naive = y[x == 1].mean() - y[x == 0].mean()
pz = np.array([np.mean(z == 0), np.mean(z == 1)])
def standardized(xv):
    return sum(y[(x == xv) & (z == k)].mean() * pz[k] for k in (0, 1))
std = standardized(1) - standardized(0)
e = np.array([x[z == 0].mean(), x[z == 1].mean()])[z]       # estimated propensity P(X=1 | Z)
ipw = np.mean(x * y / e) - np.mean((1 - x) * y / (1 - e))

# ground truth by simulated intervention: keep everyone's Z, set X for everyone
truth_sim = draw_y(np.ones(n, int), z).mean() - draw_y(np.zeros(n, int), z).mean()
print(f"naive contrast        {naive:.3f}   (exact 0.48)")
print(f"standardization       {std:.3f}")
print(f"IPW                   {ipw:.3f}   (differs from standardization by {abs(ipw - std):.1e})")
print(f"simulated do(X)       {truth_sim:.3f}   (exact 0.50 - 0.35 = 0.15)")

# the course engine's additive version: P(Y=1|X,Z) = 0.1 + 0.2 X + 0.5 Z
r = science.causal(prevalence=0.5, low=0.2, high=0.8, base=0.1, effect=0.2, confound=0.5)
risk_add = {(xv, zv): 0.1 + 0.2 * xv + 0.5 * zv for xv in (0, 1) for zv in (0, 1)}
do = {xv: sum(risk_add[(xv, zv)] * 0.5 for zv in (0, 1)) for xv in (0, 1)}
print("engine: observed", round(r["observed"], 3), " do(1) - do(0) =", round(r["do1"] - r["do0"], 3),
      " adjustment formula:", round(do[1] - do[0], 3))

blocks.title: Why IPW and standardization agree to every digit here
blocks.md: With a discrete $Z$ and propensities estimated by the stratum frequencies, the IPW sum for arm 1 is $\sum_z (n_z/n)\cdot \overline{Y}_{x=1,z}$, which is exactly the standardization with the empirical $P(z)$. With continuous covariates the propensity must be modeled, for example by logistic regression, and the two estimators differ: each relies on a different model being right [@hernan].

blocks.title: The same numbers in a library
blocks.label: ex-l4-04-dowhy
blocks.md: Causal inference libraries automate exactly these steps: declare the graph, ask the library to find a backdoor set, then choose an estimator such as standardization or weighting [@dowhy]. The graph is still the user's assumption; the software only applies the criterion.

worked_example.title: Three strata, a naive contrast, and the adjusted effect
worked_example.problem: A covariate $Z$ with three levels satisfies the backdoor criterion. $P(Z) = (0.5, 0.3, 0.2)$ and $P(X = 1) = 0.5$. The treated arm's mix is $P(Z \mid X = 1) = (0.4, 0.3, 0.3)$. Stratum risks are $0.30, 0.50, 0.70$ under $X = 1$ and $0.20, 0.35, 0.60$ under $X = 0$. Find the naive contrast, the standardized risks and the causal risk difference, and check positivity.
steps: Untreated mix: $P(z) = 0.5\,P(z \mid X = 1) + 0.5\,P(z \mid X = 0)$, so $P(Z \mid X = 0) = 2P(Z) - P(Z \mid X = 1) = (0.6, 0.3, 0.1)$.
Positivity: $P(X = 1 \mid z) = P(z \mid X = 1)P(X = 1)/P(z) = 0.4, 0.5, 0.75$, all strictly between 0 and 1, so every stratum risk is defined.
worked_example.result: The causal risk difference is $0.44 - 0.325 = 0.115$, smaller than the naive $0.195$ because the treated arm holds more of the high-risk third stratum.

exercises.prompt: Keep equal population weights $P(Z = 0) = P(Z = 1) = 0.5$ and assume $Z$ satisfies the backdoor criterion. Risks under $X = 1$ are $0.25$ and $0.65$; under $X = 0$ they are $0.15$ and $0.35$. Find both adjusted risks and their difference.
In the six-node graph of this lesson, decide whether each set satisfies the backdoor criterion: (a) $\{Z_2, Z_3\}$, (b) $\{Z_1, Z_2\}$, (c) $\{Z_1, Z_3, W\}$.
exercises.solution: (a) Valid. $Z_3$ blocks $X \leftarrow Z_3 \rightarrow Y$, $X \leftarrow Z_1 \rightarrow Z_3 \rightarrow Y$ and $X \leftarrow Z_3 \leftarrow Z_2 \rightarrow Y$ as a noncollider; on $X \leftarrow Z_1 \rightarrow Z_3 \leftarrow Z_2 \rightarrow Y$ the collider $Z_3$ is opened, but $Z_2$ is a conditioned noncollider, so the path is blocked. No member is a descendant of $X$. (b) Not valid: $X \leftarrow Z_3 \rightarrow Y$ contains no member of the set and no collider, so it stays open. (c) Not valid: $W$ is a descendant of $X$, which violates condition (i), even though the backdoor paths are all blocked.

exercises.prompt: Show that if $X$ is independent of $Z$ (for example because $X$ was assigned by a coin), the adjustment formula [](#eq-l4-04-adjust) gives the same answer as the naive conditional probability $P(y \mid x)$.
exercises.solution: Independence gives $P(z \mid x) = P(z)$. By the law of total probability $P(y \mid x) = \sum_z P(y \mid x, z) P(z \mid x) = \sum_z P(y \mid x, z) P(z)$, which is the right side of [](#eq-l4-04-adjust). Graphically, independence of $X$ and $Z$ means no arrow from $Z$ into $X$ is needed, so the empty set already blocks every backdoor path through $Z$.

exercises.prompt: A population of 1000 has $P(Z = 1) = 0.4$, $P(X = 1 \mid Z = 1) = 0.75$ and $P(X = 1 \mid Z = 0) = 0.25$. Give the four cell counts, the IPW weights, and the weighted counts. Show that in the pseudo-population $X$ is independent of $Z$.
exercises.solution: Counts: $Z = 1$ has 400 people, 300 treated and 100 untreated; $Z = 0$ has 600, 150 treated and 450 untreated. Weights $1/P(X = x \mid Z = z)$: $1/0.75$ for treated with $Z = 1$ and untreated with $Z = 0$, $1/0.25 = 4$ for the other two cells. Weighted counts: $300/0.75 = 400$, $100 \times 4 = 400$, $150 \times 4 = 600$, $450/0.75 = 600$. Each arm now has 1000 units with 40% at $Z = 1$ and 60% at $Z = 0$, so $P(Z = 1 \mid X = x) = 0.4$ for both $x$: $X$ and $Z$ are independent, and each arm is a copy of the population.

exercises.prompt: Take the graph $X \to W \to Y$ with $P(W = 1 \mid X) = 0.2 + 0.6X$ and $P(Y = 1 \mid W) = 0.1 + 0.5W$, and no other variables. Compute the true risk difference $P(Y = 1 \mid do(X = 1)) - P(Y = 1 \mid do(X = 0))$, then compute $\sum_w P(Y = 1 \mid x, w) P(w)$ for $x = 1, 0$. Which condition of the backdoor criterion does $\{W\}$ violate, and what does the violation do?
exercises.solution: No backdoor paths exist, so $P(Y = 1 \mid do(x)) = P(Y = 1 \mid x) = 0.1 + 0.5(0.2 + 0.6x)$: $0.50$ for $x = 1$ and $0.20$ for $x = 0$, a true difference of $0.30$. Since $Y$ depends on $X$ only through $W$, $P(Y = 1 \mid x, w) = 0.1 + 0.5w$ does not depend on $x$, so the 'adjusted' risks are equal for both $x$ and their difference is $0$. $W$ is a descendant of $X$, violating condition (i); adjusting for it blocks the very path that carries the effect.

exercises.prompt: The M-graph has arrows $A \to X$, $A \to M$, $B \to M$, $B \to Y$, $X \to Y$, with $A$ and $B$ unmeasured. Show that the empty set satisfies the backdoor criterion, that $\{M\}$ does not, and say which additional measured variable would make a set containing $M$ valid.
exercises.solution: The only backdoor path is $X \leftarrow A \rightarrow M \leftarrow B \rightarrow Y$, and $M$ is a collider on it. With the empty set the collider blocks the path, and no descendant of $X$ is involved, so the empty set is valid: $P(y \mid do(x)) = P(y \mid x)$. Conditioning on $M$ opens the collider, so $\{M\}$ fails condition (ii). Adding either $A$ or $B$ (if it were measured) blocks the path again as a conditioned noncollider, so $\{M, A\}$ or $\{M, B\}$ would be valid. Adjusting for a pre-treatment variable is therefore not automatically safe.

check.question: Which weights appear in the ordinary backdoor adjustment formula?
options: The treated group's distribution $P(z \mid X = 1)$ for both arms
The population distribution $P(z)$, the same for every treatment value
check.explanation: Both intervention risks are averaged over the same target distribution $P(z)$. Each arm's own mix $P(z \mid x)$ gives back the observed risks, which keep the confounding.

check.question: In the six-node graph, why does the set $\{Z_3\}$ fail the backdoor criterion?
options: It blocks the directed path $X \to W \to Y$
A valid set must contain every parent of $Y$
It opens the collider path $X \leftarrow Z_1 \rightarrow Z_3 \leftarrow Z_2 \rightarrow Y$
check.explanation: $Z_3$ is a noncollider on three backdoor paths, so conditioning on it blocks them, but it is a collider on the fourth, so conditioning on it opens that path. Adding $Z_1$ or $Z_2$ closes it again.

check.question: A treated unit lives in a stratum where $P(X = 1 \mid Z = z) = 0.2$. What is its inverse probability weight?
check.explanation: The weight is $1/P(X = x \mid Z = z)$ for the treatment actually received: $1/0.2 = 5$. Treated units are rare in that stratum, so each stands in for five.

check.question: Let $A$ and $B$ be independent fair bits and $C = \max(A, B)$. What is $P(A = 1 \mid C = 1)$?
check.explanation: Given $C = 1$ the equally likely pairs are 01, 10 and 11, and $A = 1$ in two of them. Conditioning on the collider $C$ makes $A$ and $B$ dependent, which is why a collider on a backdoor path must not be conditioned on alone.

misconceptions.claim: "Adjust for every measured pre-treatment variable; extra adjustment can only help."
misconceptions.correction: Conditioning on a collider such as $Z_3$ on the path $X \leftarrow Z_1 \rightarrow Z_3 \leftarrow Z_2 \rightarrow Y$, or $M$ in the M-graph, opens a backdoor path and creates bias. Adjustment sets come from the graph.

misconceptions.claim: "Standardization and inverse probability weighting estimate different things."
misconceptions.correction: In the population they are equal ([](#prop-l4-04-ipw)); both compute $\sum_z P(y \mid x, z)P(z)$. In finite samples with modeled covariates they rely on different models (an outcome model versus a treatment model), so their estimates differ.

misconceptions.claim: "A valid adjustment set must contain all parents of the treatment."
misconceptions.correction: The parent set is one valid choice, but not the only one. In the six-node graph the parents of $X$ are $Z_1$ and $Z_3$, yet $\{Z_2, Z_3\}$ is also valid.

misconceptions.claim: "If the arithmetic is exact, the answer is causal."
misconceptions.correction: The formula is causal only if the graph is right, the set satisfies the criterion, and positivity holds. An omitted common cause leaves an open backdoor path that no reweighting of the measured variables can close.

lessons.connect: When every backdoor path runs through an unmeasured variable, adjustment fails, but a mediator can sometimes rescue identification: that is the frontdoor criterion of [L4-05](#lesson-l4-05). Randomization in [L4-06](#lesson-l4-06) removes every arrow into $X$, so the empty set satisfies the criterion. The do-calculus of [L4-07](#lesson-l4-07) contains the backdoor theorem as a special case.
lessons.caution: The backdoor theorem identifies an effect only if the causal graph is correct; it cannot detect an omitted common cause, and the data alone cannot tell you which graph is right. The examples use binary variables and the risk difference; the same formula holds for other outcomes and effect measures, but finite-sample estimation with many or continuous covariates needs models (for the outcome, the propensity, or both), and their misspecification adds bias. Positivity and a well-defined intervention (consistency, see [L4-06](#lesson-l4-06)) are assumed throughout. Simulations here confirm the algebra; they are not evidence about any real treatment.

instructor.why: Students arrive with the regression habit of controlling for everything available. The backdoor criterion replaces that habit with a check that can be carried out by hand, and standardization shows that adjustment is only a change of weights [@pearl; @hernan].
teaching_notes: Before any formula, show the puzzle: stratum effects 0.1 and 0.2, overall difference 0.48. Ask students to explain it in words before revealing the reweighting animation.
Have students list the four backdoor paths of the six-node graph on paper before the animation. Most will miss the collider path through $Z_1$ and $Z_2$; that is the point.
Use the interactive at $c = 0$ to show that randomization makes the naive and adjusted contrasts coincide, which previews [L4-06](#lesson-l4-06).
Mark which steps of the proof of [](#thm-l4-04-backdoor) are fully proved here (the invariance of the non-descendants, and the parent-set case) and which one uses the do-calculus [@pearlcausality].
instructor.assessment: The second core exercise and the second check question test the path-by-path criterion; the worked example and the first core exercise test the computation; the challenge exercises test whether students can explain why a set fails, not only that it fails [@bradyneal].
instructor.extend: Introduce augmented IPW (doubly robust estimation), which combines an outcome model with a propensity model and stays consistent if either model is right [@robins1994; @hernan]. Students can then run the same analysis in a library [@dowhy] and compare with their own code. The Mixtape works through matching and weighting on real data sets [@seeing].

further.note: Chapters 2, 7 and 12 treat standardization, confounding and inverse probability weighting with worked data.
Chapter 4 derives the backdoor adjustment with clear figures of blocked and open paths.
Chapter 6 states adjustment criteria in the language of structural causal models.

lessons.title: Frontdoor identification
lessons.objective: State the three frontdoor conditions, derive the frontdoor formula, and compute an intervention effect when treatment and outcome share an unmeasured cause.
lessons.big_idea: When every backdoor path runs through a hidden cause, a measured mediator that carries all of the effect and is shielded from that cause lets us identify the effect in two backdoor steps: treatment to mediator, then mediator to outcome.
outcomes: State the three frontdoor conditions and check each one on a graph, including graphs with a direct arrow or a hidden cause of the mediator, where they fail.
Derive the frontdoor formula for the canonical graph from the truncated factorization with the hidden variable, naming the conditional independence used at each step.
Compute $P(y \mid do(x))$ from the two identified pieces, $P(m \mid x)$ and the standardized mediator response, and compare it with the naive contrast.
Verify the formula by simulation and measure how far it moves from the truth when a frontdoor condition is violated.

key_terms.meaning: A common cause of treatment and outcome that is not recorded, drawn as a dashed node $U$; it opens a backdoor path that no measured set can block.
A variable $M$ on a directed path $X \to M \to Y$, through which part or all of the effect of $X$ on $Y$ passes.
Three graphical conditions on a set $M$: it intercepts every directed path from $X$ to $Y$, there is no open backdoor path from $X$ to $M$, and $X$ blocks every backdoor path from $M$ to $Y$.
$r(m) = \sum_{x'} P(y \mid m, x')P(x')$, the outcome risk at mediator value $m$ averaged over the population distribution of the treatment; it equals $P(y \mid do(m))$ under the frontdoor conditions.
A dummy treatment value summed over in $r(m)$, distinct from the intervention value $x$.

motivation: Backdoor adjustment ([L4-04](#lesson-l4-04)) needs a measured set that blocks every backdoor path. Often there is none. Suppose a hidden factor $U$ raises both the chance of exposure $X$ and the risk of the outcome $Y$. Every backdoor path runs through $U$, and $U$ is not in the data. It seems that the effect of $X$ on $Y$ cannot be computed from observational data at all.

Pearl showed that it sometimes can [@frontdoor]. His illustration was hypothetical: if smoking affected cancer only through tar deposits in the lungs, and a hidden genotype affected smoking and cancer but not tar, then the effect of smoking would be identified from data on smoking, tar and cancer, even with the genotype unmeasured. The trick is to identify two smaller effects, each by a backdoor argument, and chain them. This lesson proves the formula, computes it, and shows how quickly it breaks when its conditions fail. The smoking story is used only as an illustration of the graph, not as a claim about real biology.

blocks.md: Here is the running model. All variables are binary. The hidden $U$ is fair, $P(U = 1) = 0.5$. Treatment depends on $U$: $P(X = 1 \mid U) = 0.25 + 0.5U$. The mediator depends only on treatment: $P(M = 1 \mid X) = 0.2 + 0.6X$. The outcome depends on the mediator and on $U$: $P(Y = 1 \mid M, U) = 0.6M + 0.4U$. We observe only $X$, $M$ and $Y$.

blocks.mermaid:
graph LR
  U((U hidden)) -.-> X
  U -.-> Y
  X --> M
  M --> Y
blocks.caption: The canonical frontdoor graph. The dashed arrows come from the unmeasured $U$. The only directed path from $X$ to $Y$ passes through the measured mediator $M$.

blocks.title: Frontdoor criterion
blocks.label: def-l4-05-frontdoor

blocks.alt: A graph with X, M, Y in a row and a dashed unmeasured U above with arrows to X and Y. The backdoor path is highlighted, then the three frontdoor conditions are checked one at a time, then a direct X to Y arrow and a U to M arrow are added to show failures.
blocks.caption: The backdoor path $X \leftarrow U \rightarrow Y$ cannot be blocked, but the three frontdoor conditions hold. A direct arrow $X \to Y$ breaks condition 1; an arrow $U \to M$ breaks conditions 2 and 3.
blocks.describe: The graph shows $X \to M \to Y$ and a dashed node $U$, labeled unmeasured, with dashed arrows to $X$ and $Y$. The backdoor path $X \leftarrow U \rightarrow Y$ is highlighted in red: it cannot be blocked because $U$ is not observed, so backdoor adjustment is unavailable. Three condition cards then appear. Condition 1: the directed path $X \to M \to Y$ is the only directed path from $X$ to $Y$, and it passes through $M$. Condition 2: the only backdoor path from $X$ to $M$, $X \leftarrow U \rightarrow Y \leftarrow M$, is blocked by the collider $Y$. Condition 3: the backdoor path from $M$ to $Y$, $M \leftarrow X \leftarrow U \rightarrow Y$, is blocked by conditioning on $X$. Then a curved red arrow from $X$ to $Y$ is added, and condition 1 fails. It is removed, and a red arrow from $U$ to $M$ is added, and conditions 2 and 3 fail. The final line says that a measured mediator alone is not enough.

blocks.md: Check the conditions by hand on the canonical graph. The only directed path from $X$ to $Y$ is $X \to M \to Y$, so condition 1 holds. The only path from $X$ to $M$ that starts with an arrow into $X$ is $X \leftarrow U \rightarrow Y \leftarrow M$, and $Y$ is a collider on it, so with nothing conditioned it is blocked: condition 2 holds. The only backdoor path from $M$ to $Y$ is $M \leftarrow X \leftarrow U \rightarrow Y$; $X$ is a noncollider on it, so conditioning on $X$ blocks it: condition 3 holds.

blocks.title: Two independences in the canonical graph
blocks.label: lem-l4-05-indep
blocks.md: In the graph $U \to X \to M \to Y \leftarrow U$, the d-separation rule gives $Y \perp\!\!\!\perp X \mid M, U$ and $U \perp\!\!\!\perp M \mid X$.

The paths between $Y$ and $X$ are $Y \leftarrow M \leftarrow X$, blocked by the conditioned noncollider $M$, and $Y \leftarrow U \rightarrow X$, blocked by the conditioned noncollider $U$. The paths between $U$ and $M$ are $U \rightarrow X \rightarrow M$, blocked by the conditioned noncollider $X$, and $U \rightarrow Y \leftarrow M$, blocked because the collider $Y$ is not conditioned on and has no descendants. By the Markov property of the DAG ([L4-02](#lesson-l4-02)), d-separation implies conditional independence.

blocks.title: Frontdoor formula for the canonical graph
blocks.label: thm-l4-05-canonical
blocks.md: In the canonical graph, with $U$ unmeasured, suppose $P(x, m) > 0$ for every pair $(x, m)$. Then [](#eq-l4-05-frontdoor) holds, where $x'$ is a summation index that runs over the values of $X$.

blocks.latex: P(y \mid do(x)) = \sum_m P(m \mid x) \sum_{x'} P(y \mid m, x')\, P(x')
blocks.label: eq-l4-05-frontdoor

blocks.md:
*Proof for the canonical graph.* Apply the truncated factorization ([L4-04](#lesson-l4-04), equation [](#eq-l4-04-truncated)) to the full graph, $U$ included, and remove the factor of $X$:

$P(u, m, y \mid do(x)) = P(u)\, P(m \mid x)\, P(y \mid m, u)$.

Sum over $u$ and $m$ and collect the terms that depend on $u$:

$P(y \mid do(x)) = \sum_m P(m \mid x) \sum_u P(y \mid m, u)\, P(u)$.

The inner sum involves the hidden $U$. Rewrite it with observed quantities. For each $x'$, condition on $U$:

$P(y \mid m, x') = \sum_u P(y \mid m, u, x')\, P(u \mid m, x') = \sum_u P(y \mid m, u)\, P(u \mid x')$,

using $Y \perp\!\!\!\perp X \mid M, U$ for the first factor and $U \perp\!\!\!\perp M \mid X$ for the second ([](#lem-l4-05-indep)). Multiply by $P(x')$ and sum over $x'$; since $\sum_{x'} P(u \mid x')P(x') = P(u)$,

$\sum_{x'} P(x')\, P(y \mid m, x') = \sum_u P(y \mid m, u)\, P(u)$.

Substituting this into the inner sum gives [](#eq-l4-05-frontdoor). Positivity makes every conditional probability on the right defined.

blocks.alt: The frontdoor derivation written as a chain of equations whose terms slide into new positions, with the hidden-variable average boxed and then replaced by an average over treatment values.
blocks.caption: The derivation term by term: truncated factorization with $U$, collect the $u$ terms, replace the hidden average by an observed one using two independences, then plug in the numbers.
blocks.describe: The first line is $P(y \mid do(x)) = \sum_u \sum_m P(u) P(m \mid x) P(y \mid m, u)$, labeled as the truncated factorization on the full graph. Its terms slide into $\sum_m P(m \mid x) \sum_u P(y \mid m, u) P(u)$. The inner sum is boxed with the warning that $U$ is unmeasured. Below, a second chain shows $\sum_{x'} P(x') P(y \mid m, x') = \sum_{x'} P(x') \sum_u P(y \mid m, u, x') P(u \mid m, x')$, then, using $Y \perp\!\!\!\perp X \mid M, U$ and $U \perp\!\!\!\perp M \mid X$, $\sum_{x'} P(x') \sum_u P(y \mid m, u) P(u \mid x')$, then $\sum_u P(y \mid m, u) P(u)$. The boxed term is replaced, giving the frontdoor formula in which every term is observable. Finally the numbers: $P(Y=1 \mid do(X=1)) = 0.8(0.8) + 0.2(0.2) = 0.68$ and $P(Y=1 \mid do(X=0)) = 0.2(0.8) + 0.8(0.2) = 0.32$.

blocks.title: Frontdoor adjustment (general graphs)
blocks.label: thm-l4-05-general
blocks.md: If a set $M$ satisfies the frontdoor criterion relative to $(X, Y)$ and $P(x, m) > 0$ for all $x$ and $m$, then the effect of $X$ on $Y$ is identified by [](#eq-l4-05-frontdoor), with $m$ running over the joint values of $M$ [@pearlcausality; @frontdoor].

blocks.title: Why the general proof is two backdoor steps
blocks.md: *Proof sketch.* Condition 2 says the empty set satisfies the backdoor criterion for $(X, M)$, so $P(m \mid do(x)) = P(m \mid x)$. Condition 3 says $\{X\}$ satisfies the backdoor criterion for $(M, Y)$, so $P(y \mid do(m)) = \sum_{x'} P(y \mid m, x')P(x')$: this is the standardized response $r(m)$. Condition 1 lets the two be chained, $P(y \mid do(x)) = \sum_m P(m \mid do(x))\, P(y \mid do(m))$; making that chaining step rigorous in an arbitrary graph uses the do-calculus of [L4-07](#lesson-l4-07) [@pearlcausality]. The proof above with $U$ is a complete proof for the canonical graph only.

Compute the pieces from the observed distribution of the running model. Bayes' rule gives $P(X = 1) = 0.5$, $P(U = 1 \mid X = 1) = 0.75$ and $P(U = 1 \mid X = 0) = 0.25$. Piece 1 is $P(M = 1 \mid X = 1) = 0.8$ and $P(M = 1 \mid X = 0) = 0.2$. The observed outcome risks are $P(Y = 1 \mid M = 1, X = 0) = 0.7$ and $P(Y = 1 \mid M = 1, X = 1) = 0.9$, and $0.1$ and $0.3$ when $M = 0$. Piece 2 averages over $x'$ with $P(x') = 0.5$: $r(1) = 0.5(0.7) + 0.5(0.9) = 0.8$ and $r(0) = 0.5(0.1) + 0.5(0.3) = 0.2$.

blocks.alt: Two bar charts: P(M = 1 | x) with bars 0.2 and 0.8, and the standardized response r(m) with bars 0.2 and 0.8. The two formula pieces then fly into the full frontdoor formula, and the results 0.68, 0.32 and effect 0.36 appear.
blocks.caption: Piece 1 is the effect of $X$ on $M$; piece 2 is the effect of $M$ on $Y$, adjusted for $X$. Assembled, they give the effect $0.36$, while the naive contrast is $0.56$.
blocks.describe: On the left, piece 1, $P(m \mid x)$, is drawn as bars 0.2 at $x = 0$ and 0.8 at $x = 1$; it needs no adjustment because there is no open backdoor path from $X$ to $M$. On the right, piece 2, $\sum_{x'} P(y \mid m, x') P(x')$, is computed as $r(1) = 0.5(0.7) + 0.5(0.9) = 0.8$ and $r(0) = 0.5(0.1) + 0.5(0.3) = 0.2$ and drawn as bars. The two formula pieces then move into the full formula $P(y \mid do(x)) = \sum_m P(m \mid x) \sum_{x'} P(y \mid m, x') P(x')$. The results appear: $do(X = 1)$ gives 0.68, $do(X = 0)$ gives 0.32, and the effect is 0.36. A last line notes that the naive contrast $0.78 - 0.22 = 0.56$ is biased by $U$.

blocks.md: The effect is $0.68 - 0.32 = 0.36$. Because the model is explicit, we can check it against the truth computed with $U$: $P(Y = 1 \mid do(x)) = \sum_m P(m \mid x)\,(0.6m + 0.4 \cdot 0.5)$, which is $0.68$ and $0.32$. The naive contrast is $P(Y = 1 \mid X = 1) - P(Y = 1 \mid X = 0) = 0.78 - 0.22 = 0.56$: people who take the treatment also tend to have $U = 1$. With a binary mediator the effect factorizes, $[P(M = 1 \mid 1) - P(M = 1 \mid 0)]\,[r(1) - r(0)] = 0.6 \times 0.6 = 0.36$: the effect of $X$ on $M$ times the effect of $M$ on $Y$.

blocks.title: Why piece 2 averages over $x'$
blocks.md: Conditioning on $X$ blocks the backdoor path $M \leftarrow X \leftarrow U \rightarrow Y$, so within each value $x'$ the association of $M$ with $Y$ is causal. Averaging over the population distribution $P(x')$ is backdoor standardization with $\{X\}$ as the adjustment set. Using $P(y \mid m)$ instead would leave that path open.

blocks.caption: 400 simulated studies of 2000 units each from the running model. The frontdoor estimate centers on the true effect 0.36; the naive contrast centers on 0.56. Finite samples add spread, not bias.

blocks.md: The formula is exact only on a graph that satisfies the criterion. Two small edits break it. A **direct arrow** $X \to Y$, modeled as $P(Y = 1 \mid M, U, X) = (1 - s)(0.6M + 0.4U) + sX$, violates condition 1: part of the effect bypasses $M$, and the formula misses it. A **hidden arrow** $U \to M$, modeled as $P(M = 1 \mid X, U) = (1 - s)(0.2 + 0.6X) + sU$, violates conditions 2 and 3: piece 1 is now confounded, and $X$ no longer blocks every path from $M$ to $Y$.

blocks.mermaid:
graph LR
  U((U hidden)) -.-> X
  U -.-> Y
  U -.->|violation B| M
  X --> M
  M --> Y
  X -->|violation A| Y
blocks.caption: The two violations explored below: a direct arrow $X \to Y$ (A) and an arrow from the hidden $U$ into the mediator (B). Either one makes the frontdoor formula biased.
Increase the violation strength $s$. With $s = 0$ the frontdoor formula equals the truth; as $s$ grows, it drifts away in both violated models.
blocks.describe: The first panel shows three bars for each violated model: the true risk difference, the value of the frontdoor formula computed from the exact observed distribution, and the naive contrast. The second panel plots the frontdoor formula minus the truth against $s$ from 0 to 0.5 for both models, with markers at the chosen $s$. At $s = 0$ both biases are 0. With the direct arrow at $s = 0.5$ the truth is 0.68 and the formula gives 0.18; with the arrow $U \to M$ at $s = 0.5$ the truth is 0.18 and the formula gives about 0.45.

blocks.title: The conditions cannot be checked from the data
blocks.md: In the canonical graph every pair of observed variables is connected by an arrow or by a path that no observed set blocks, so the graph implies no conditional independence among $X$, $M$ and $Y$ that the data could test. Whether the mediator carries all of the effect and is unconfounded with the outcome is a substantive assumption. The frontdoor criterion is sufficient for identification, not necessary; other graphs are identified by other arguments ([L4-07](#lesson-l4-07)).

blocks.explain: Check the two independences with `networkx`, compute the frontdoor formula exactly from the model's observed distribution, then estimate it from 120,000 simulated rows of $(X, M, Y)$ only. The 'backdoor on $U$' line is an oracle that uses the hidden variable, for comparison.

blocks.title: Estimation
blocks.md: The plug-in estimator replaces each probability in [](#eq-l4-05-frontdoor) by a sample frequency, as in the code. With many mediator values or continuous variables, the two pieces are fitted with models, and their errors combine; the delta method or the bootstrap gives uncertainty intervals ([L3-10](#lesson-l3-10)). Identification guarantees only that the target is a function of the observed distribution; it says nothing about how many samples are needed [@bradyneal].

worked_example.title: A frontdoor calculation from an observed table
worked_example.problem: Assume a valid frontdoor graph. The observed distribution has $P(X = 1) = 0.4$, $P(M = 1 \mid X = 1) = 0.7$, $P(M = 1 \mid X = 0) = 0.1$, and outcome risks $P(Y = 1 \mid M = m, X = x)$ of $0.5$ for $(1, 1)$, $0.3$ for $(1, 0)$, $0.4$ for $(0, 1)$ and $0.2$ for $(0, 0)$. Find $P(Y = 1 \mid do(X = x))$ for both $x$, the effect, and the naive contrast.
steps: Check with the binary shortcut: $[0.7 - 0.1]\,[0.38 - 0.28] = 0.6 \times 0.10 = 0.06$.
worked_example.result: The frontdoor effect is $0.35 - 0.29 = 0.06$, far smaller than the naive $0.26$; most of the observed association comes from the hidden common cause.

exercises.prompt: Assume a valid frontdoor graph. The standardized responses for $M = 1$ and $M = 0$ are $0.6$ and $0.2$. The probabilities of $M = 1$ at $X = 1$ and $X = 0$ are $0.75$ and $0.25$. Find both intervention risks and their difference.

For each graph, say whether $\{M\}$ satisfies the frontdoor criterion relative to $(X, Y)$, and name the failing condition if not. (a) $U \to X$, $U \to Y$, $X \to M \to Y$. (b) Graph (a) plus $X \to Y$. (c) Graph (a) plus $U \to M$. (d) Graph (a) plus a second hidden $V$ with $V \to M$ and $V \to Y$.
exercises.solution: (a) Yes, all three conditions hold. (b) No: the directed path $X \to Y$ avoids $M$, so condition 1 fails. (c) No: $X \leftarrow U \rightarrow M$ is an open backdoor path from $X$ to $M$ (condition 2), and $M \leftarrow U \rightarrow Y$ is a backdoor path from $M$ to $Y$ that $X$ does not block (condition 3). (d) No: $M \leftarrow V \rightarrow Y$ is a backdoor path from $M$ to $Y$ that does not pass through $X$, so condition 3 fails; condition 2 still holds because $X \leftarrow U \rightarrow Y \leftarrow V \rightarrow M$ is blocked at the collider $Y$.

exercises.prompt: Show that for a binary mediator, $P(y \mid do(X = 1)) - P(y \mid do(X = 0)) = [P(M = 1 \mid X = 1) - P(M = 1 \mid X = 0)]\,[r(1) - r(0)]$, and interpret each factor.
exercises.solution: From [](#eq-l4-05-frontdoor), $P(y \mid do(x)) = r(0) + P(M = 1 \mid x)\,[r(1) - r(0)]$, since $P(M = 0 \mid x) = 1 - P(M = 1 \mid x)$. Subtracting the $x = 0$ value from the $x = 1$ value cancels $r(0)$ and leaves the product. The first factor is the causal effect of $X$ on $M$ (identified because condition 2 holds); the second is the causal effect of $M$ on $Y$, $P(y \mid do(M = 1)) - P(y \mid do(M = 0))$ (identified by adjusting for $X$).

exercises.prompt: In the running model, someone computes piece 2 as $P(Y = 1 \mid M = m)$ instead of $r(m)$. Find $P(Y = 1 \mid M = 1)$, $P(Y = 1 \mid M = 0)$ and the resulting 'effect'. Why is it wrong?
exercises.solution: $P(M = 1) = 0.5(0.8) + 0.5(0.2) = 0.5$, so $P(X = 1 \mid M = 1) = 0.4/0.5 = 0.8$ and $P(X = 1 \mid M = 0) = 0.1/0.5 = 0.2$. Then $P(Y = 1 \mid M = 1) = 0.8(0.9) + 0.2(0.7) = 0.86$ and $P(Y = 1 \mid M = 0) = 0.2(0.3) + 0.8(0.1) = 0.14$. The 'effect' is $0.6 \times (0.86 - 0.14) = 0.432$ instead of $0.36$. Without conditioning on $X$, the path $M \leftarrow X \leftarrow U \rightarrow Y$ is open, so $P(y \mid m)$ mixes the effect of $M$ with confounding by $U$.

exercises.prompt: Show directly that in the canonical model the frontdoor formula agrees with the backdoor formula you could use if $U$ were measured, $\sum_u P(y \mid x, u) P(u)$.
exercises.solution: By [](#lem-l4-05-indep) and the chain rule, $P(y \mid x, u) = \sum_m P(m \mid x, u)\, P(y \mid m, x, u) = \sum_m P(m \mid x)\, P(y \mid m, u)$, because $M$ depends on $(X, U)$ only through $X$ ($U \perp\!\!\!\perp M \mid X$) and $Y \perp\!\!\!\perp X \mid M, U$. Hence $\sum_u P(u) P(y \mid x, u) = \sum_m P(m \mid x) \sum_u P(y \mid m, u) P(u)$, which is the second line of the proof of [](#thm-l4-05-canonical), and that equals [](#eq-l4-05-frontdoor). Both formulas compute the same $P(y \mid do(x))$; only the frontdoor one avoids $U$.

exercises.prompt: A treatment acts through two measured mediators in parallel, $X \to M_1 \to Y$ and $X \to M_2 \to Y$, and a hidden $U$ causes $X$ and $Y$. Show that $\{M_1, M_2\}$ satisfies the frontdoor criterion and write the identifying formula.
exercises.solution: Condition 1: the directed paths from $X$ to $Y$ are $X \to M_1 \to Y$ and $X \to M_2 \to Y$, and both pass through the set. Condition 2: every backdoor path from $X$ to $M_1$ or $M_2$ starts $X \leftarrow U \rightarrow Y$ and then enters a mediator against an arrow ($Y \leftarrow M_j$), so $Y$ is a collider and the path is blocked. Condition 3: the backdoor paths from the mediators to $Y$ are $M_j \leftarrow X \leftarrow U \rightarrow Y$ and $M_1 \leftarrow X \rightarrow M_2 \rightarrow Y$ (and the mirror image), and each has $X$ as a noncollider, so conditioning on $X$ blocks them. The formula is $P(y \mid do(x)) = \sum_{m_1, m_2} P(m_1, m_2 \mid x) \sum_{x'} P(y \mid m_1, m_2, x')\, P(x')$, given positivity.

check.question: Which condition is part of the ordinary frontdoor criterion?
options: The mediator must be a parent of $X$
The mediator may skip some directed paths from $X$ to $Y$
The mediator must intercept every directed path from $X$ to $Y$
All hidden causes must be measured
check.explanation: Condition 1 requires every directed path from treatment to outcome to pass through the mediator. Hidden treatment-outcome confounding is allowed; that is the point of the criterion.

check.question: In a valid frontdoor graph, $r(1) = 0.8$, $r(0) = 0.2$ and $P(M = 1 \mid X = x) = 0.5$. What is $P(Y = 1 \mid do(X = x))$?
check.explanation: $0.5(0.8) + 0.5(0.2) = 0.5$. The frontdoor formula is a weighted average of the standardized responses with weights $P(m \mid x)$.

check.question: Why does piece 2 average $P(y \mid m, x')$ over $x'$ with weights $P(x')$ instead of using $P(y \mid m)$?
options: To remove the effect of $M$ on $Y$
Because $X$ is a collider between $M$ and $Y$
Conditioning on $X$ blocks the backdoor path $M \leftarrow X \leftarrow U \rightarrow Y$
check.explanation: This is backdoor adjustment for the effect of $M$ on $Y$, with $\{X\}$ as the adjustment set. Without $X$ the path through the hidden $U$ stays open.

check.question: In backdoor adjustment, why may an adjustment set not contain a descendant of the treatment?
options: Conditioning on it can block part of the effect or open new paths
It makes the formula use $P(z \mid x)$ instead of $P(z)$
check.explanation: A descendant such as a mediator carries part of the effect, so conditioning on it removes that part; a descendant can also be a collider. Condition (i) of the backdoor criterion excludes descendants for this reason.

misconceptions.claim: "Any measured mediator lets you identify the effect by the frontdoor formula."
misconceptions.correction: All three conditions are needed. A direct arrow $X \to Y$ or a hidden cause of both $M$ and $Y$ makes the formula biased, as the interactive shows.

misconceptions.claim: "The frontdoor formula works by estimating the hidden $U$."
misconceptions.correction: Nothing about $U$ is estimated. The proof shows that the one place $U$ enters, $\sum_u P(y \mid m, u)P(u)$, equals an average over $x'$ of observed quantities.

misconceptions.claim: "Frontdoor adjustment means adjusting for the mediator."
misconceptions.correction: Adjusting for $M$ in the usual way would block the effect. The frontdoor formula instead uses $M$ as a stepping stone: the effect of $X$ on $M$, chained with the effect of $M$ on $Y$.

misconceptions.claim: "If the frontdoor estimate and the naive contrast differ, the data have proved confounding."
misconceptions.correction: The difference is evidence only under the assumed graph. The frontdoor conditions imply no testable independence among $X$, $M$ and $Y$, so the data cannot confirm the graph.

lessons.connect: [L4-07](#lesson-l4-07) shows that backdoor and frontdoor adjustment are both special cases of the do-calculus, and that some graphs with hidden variables are not identified at all. Counterfactual questions in [L4-09](#lesson-l4-09) need more than the interventional distribution computed here.
lessons.caution: The frontdoor formula identifies the effect only if the causal graph is right, in particular if the mediator carries all of the effect and shares no hidden cause with the outcome. These assumptions cannot be tested from data on $X$, $M$ and $Y$ alone. Positivity $P(x, m) > 0$ is required. The criterion is sufficient, not necessary. The smoking and tar story is a hypothetical illustration of the graph, not a claim about real smoking data, and the numbers come from a made-up model. Simulations confirm the algebra; they are not evidence about the world.

instructor.why: The frontdoor criterion is the clearest example that identification is a property of the graph and the observed distribution together, not of which variables happen to be confounded. Its proof is short enough to do completely for the canonical graph and shows the logic of the do-calculus without the full calculus [@frontdoor; @pearlcausality].
teaching_notes: Start by asking students to try backdoor adjustment on the canonical graph and to explain why every candidate set fails. The puzzle motivates the rest.
Write the derivation on the board in the same order as the animation, and ask students to name the independence used at each step before revealing it.
Stress the averaging index: $x$ is the intervention value and $x'$ is summed over. Many errors come from merging them.
Use the interactive to show that a small direct effect produces a large bias; then discuss how rarely the conditions are believable in real applications [@bradyneal].
instructor.assessment: The second core exercise tests the conditions on modified graphs; the stretch exercises test the formula's structure; the first challenge exercise tests whether students can connect the frontdoor and backdoor formulas algebraically [@pearl].
instructor.extend: Read Pearl's original presentation of the frontdoor graph and compare the do-calculus derivation there with the proof given here [@frontdoor]. Then show that the conditional frontdoor formula, with measured covariates $C$ that block some backdoor paths, is obtained by applying the same argument within each stratum of $C$ [@pearlcausality].

further.note: The original paper, which introduces the frontdoor criterion with the hypothetical smoking, tar and cancer illustration.
Chapter 6 presents frontdoor adjustment as a sequence of backdoor steps, with figures.
Section 3.3.2 states the frontdoor theorem and Section 3.4 derives it with the do-calculus.

lessons.title: Potential outcomes and randomization
lessons.objective: Define potential outcomes and the average treatment effect, state the four assumptions that identify it from a treated-versus-control contrast, and show why randomization delivers them.
lessons.big_idea: Each unit has an outcome for every treatment but shows only one, so causal effects are averages over a table we can never see in full; randomization makes the visible half a fair sample of each invisible column.
outcomes: Write a potential outcomes table, compute individual effects, the ATE and the ATT, and explain the fundamental problem of causal inference.
Decompose a naive treated-minus-control contrast into the effect on the treated plus selection bias, and compute both parts.
State SUTVA, consistency, exchangeability and positivity, prove that together they identify the ATE, and prove that the difference in means is unbiased under complete randomization.
Enumerate or simulate a randomization distribution and explain why it is centered on the ATE although single experiments miss it.

key_terms.meaning: $Y_i(x)$, the outcome unit $i$ would have if the treatment were set to $x$; with two options each unit has a pair $(Y_i(0), Y_i(1))$.
$E[Y(1) - Y(0)] = E[Y(1)] - E[Y(0)]$, the mean of the individual effects over the population.
For each unit at most one potential outcome is observed, so no individual effect $Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)$ is ever seen directly.
Stable unit treatment value assumption: a unit's outcome depends only on its own treatment (no interference), and each treatment value has one version.
If unit $i$ actually receives $X_i = x$, its observed outcome is $Y_i = Y_i(x)$.
$Y(x) \perp\!\!\!\perp X$ for each $x$: the potential outcomes carry no information about which treatment was received.
Every treatment value being compared has a positive probability, $0 < P(X = 1) < 1$ (within each stratum, for conditional versions).

motivation: A tutoring program is open to anyone who signs up. At the end of term, students who signed up score $6.25$ points higher than those who did not. Is $6.25$ the effect of tutoring? Not necessarily: the students who sign up may be the ones who would have scored higher anyway. In the example of this lesson the true average effect is $4$, and the extra $2.25$ comes from who chose the program.

Lessons [L4-01](#lesson-l4-01) to [L4-05](#lesson-l4-05) described causal effects with graphs and the $do$ operator. This lesson uses the second great language of causal inference, potential outcomes, which writes the same questions as comparisons between outcomes under different treatments [@neyman1990; @rubin1974; @hernan]. It makes one fact impossible to miss: half of the data we would need is always missing. It also explains, line by line, why a randomized experiment is trusted more than any adjustment: randomization makes the key assumption true by design instead of by argument.

sections.heading: Two outcomes per unit, one observed

blocks.title: Potential outcomes and average effects
blocks.label: def-l4-06-po
blocks.md: For a binary treatment, each unit $i$ in a population has two **potential outcomes**, $Y_i(1)$ under treatment and $Y_i(0)$ under control. Its **individual effect** is $\tau_i = Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)$. The **average treatment effect** is [](#eq-l4-06-ate), and the **average effect on the treated** is $\text{ATT} = E[Y(1) - Y(0) \mid X = 1]$, the average over units that actually receive treatment.

The table below the animation lists eight units, A to H, with both potential outcomes, a view only an oracle could have. The $Y(0)$ column is $0, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4$ (mean 2) and the $Y(1)$ column is $3, 5, 7, 4, 8, 6, 7, 8$ (mean 6). The individual effects $3, 4, 6, 2, 6, 3, 4, 4$ differ from unit to unit, and their mean is the ATE, $6 - 2 = 4$. Effects are heterogeneous; the ATE is one summary of them, not the effect on every unit.

blocks.alt: A table of eight units with columns Y(0), Y(1) and the individual effect. Then a treatment column appears and one potential outcome per row turns into a question mark, as does every individual effect. The naive contrast 6.25 is split into 4.25 plus 2.00.
blocks.caption: The science table, then reality: each unit reveals only the column of the treatment it chose. The naive contrast $6.25$ is the effect on the treated, $4.25$, plus selection bias, $2.00$.
blocks.describe: Eight rows, units A to H, show $Y(0)$ in blue, $Y(1)$ in violet and the effect $Y(1) - Y(0)$. The column means are 2, 6 and 4, and the oracle's ATE is $E[Y(1)] - E[Y(0)] = 6 - 2 = 4$. Then reality takes over: the four units with the highest $Y(0)$, E to H, choose treatment, so a column $X$ appears with values 0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1. For treated units the $Y(0)$ entry becomes a question mark; for control units the $Y(1)$ entry does; every individual effect becomes a question mark. The naive contrast is the treated mean of $Y(1)$ minus the control mean of $Y(0)$: $7.25 - 1.00 = 6.25$. It splits into $4.25$, the effect on the treated, plus $2.00$, the selection bias $E[Y(0) \mid X=1] - E[Y(0) \mid X=0] = 3 - 1$.

blocks.title: The fundamental problem
blocks.md: No unit ever shows both potential outcomes, so no individual effect is ever observed [@hernan]. Every causal estimate compares *different* units (or the same unit at different times, which needs its own assumptions). The question is always which assumptions make the units in one arm stand in for the units in the other.

blocks.title: Decomposition of the naive contrast
blocks.label: prop-l4-06-decomp
blocks.md: Under consistency, $E[Y \mid X = 1] - E[Y \mid X = 0] = \text{ATT} + \big(E[Y(0) \mid X = 1] - E[Y(0) \mid X = 0]\big)$. The second term is the **selection bias**: the difference the two groups would show if nobody were treated [@seeing].

By consistency, $E[Y \mid X = 1] = E[Y(1) \mid X = 1]$ and $E[Y \mid X = 0] = E[Y(0) \mid X = 0]$. Add and subtract $E[Y(0) \mid X = 1]$: $E[Y(1) \mid X = 1] - E[Y(0) \mid X = 1] + E[Y(0) \mid X = 1] - E[Y(0) \mid X = 0]$. The first difference is the ATT; the second is the selection bias.

In the self-selected example the treated units E to H have $Y(1)$ values $8, 6, 7, 8$ (mean $7.25$) and the control units A to D have $Y(0)$ values $0, 1, 1, 2$ (mean $1.00$), so the naive contrast is $6.25$. The treated units' own effects are $6, 3, 4, 4$, so $\text{ATT} = 4.25$. Their $Y(0)$ values average $3$ against $1$ for the controls, a selection bias of $2.00$. Check: $4.25 + 2.00 = 6.25$. The ATT differs from the ATE ($4.25$ versus $4$) because the effects are heterogeneous.
