sections.heading: Four assumptions that identify the ATE

blocks.title: SUTVA
blocks.label: asm-l4-06-sutva
blocks.md: Each unit's outcome depends only on its own treatment, $Y_i(x_1, \dots, x_n) = Y_i(x_i)$ (no interference), and there is only one version of each treatment value. Vaccines in a household and classroom peer effects are standard violations.

blocks.title: Consistency
blocks.label: asm-l4-06-consistency
blocks.md: If $X_i = x$ then $Y_i = Y_i(x)$: the observed outcome is the potential outcome of the treatment actually received. In graph language this is what links the observed $Y$ to the intervention $do(X = x)$ ([L4-01](#lesson-l4-01)).

blocks.title: Exchangeability
blocks.label: asm-l4-06-exch
blocks.md: $Y(x) \perp\!\!\!\perp X$ for $x = 0, 1$: the treated and control groups would have had the same distribution of $Y(1)$, and of $Y(0)$, had they received the same treatment. In the graph language of [L4-04](#lesson-l4-04) this corresponds to the empty set satisfying the backdoor criterion.

blocks.title: Positivity
blocks.label: asm-l4-06-pos
blocks.md: $0 < P(X = 1) < 1$, so both conditional means $E[Y \mid X = x]$ are defined.

blocks.title: Identification of the ATE
blocks.label: thm-l4-06-ident
blocks.md: Under SUTVA, consistency, exchangeability and positivity, $E[Y(x)] = E[Y \mid X = x]$ for $x = 0, 1$, and therefore $\text{ATE} = E[Y \mid X = 1] - E[Y \mid X = 0]$ [@hernan].

SUTVA makes $Y_i(1)$ and $Y_i(0)$ well-defined numbers for each unit. Positivity makes $E[Y \mid X = x]$ defined. Then $E[Y \mid X = 1] = E[Y(1) \mid X = 1]$ by consistency, because among units with $X = 1$ the observed $Y$ is $Y(1)$. Next, $E[Y(1) \mid X = 1] = E[Y(1)]$ by exchangeability, because $Y(1)$ is independent of $X$. The same two steps give $E[Y \mid X = 0] = E[Y(0)]$. Subtract and use [](#eq-l4-06-ate).

blocks.alt: Four cards labeled SUTVA, consistency, exchangeability and positivity with their formulas. Below, the chain E[Y | X = 1] = E[Y(1) | X = 1] = E[Y(1)] grows term by term while the card used at each step flashes.
blocks.caption: Each step of the identification proof uses one card: SUTVA defines the potential outcomes, consistency swaps $Y$ for $Y(1)$, exchangeability removes the conditioning, positivity keeps both sides defined.
blocks.describe: Four cards appear: SUTVA with $Y_i(x_1, \dots, x_n) = Y_i(x_i)$, consistency with $X_i = x \Rightarrow Y_i = Y_i(x)$, exchangeability with $Y(x) \perp\!\!\!\perp X$, and positivity with $0 < P(X = 1) < 1$. The SUTVA card flashes: it makes $Y(1)$ and $Y(0)$ well defined. The expression $E[Y \mid X = 1]$ appears and grows into $E[Y \mid X = 1] = E[Y(1) \mid X = 1]$ while the consistency card flashes, then into $= E[Y(1)]$ while the exchangeability card flashes. The positivity card flashes to show that both sides are defined. The final line reads $E[Y \mid X=1] - E[Y \mid X=0] = E[Y(1)] - E[Y(0)] = \text{ATE}$.

blocks.title: Conditional exchangeability gives standardization
blocks.label: cor-l4-06-cond
blocks.md: If instead $Y(x) \perp\!\!\!\perp X \mid Z$ (conditional exchangeability) and $0 < P(X = 1 \mid Z = z) < 1$ for every $z$, then $E[Y(x)] = \sum_z E[Y \mid X = x, Z = z]\, P(z)$, the standardization formula of [L4-04](#lesson-l4-04).

$E[Y(x)] = \sum_z E[Y(x) \mid Z = z] P(z) = \sum_z E[Y(x) \mid X = x, Z = z] P(z) = \sum_z E[Y \mid X = x, Z = z] P(z)$, using the law of total expectation, then conditional exchangeability within each stratum, then consistency. Positivity makes every term defined. Graphically, a set $Z$ that satisfies the backdoor criterion delivers conditional exchangeability, so the two languages give the same formula [@pearlcausality].

In **complete randomization** exactly $n_1$ of the $N$ units are treated and every one of the $\binom{N}{n_1}$ subsets is equally likely. With $N = 8$ and $n_1 = 4$ there are $\binom{8}{4} = 70$ assignments. Because the assignment is generated by a device that never looks at the units, it is independent of their potential outcomes: exchangeability holds by design [@openstax_design].

blocks.title: The difference in means is unbiased
blocks.label: prop-l4-06-unbiased
blocks.md: Under SUTVA, consistency and complete randomization with $0 < n_1 < N$, the difference in means $\hat\tau = \frac{1}{n_1}\sum_{i: X_i = 1} Y_i - \frac{1}{n_0}\sum_{i: X_i = 0} Y_i$, with $n_0 = N - n_1$, satisfies $E[\hat\tau] = \frac1N \sum_i \big(Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)\big)$, the ATE of the $N$ units. The expectation is over the random assignment; the potential outcomes are fixed [@imbensrubin2015].

By consistency, $\hat\tau = \frac{1}{n_1}\sum_i X_i Y_i(1) - \frac{1}{n_0}\sum_i (1 - X_i) Y_i(0)$, where only the indicators $X_i$ are random. Each unit is in the treated subset of exactly $\binom{N-1}{n_1-1}$ of the $\binom{N}{n_1}$ equally likely subsets, so $E[X_i] = n_1/N$ and $E[1 - X_i] = n_0/N$. By linearity, $E[\hat\tau] = \frac{1}{n_1}\sum_i \frac{n_1}{N} Y_i(1) - \frac{1}{n_0}\sum_i \frac{n_0}{N} Y_i(0) = \frac1N\sum_i Y_i(1) - \frac1N\sum_i Y_i(0)$.

blocks.alt: Eight unit circles at the top; at each draw four turn violet (treated) and four blue. Each draw drops one dot into a dot plot of the difference in means and one into a dot plot of baseline imbalance. After ten draws, the dots of all 70 assignments fill in, centered on 4 and on 0.
blocks.caption: One random assignment at a time: estimates scatter around the ATE and baseline imbalance scatters around 0. Over all $70$ assignments the estimates average exactly 4, with variance $29/28$.
blocks.describe: Eight circles, A to H, show each unit's $Y(0)$. A draw of complete randomization colors four circles violet for treatment and four blue for control. For each draw the screen shows the difference in means $\hat\tau$ and the baseline imbalance, the treated mean of $Y(0)$ minus the control mean of $Y(0)$, and drops a dot into one dot plot for each. Ten draws are shown one by one; single estimates land as far from 4 as 2 or 6, and imbalances land away from 0. Then the dots of all 70 possible assignments fill in. The estimates average exactly 4, the ATE, with variance $29/28$, and the imbalances average exactly 0.

blocks.caption: The exact randomization distribution of $\hat\tau$ for the eight-unit table: one bar per possible value, height the number of the 70 assignments that give it. The mean is the ATE, 4. The self-selected assignment E to H is one of the 70 and gives the extreme value $6.25$; the problem with self-selection is not that assignment but that it was chosen because of $Y(0)$.

blocks.title: How spread out is one experiment?
blocks.md: The variance of $\hat\tau$ over the 70 assignments is $29/28 \approx 1.04$. A classical formula due to Neyman [@neyman1990; @imbensrubin2015] gives it exactly as $S_1^2/n_1 + S_0^2/n_0 - S_\tau^2/N$, where $S_1^2$, $S_0^2$ and $S_\tau^2$ are the variances (divisor $N - 1$) of the $Y(1)$ column, the $Y(0)$ column and the individual effects: $\tfrac{24/7}{4} + \tfrac{12/7}{4} - \tfrac{2}{8} = \tfrac{29}{28}$. The last term needs both columns and can never be estimated, so the usual standard error, which drops it, is conservative. The code below checks the formula by enumeration.

blocks.caption: Change the number of units $N$ (the eight-unit table copied $N/8$ times, half treated). Both histograms narrow around their centers as $N$ grows; the self-selected value $6.25$ never moves.
blocks.describe: The first panel is a histogram of the difference in means over 2000 simulated complete randomizations, with a solid line at the true ATE 4 and a dashed line at the self-selected contrast 6.25. The second panel is a histogram of the baseline imbalance in $Y(0)$. At $N = 8$ the estimates spread from about 2 to 6 (standard deviation about 1.0) and the imbalance from $-2$ to $2$. At $N = 256$ the estimates concentrate near 4 (standard deviation under 0.2) and the imbalance near 0. Self-selection stays biased at every $N$.

blocks.title: What randomization does not do
blocks.md: It does not balance every realized sample: one experiment can be unlucky, as the dot plots show. It does not make participants follow their assignment: with nonadherence, the comparison of randomized groups estimates the effect of *assignment* (intention to treat), not of treatment received. It does not repair missing outcomes or interference between units. Each of these changes the target or the analysis.

blocks.explain: Exact arithmetic with `fractions`: the ATE of the table, the decomposition of the self-selected contrast, the 70-assignment randomization distribution with Neyman's variance formula, and a Bernoulli design (an independent coin per unit, from the course engine's seeded generator `qcai.science.rng`) in which an arm can come out empty and must be skipped.
blocks.source:
import itertools
from fractions import Fraction as F
from qcai import science

Y0 = [0, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4]          # the science table of the lesson (units A to H)
Y1 = [3, 5, 7, 4, 8, 6, 7, 8]
N = len(Y0)
tau = [b - a for a, b in zip(Y0, Y1)]
print("ATE =", F(sum(tau), N))

def diff_in_means(T):
    """Treated mean of Y(1) minus control mean of Y(0): what we see when T is treated (consistency)."""
    C = [i for i in range(N) if i not in T]
    return F(sum(Y1[i] for i in T), len(T)) - F(sum(Y0[i] for i in C), len(C))

# self-selection: the four units with the largest Y(0) take the treatment
T_self = (4, 5, 6, 7)
att = F(sum(tau[i] for i in T_self), 4)
bias = F(sum(Y0[i] for i in T_self), 4) - F(sum(Y0[i] for i in range(4)), 4)
print("self-selected contrast", diff_in_means(T_self), "= ATT", att, "+ selection bias", bias)

# complete randomization: all C(8, 4) = 70 assignments equally likely
est = [diff_in_means(T) for T in itertools.combinations(range(N), 4)]
mean = sum(est) / len(est)
var = sum((e - mean) ** 2 for e in est) / len(est)
def S2(v):                                 # finite-population variance with divisor N - 1
    mu = F(sum(v), len(v))
    return sum((x - mu) ** 2 for x in v) / (len(v) - 1)
neyman = S2(Y1) / 4 + S2(Y0) / 4 - S2(tau) / N
print(len(est), "assignments: mean", mean, " variance", var, " Neyman's formula", neyman)
print("range of estimates:", float(min(est)), "to", float(max(est)))

# Bernoulli design: one fair coin per unit (the course engine's seeded generator); an arm can be empty
coin = science.rng(2024)
total, kept, empty = F(0), 0, 0
for _ in range(20000):
    T = tuple(i for i in range(N) if coin() < 0.5)
    if len(T) in (0, N):
        empty += 1
        continue
    total += diff_in_means(T)
    kept += 1
print(f"coin flips: mean estimate {float(total / kept):.3f} over {kept} experiments; {empty} had an empty arm")

blocks.title: Two designs
blocks.md: Complete randomization fixes the arm sizes, so both arms are never empty. Independent coin flips (a Bernoulli design) can leave an arm empty, with probability $2/2^N = 1/128$ for $N = 8$; then $\hat\tau$ is undefined. Given the number of treated units, a Bernoulli design is a complete randomization, so the estimator is still unbiased once empty-arm draws are excluded, as the simulation shows.

worked_example.title: Every possible experiment on four units
worked_example.problem: Four units have $(Y(0), Y(1))$ equal to $a = (1, 3)$, $b = (2, 2)$, $c = (4, 7)$ and $d = (3, 2)$. Compute the ATE. Then list all complete randomizations with two treated units, the difference in means for each, and their average.
steps: Individual effects are $2, 0, 3, -1$; their mean is the ATE, $4/4 = 1$.
Average of the six estimates: $(-1 + 2.5 - 0.5 + 2.5 - 0.5 + 3)/6 = 6/6 = 1$.
worked_example.result: The ATE is 1. Single experiments give anything from $-1$ to $3$, even the wrong sign, but the average over the assignment distribution is exactly the ATE, as [](#prop-l4-06-unbiased) promises.

exercises.prompt: Four model units have potential outcome pairs $(Y(0), Y(1))$ of $(1, 3)$, $(2, 2)$, $(4, 7)$ and $(3, 2)$. Calculate each individual effect and the population ATE. Is the treatment good for every unit?
exercises.solution: The individual effects are $2, 0, 3, -1$. Their sum is 4 over four units, so the ATE is 1 outcome unit. No: one unit is unaffected and one is harmed ($-1$), although the average effect is positive.

exercises.prompt: In the eight-unit table, suppose units C, E, G and H choose treatment. Compute the naive contrast, the ATT and the selection bias, and check the decomposition.
exercises.solution: Treated $Y(1)$: $7, 8, 7, 8$, mean $7.5$. Control (A, B, D, F) $Y(0)$: $0, 1, 2, 3$, mean $1.5$. Naive contrast $6.0$. ATT: effects of C, E, G, H are $6, 6, 4, 4$, mean $5.0$. Selection bias: treated $Y(0)$ are $1, 2, 3, 4$, mean $2.5$, minus $1.5$, giving $1.0$. Check: $5.0 + 1.0 = 6.0$.

exercises.prompt: Show that under exchangeability the ATT equals the ATE. Then explain in one sentence why they differ in the self-selected example.
exercises.solution: $\text{ATT} = E[Y(1) \mid X = 1] - E[Y(0) \mid X = 1] = E[Y(1)] - E[Y(0)] = \text{ATE}$, using $Y(x) \perp\!\!\!\perp X$ for each $x$. In the self-selected example $Y(0)$ and $Y(1)$ depend on $X$ (the treated have high $Y(0)$), so exchangeability fails and the treated units' average effect, $4.25$, differs from the population's, $4$.

exercises.prompt: In a Bernoulli design each of $N$ units is treated by an independent fair coin. Find the probability that an arm is empty, evaluate it for $N = 8$ and $N = 20$, and explain why the difference in means is still unbiased if such draws are discarded.
exercises.solution: An arm is empty when all coins agree: $P = 2 \cdot (1/2)^N = 2^{1-N}$. For $N = 8$ this is $1/128 \approx 0.0078$; for $N = 20$ it is $2^{-19} \approx 1.9 \times 10^{-6}$. Conditional on the number of treated units $n_1$, every subset of size $n_1$ is equally likely, which is complete randomization, so by [](#prop-l4-06-unbiased) the conditional mean of $\hat\tau$ is the ATE for each $n_1$ from 1 to $N - 1$. Averaging over $n_1$ (with empty arms excluded) still gives the ATE.

exercises.prompt: Two roommates can each be vaccinated. Unit 1's probability of illness depends on both treatments: $0.4$ if neither is vaccinated, $0.1$ if only unit 1 is, $0.3$ if only the roommate is, $0.05$ if both are. Which assumption fails? Compute unit 1's effect of its own vaccination for each roommate status, and the effect a trial would estimate if each person were vaccinated by an independent fair coin.
exercises.solution: SUTVA (no interference) fails: unit 1's outcome depends on the roommate's treatment, so '$Y_1(1)$' is not one number. The effect of own vaccination on the risk is $0.1 - 0.4 = -0.3$ when the roommate is unvaccinated and $0.05 - 0.3 = -0.25$ when the roommate is vaccinated. With independent fair coins the roommate is vaccinated half the time, so the trial estimates the average $0.5(-0.3) + 0.5(-0.25) = -0.275$, an effect that depends on the vaccination policy for others, not a property of unit 1 alone.

exercises.prompt: A trial randomizes within two strata of $Z$, each half of the population, treating 80% of units with $Z = 1$ and 20% with $Z = 0$. Mean potential outcomes are $E[Y(0) \mid Z = 0] = 1$, $E[Y(1) \mid Z = 0] = 3$, $E[Y(0) \mid Z = 1] = 4$, $E[Y(1) \mid Z = 1] = 7$. Compute the ATE, the naive contrast, and the standardized contrast. Which version of exchangeability holds?
exercises.solution: ATE $= 0.5(3 - 1) + 0.5(7 - 4) = 2.5$. By Bayes' rule $P(Z = 1 \mid X = 1) = 0.8$ and $P(Z = 1 \mid X = 0) = 0.2$, so $E[Y \mid X = 1] = 0.2(3) + 0.8(7) = 6.2$ and $E[Y \mid X = 0] = 0.8(1) + 0.2(4) = 1.6$: a naive contrast of $4.6$. Standardizing with $P(Z) = (0.5, 0.5)$: $0.5(3) + 0.5(7) - [0.5(1) + 0.5(4)] = 5 - 2.5 = 2.5$, the ATE. Randomization within strata gives conditional exchangeability $Y(x) \perp\!\!\!\perp X \mid Z$, not marginal exchangeability, so [](#cor-l4-06-cond) applies.

check.question: What does random assignment establish in its assignment distribution?
options: Every finite sample is perfectly balanced
Every participant receives the assigned treatment
Every unit has the same treatment effect
Treatment is independent of the potential outcomes
check.explanation: Random assignment provides exchangeability by design. Perfect realized balance, full adherence and homogeneous effects are different properties and do not follow.

check.question: In the eight-unit example, the naive contrast is $6.25$ and the effect on the treated is $4.25$. What is the selection bias?
check.explanation: Naive contrast = ATT + selection bias, so the bias is $6.25 - 4.25 = 2.00$, the difference in average $Y(0)$ between the groups, $3 - 1$. The remaining $0.25$ between the ATT and the ATE comes from heterogeneous effects.

check.question: Which step of the identification proof uses consistency?
check.explanation: Consistency replaces the observed $Y$ by $Y(1)$ among units that received $X = 1$. Removing the conditioning uses exchangeability; the third step is linearity of expectation; the last is positivity.

check.question: A sample mean has standard error $s$ with $n$ independent observations. What is its standard error with $4n$ observations?
check.explanation: The standard error scales as $1/\sqrt{n}$, so four times as many observations halve it. The randomization explorer shows the same narrowing of the distribution of $\hat\tau$.

misconceptions.claim: "Randomization guarantees that the two groups are balanced."
misconceptions.correction: It guarantees balance on average over the assignment distribution. A single experiment can be unbalanced, as the dot plots show; the uncertainty calculation accounts for that.

misconceptions.claim: "The ATE is the effect on each unit."
misconceptions.correction: It is the mean of individual effects that can differ in size and sign. In the four-unit example the ATE is 1 while one unit is harmed.

misconceptions.claim: "Potential outcomes and causal graphs are rival theories."
misconceptions.correction: They describe the same causal quantities. Consistency links $Y$ to $Y(x)$ as the do operator links $Y$ to an intervention, and a valid backdoor set gives conditional exchangeability [@pearlcausality].

misconceptions.claim: "A randomized trial always measures the effect of taking the treatment."
misconceptions.correction: It measures the effect of assignment. If some participants do not follow their assignment, the effect of treatment actually received needs further assumptions.

lessons.connect: [L4-07](#lesson-l4-07) asks in general when a causal quantity is determined by the observed distribution. [L4-09](#lesson-l4-09) studies counterfactuals for individual units, which need a structural causal model rather than only the averages used here. [L4-10](#lesson-l4-10) asks when an effect measured in one population carries over to another.
lessons.caution: This lesson uses a finite population with fixed potential outcomes and the expectation over random assignment; the superpopulation view, where units are also sampled, leads to the same identification argument with different variance formulas. Identification by randomization relies on SUTVA, consistency, adherence to the assigned treatment and complete outcome data; none of these is guaranteed by the coin. All tables and numbers are made up for teaching, and the simulations check the algebra, not any real program.

instructor.why: Students who first meet causal inference through graphs often treat 'correlation is not causation' as a slogan. The potential outcomes table makes the missing-data structure concrete, and the selection-bias decomposition says exactly what goes wrong [@hernan; @seeing].
teaching_notes: Hand out the eight-unit table with both columns, let groups compute the ATE, then cover one column per row according to self-selection and ask them to estimate it again.
Run the 70-assignment enumeration as a class activity: each group draws a few assignments by hand, the class pools the estimates, and the pooled mean approaches 4.
Map each assumption to its graph counterpart: exchangeability to an empty backdoor set, conditional exchangeability to a valid adjustment set, consistency to the do operator [@pearlcausality].
Separate the two sources of randomness explicitly: random assignment (used here) and random sampling of units ([L3-10](#lesson-l3-10)).
instructor.assessment: The second core exercise and the second check question test the decomposition; the third check question and the stretch exercise test the identification argument; the challenge exercises test whether students can spot violated assumptions (interference) and use conditional exchangeability [@bradyneal].
instructor.extend: Introduce Fisher's randomization test: under the sharp null $Y_i(1) = Y_i(0)$ for every unit, all 70 assignments are known, so the observed $\hat\tau$ can be ranked among them to give an exact p-value. Then compare it with the large-sample interval for the ATE. Hernán and Robins develop the potential outcomes view with many examples [@hernan].

further.note: Chapters 1 to 3 define potential outcomes, exchangeability, positivity and consistency, and treat randomized experiments.
The potential outcomes chapter derives the decomposition of the simple difference in outcomes into effect and selection bias.
Chapter 2 introduces potential outcomes and the identification assumptions with small tables.

lessons.title: Identification before estimation
lessons.objective: Decide whether a causal quantity is fixed by a graph and an observational distribution, derive its estimand by truncated factorization or do-calculus, and only then estimate it.
lessons.big_idea: If two models that fit the same exact distribution disagree about an intervention, no estimator and no sample size can settle the question; identification depends on assumptions and distributions, estimation on data.
outcomes: Build two structural models, compatible with one graph, that share an observational distribution and disagree about $P(y \mid do(x))$, and use the pair to prove that the effect is not identified.
Derive $P(v \mid do(x))$ in a fully observed Markovian model by the truncated factorization, stating the positivity condition it needs.
Apply the three rules of do-calculus, checking each rule's separation condition in the correct mutilated graph.
Split the error of a causal estimate into an estimation part that shrinks with the sample size and an identification part that does not.

key_terms.meaning: A causal quantity is identifiable in a class of models if every two models in the class that produce the same observational distribution give it the same value.
A formula that writes the causal quantity as a function of the observational distribution, such as $\sum_z P(y \mid x, z)P(z)$.
A rule that turns a finite sample into a number that approximates an estimand, such as plugging in sample frequencies.
In a fully observed Markovian model, $P(v \mid do(x))$ is the usual product of $P(v_i \mid pa_i)$ with the factors of the intervened variables deleted.
A graph with some arrows deleted: $G_{\overline{X}}$ removes the arrows into $X$, $G_{\underline{X}}$ removes the arrows out of $X$.
Three rules that rewrite expressions containing $do(\cdot)$, each licensed by a d-separation statement in a mutilated graph.
Every conditional probability the formula uses is defined: the conditioning values occur with positive probability.

motivation: A health system holds ten million records. Among treated patients 80 percent recover; among untreated patients 20 percent do. A manager asks for another ten million records to pin down the effect of treatment. The request sounds reasonable and is useless. This lesson exhibits two models of the clinic that produce exactly the same table of frequencies, to every decimal place, while one says treatment raises recovery by 60 percentage points and the other says it does nothing at all. More records sharpen the table. They cannot choose between the models.

That is why causal inference has two stages with different jobs. **Identification** asks whether the assumptions (a graph, the absence of certain hidden causes, positivity) force a unique answer from the exact distribution, and if so, which formula of that distribution equals the causal quantity. **Estimation** then approximates that formula from finite data, with an uncertainty statement. Skipping the first stage produces confident intervals around the wrong number. The tools in this lesson, the truncated factorization and Pearl's do-calculus, are the machinery of the first stage [@pearlcausality; @pearl].

sections.heading: Two models that no data can tell apart

blocks.md:
Take binary $X$ (treatment) and $Y$ (recovery) with $P(X{=}1) = 0.5$, $P(Y{=}1 \mid X{=}1) = 0.8$ and $P(Y{=}1 \mid X{=}0) = 0.2$. Two structural models produce these numbers.

- **Model A** (treatment works): draw $X$ with $P(X{=}1) = 0.5$, then draw $Y$ from $P(y \mid x)$.
- **Model B** (treatment is inert): draw a hidden $U$ with $P(U{=}1) = 0.5$, draw $X$ with $P(X{=}1 \mid U{=}1) = 0.8$ and $P(X{=}1 \mid U{=}0) = 0.2$, and set $Y = U$.

In model B, $P(X{=}1, Y{=}1) = P(U{=}1)\,P(X{=}1 \mid U{=}1) = 0.5 \cdot 0.8 = 0.4$, the same as $0.5 \cdot 0.8$ in model A. The other three cells match too: $0.4, 0.1, 0.1, 0.4$ for $(x, y) = (0,0), (0,1), (1,0), (1,1)$.

blocks.mermaid:
graph LR
  U((U hidden)) -.-> X
  U -.-> Y
  X --> Y
blocks.caption: Both models fit this graph, with a hidden $U$ (dashed) pointing into $X$ and $Y$. Model A gives the dashed arrows no influence; model B gives the solid arrow $X \to Y$ no influence. A graph allows an arrow to matter; it does not force it to.

blocks.alt: Two small causal graphs on the left, model A with X to Y and model B with a hidden U pointing to X and Y. On the right, violet and cyan bars for P(x, y) are identical; after the arrows into X are cut, the bars for P(Y=1 given do(X=x)) differ.
blocks.caption: Observational bars are identical; interventional bars are not. The data fix the left chart and leave the right chart open.
blocks.describe: Model A (violet) is the graph $X \to Y$ with $Y \sim P(y \mid x)$. Model B (cyan) has a hidden $U$ pointing to $X$ and to $Y$, with $Y = U$. Each model draws its four bars for $P(x, y)$; the bars coincide at $0.4, 0.1, 0.1, 0.4$ and the label reads that they are identical for every $(x, y)$. Then the intervention $do(X{=}x)$ is performed by graph surgery: the arrow from $U$ into $X$ is cut, and $X$ becomes a square holding the set value $x$. The chart becomes $P(Y{=}1 \mid do(X{=}x))$: model A gives $0.2$ and $0.8$, model B gives $0.5$ and $0.5$. The effects are written as A: $0.8 - 0.2 = 0.6$ and B: $0.5 - 0.5 = 0$, and the closing line reads: same $P(x, y)$, different effects, so more data cannot decide.

blocks.latex: P_A(Y{=}1 \mid do(X{=}x)) = P(Y{=}1 \mid X{=}x), \qquad P_B(Y{=}1 \mid do(X{=}x)) = P(Y{=}1) = 0.5
blocks.label: eq-l4-07-two

blocks.md: In model A the mechanism for $Y$ is $P(y \mid x)$ itself, so setting $X$ by hand leaves it in force and the effect is $0.8 - 0.2 = 0.6$. In model B the mechanism for $Y$ is $Y = U$, and cutting the arrow $U \to X$ does not touch $U$, so the effect is $0.5 - 0.5 = 0$. Equation [](#eq-l4-07-two) is the whole disagreement.

blocks.title: Identifiability
blocks.label: def-l4-07-ident
blocks.md: Let $\mathcal{M}$ be a class of structural causal models over observed variables $V$, for example all models compatible with a graph $G$ (possibly with hidden variables) whose observational distribution is positive. A causal quantity $Q$, such as $P(y \mid do(x))$, is **identifiable in $\mathcal{M}$** if for all $M_1, M_2 \in \mathcal{M}$, equality of the observational distributions, $P_{M_1}(v) = P_{M_2}(v)$ for all $v$, implies $Q(M_1) = Q(M_2)$. Then $Q$ is a function of $P(v)$ alone, and any formula for that function is an **estimand** [@pearlcausality].

blocks.title: No identification in the bow graph
blocks.label: prop-l4-07-bow
blocks.md: In the class of models compatible with the graph $X \to Y$ plus a hidden common cause of $X$ and $Y$, the effect $P(Y{=}1 \mid do(X{=}1))$ is not identifiable, even when $P(x, y)$ is positive.

Models A and B above both belong to the class, produce the same positive joint $P(x, y)$, and give $P(Y{=}1 \mid do(X{=}1)) = 0.8$ and $0.5$ respectively. By the definition, one counterexample pair suffices.

blocks.caption: A hidden coin chooses model A with probability $\lambda$ and model B otherwise. Move $\lambda$: the observational bars never move, while $P(Y{=}1 \mid do(X{=}x))$ slides. The gray bars are the bounds that hold with no assumption at all.
blocks.describe: The first panel shows the fixed observational distribution: $0.4, 0.1, 0.1, 0.4$ for $(x, y) = (0,0), (0,1), (1,0), (1,1)$. The second panel shows $P(Y{=}1 \mid do(X{=}0)) = 0.5 - 0.3\lambda$ and $P(Y{=}1 \mid do(X{=}1)) = 0.5 + 0.3\lambda$ as cyan bars, the seen conditional probabilities $0.2$ and $0.8$ as orange diamonds, and gray intervals from $0.1$ to $0.6$ and from $0.4$ to $0.9$. At $\lambda = 1$ the bars meet the diamonds; at $\lambda = 0$ both bars are $0.5$. The effect is $0.6\lambda$.

blocks.title: A continuum, not a pair
blocks.md: The mixture with weight $\lambda$ is itself a structural model with the same graph (the coin is part of the hidden cause), and its effect is $0.6\lambda$. So every effect between $0$ and $0.6$ fits the data exactly. Without assumptions the possible values of $P(Y{=}1 \mid do(X{=}1))$ fill the interval $[P(X{=}1, Y{=}1),\; P(X{=}1, Y{=}1) + P(X{=}0)] = [0.4, 0.9]$ (exercise 3).

sections.heading: When the graph is enough: the truncated factorization

blocks.title: Markovian model and positivity
blocks.label: asm-l4-07-markov
blocks.md: The model is an SCM $V_i := f_i(PA_i, N_i)$ on an acyclic graph $G$, every $V_i$ is observed, and the noise terms $N_1, \dots, N_d$ are mutually independent (no hidden common causes). For the target $do(X{=}x)$, every parent configuration $pa_i$ that the formula below uses has $P(pa_i) > 0$.

blocks.title: Truncated factorization
blocks.label: thm-l4-07-trunc
blocks.md: Under the assumption above, for every $v$ consistent with $x$, $P(v \mid do(X{=}x)) = \prod_{i:\, V_i \notin X} P(v_i \mid pa_i)$, with the values $x$ substituted wherever $X$ appears among the parents, and $P(v \mid do(X{=}x)) = 0$ for $v$ inconsistent with $x$ [@pearlcausality; @peters].

This is Theorem [](#thm-l4-01-truncated), proved in [L4-01](#lesson-l4-01). In brief: $M_x$ is Markovian with respect to $G_{\overline{X}}$, and each remaining factor is the same number $P(f_i(pa_i, N_i) = v_i)$ in $M$ and in $M_x$, because in both models $PA_i$ depends only on noises that are independent of $N_i$; positivity makes the factor defined in $M$.

blocks.latex: P(z, y \mid do(x)) = P(z)\,P(y \mid x, z) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad P(y \mid do(x)) = \sum_z P(y \mid x, z)\,P(z)
blocks.label: eq-l4-07-trunc

blocks.md: For the graph $Z \to X \to Y$, $Z \to Y$, the observational factorization is $P(z)P(x \mid z)P(y \mid x, z)$. Deleting the factor $P(x \mid z)$ of the intervened variable and summing out $z$ gives [](#eq-l4-07-trunc), which is the backdoor formula of [L4-04](#lesson-l4-04). The theorem says more: in a Markovian model **every** interventional distribution is identified, because every factor $P(v_i \mid pa_i)$ is observable. Hidden common causes are exactly what breaks this, as model B showed.

With hidden variables some factors are unobservable, and the question becomes whether $P(y \mid do(x))$ can still be rewritten as an expression with no $do$ in it. Pearl's do-calculus gives three rewriting rules [@frontdoor; @pearlcausality]. Write $G_{\overline{X}}$ for $G$ with the arrows into $X$ removed, $G_{\underline{X}}$ for $G$ with the arrows out of $X$ removed, and $(Y \perp\!\!\!\perp Z \mid W)_{H}$ for d-separation in a graph $H$, as in [L4-02](#lesson-l4-02).

blocks.title: The rules of do-calculus (Pearl 1995)
blocks.label: thm-l4-07-docalc
blocks.md:
Let $X, Y, Z, W$ be disjoint sets of nodes in a causal graph $G$ (hidden variables allowed). Whenever the conditional probabilities are defined:

1. **Insert or delete an observation.** $P(y \mid do(x), z, w) = P(y \mid do(x), w)$ if $(Y \perp\!\!\!\perp Z \mid X, W)_{G_{\overline{X}}}$.
2. **Exchange an action and an observation.** $P(y \mid do(x), do(z), w) = P(y \mid do(x), z, w)$ if $(Y \perp\!\!\!\perp Z \mid X, W)_{G_{\overline{X}\underline{Z}}}$.
3. **Insert or delete an action.** $P(y \mid do(x), do(z), w) = P(y \mid do(x), w)$ if $(Y \perp\!\!\!\perp Z \mid X, W)_{G_{\overline{X}\,\overline{Z(W)}}}$, where $Z(W)$ is the set of $Z$-nodes that are not ancestors of any $W$-node in $G_{\overline{X}}$.

blocks.alt: A three-node graph Z to X, Z to Y, X to Y beside a derivation. Each step cuts arrows in the graph, states a d-separation, and rewrites one factor; it ends with the backdoor formula, the number 0.72 and the truncated factorization with one factor crossed out.
blocks.caption: Each rewrite is licensed by a d-separation in a cut graph: $G_{\overline{X}}$ for Rule 3, $G_{\underline{X}}$ for Rule 2.
blocks.describe: The graph has arrows $Z \to X$, $Z \to Y$ and $X \to Y$. The derivation starts with $P(y \mid do(x)) = \sum_z P(y \mid do(x), z)P(z \mid do(x))$, conditioning on $Z$ inside the intervened model. The arrow $Z \to X$ is cut to form $G_{\overline{X}}$; there the only path between $Z$ and $X$ is $Z \to Y \leftarrow X$, blocked at the collider $Y$, so $(Z \perp\!\!\!\perp X)_{G_{\overline{X}}}$ and Rule 3 turns $P(z \mid do(x))$ into $P(z)$. The arrow is restored and $X \to Y$ is cut to form $G_{\underline{X}}$; the only remaining path $X \leftarrow Z \to Y$ is blocked by conditioning on $Z$, so Rule 2 turns $P(y \mid do(x), z)$ into $P(y \mid x, z)$. The boxed result is $\sum_z P(y \mid x, z)P(z)$, and with the worked-example numbers $P(Y{=}1 \mid do(X{=}1)) = 0.6 \cdot 0.6 + 0.9 \cdot 0.4 = 0.72$. Finally the observational factorization $P(z)P(x \mid z)P(y \mid x, z)$ appears, the factor $P(x \mid z)$ is crossed out, and what remains is the same formula.

blocks.md: Read the animation as a proof. Line one is the law of total probability inside the model $M_x$. Line two uses Rule 3 with target $Z$, action $X$ and no $W$, so the graph to check is $G_{\overline{X}}$. Line three uses Rule 2 with target $Y$, action $X$ and $W = \{Z\}$, so the graph to check is $G_{\underline{X}}$. Every equality has a stated reason, and none of them is available in the bow graph of the first section: there, $X$ and $Y$ stay connected through the hidden $U$ in $G_{\underline{X}}$, so Rule 2 fails, and no other rule produces a $do$-free expression. The frontdoor formula of [L4-05](#lesson-l4-05) is derived the same way (exercise 5).

blocks.title: Not a license to delete do
blocks.md: A derivation that replaces $P(y \mid do(x))$ by $P(y \mid x)$ without checking $(Y \perp\!\!\!\perp X)_{G_{\underline{X}}}$ is wrong whenever a backdoor path is open; model B is a case where the replacement gives $0.8$ instead of $0.5$. State the graph, the target and the available distributions first, then justify each step. When the rules cannot remove every $do$, report that the quantity is not identified under these assumptions, and either add justified assumptions, collect experimental data, or report bounds.

blocks.mermaid:
graph LR
  Q[Causal question] --> G[Graph and assumptions]
  G --> I{Identified?}
  I -- yes --> E[Estimand as a formula of P]
  E --> S[Estimator on finite data]
  S --> R[Estimate with uncertainty]
  I -- no --> A[More assumptions, experiments, or bounds]
  A --> G
blocks.caption: The two stages. Only the right half involves data; the identification step is settled before any record is read.

blocks.md: Once an estimand $\theta(P)$ is in hand, estimation is ordinary statistics: replace $P$ by sample frequencies (a plug-in estimator), regress, or weight, and attach an uncertainty statement as in [L3-10](#lesson-l3-10). For an estimate $\hat\tau_n$ of a true effect $\tau$, the error splits into two parts:

blocks.latex: \hat\tau_n - \tau = \underbrace{\big(\hat\tau_n - \theta(P)\big)}_{\text{estimation error}} + \underbrace{\big(\theta(P) - \tau\big)}_{\text{identification gap}}
blocks.label: eq-l4-07-split

blocks.md: The first part shrinks as $n$ grows. For the observed contrast in the first section, $\hat\theta = \hat p(Y{=}1 \mid X{=}1) - \hat p(Y{=}1 \mid X{=}0)$ with $n$ records has standard error $\sqrt{0.8 \cdot 0.2/(0.5n) + 0.2 \cdot 0.8/(0.5n)} = 0.8/\sqrt{n}$. The second part does not depend on $n$ at all: it is $0$ if model A is true and $0.6 - 0 = 0.6$ if model B is true.

blocks.alt: Histograms of the observed contrast across 800 simulated studies, at sample sizes 25, 100, 400, 1600 and 6400, narrowing around 0.6. Dashed lines mark model B's effect 0 and model A's effect 0.6.
blocks.caption: Each histogram is 800 simulated studies of the same size. The spread follows $0.8/\sqrt{n}$; the center stays at 0.6 whichever model generated the data.
blocks.describe: A horizontal axis runs from $-0.2$ to $1.0$ for the estimated contrast $p(Y{=}1 \mid X{=}1) - p(Y{=}1 \mid X{=}0)$. A cyan dashed line at $0$ is labeled as model B's effect and a violet dashed line at $0.6$ as model A's effect. An orange histogram of 800 simulated studies appears for $n = 25$, with standard error $0.8/\sqrt{n} = 0.160$, and then morphs through $n = 100$ (SE $0.080$), $400$ ($0.040$), $1600$ ($0.020$) and $6400$ ($0.010$), becoming a narrow spike at $0.6$. The closing equation splits the error against model B's effect into an estimation part $(\hat\tau_n - 0.6)$ that tends to zero and an identification part $(0.6 - 0)$ that stays.

blocks.caption: Root-mean-square error against the true effect $0.5$ in the worked-example model, 300 simulated studies per sample size. The backdoor plug-in estimator targets the identified estimand, and its error falls like $1/\sqrt{n}$. The naive contrast estimates a different quantity, $0.81 - 0.16 = 0.65$, and its error levels off at the bias $0.15$.

blocks.explain: Exact arithmetic with fractions: the two models of the first section give the same joint distribution and different interventional answers, and the mixture with weight $\lambda$ has effect $0.6\lambda$ with the joint unchanged.

Estimation after identification. Simulate the worked-example model, compare the naive contrast with the backdoor plug-in estimate and its bootstrap interval, and cross-check the exact values with `qcai.science.causal`, which implements the same model. Then sample model B: the observed contrast settles at $0.6$ while the true effect is $0$.
blocks.source:
import numpy as np
from qcai import science

# Worked-example model: Z -> X -> Y and Z -> Y, all observed (Markovian)
rng = np.random.default_rng(2024)
n = 20000
z = rng.random(n) < 0.4
x = rng.random(n) < np.where(z, 0.7, 0.2)
y = rng.random(n) < 0.1 + 0.5 * x + 0.3 * z

def naive(x, y):
    return y[x].mean() - y[~x].mean()

def backdoor(x, y, z):
    """Plug-in estimate of sum_z P(z) [P(Y=1 | X=1, z) - P(Y=1 | X=0, z)]."""
    return sum(np.mean(z == v) * (y[x & (z == v)].mean() - y[~x & (z == v)].mean()) for v in (False, True))

exact = science.causal(prevalence=0.4, low=0.2, high=0.7, base=0.1, effect=0.5, confound=0.3)
print("exact: do(1) =", round(exact["do1"], 4), " do(0) =", round(exact["do0"], 4),
      " effect =", round(exact["ate"], 4), " naive contrast =", round(exact["observed"], 4))
est = backdoor(x, y, z)
boot = []
for b in range(200):                      # nonparametric bootstrap of the plug-in estimator
    i = rng.integers(0, n, n)
    boot.append(backdoor(x[i], y[i], z[i]))
lo, hi = np.percentile(boot, [2.5, 97.5])
print(f"n = {n}: naive {naive(x, y):.3f}, backdoor {est:.3f}  (95% bootstrap interval {lo:.3f} to {hi:.3f})")

# Model B from the first section: the observed contrast converges to 0.6, its true effect is 0
for m in (100, 10_000, 1_000_000):
    u = rng.random(m) < 0.5
    xb = rng.random(m) < np.where(u, 0.8, 0.2)
    print(f"model B, n = {m:>9,}: observed contrast {naive(xb, u):.3f}   true effect 0   SE about {0.8 / np.sqrt(m):.4f}")

blocks.title: What the bootstrap interval does and does not cover
blocks.md: The bootstrap interval describes sampling variability of the plug-in estimator, the first term of [](#eq-l4-07-split). It says nothing about the second term. An interval computed for the naive contrast in model B would be narrow, centered near $0.6$, and would miss the true effect $0$.

worked_example.title: Truncated factorization in a confounded model
worked_example.problem: In a Markovian model with graph $Z \to X \to Y$, $Z \to Y$ (all binary and observed), $P(Z{=}1) = 0.4$, $P(X{=}1 \mid Z{=}0) = 0.2$, $P(X{=}1 \mid Z{=}1) = 0.7$ and $P(Y{=}1 \mid X, Z) = 0.1 + 0.5X + 0.3Z$. Find $P(Y{=}1 \mid do(X{=}x))$ for $x = 0, 1$, the average effect, and the naive observed contrast.
steps: Identification: the model is Markovian, so by the truncated factorization $P(y \mid do(x)) = \sum_z P(z)P(y \mid x, z)$, equation [](#eq-l4-07-trunc). Positivity holds because every $(x, z)$ cell has positive probability.
Untreated: $P(Y{=}1 \mid do(X{=}0)) = 0.1 \cdot 0.6 + 0.4 \cdot 0.4 = 0.22$, so the average effect is $0.72 - 0.22 = 0.5$, the coefficient of $X$.
Comparison: the naive contrast $0.81 - 0.16 = 0.65$ overstates the effect by $0.15$ because treated units more often have $Z = 1$, which raises $Y$ on its own.
worked_example.result: $P(Y{=}1 \mid do(X{=}1)) = 0.72$, $P(Y{=}1 \mid do(X{=}0)) = 0.22$, average effect $0.5$; the naive contrast $0.65$ answers a different question.

exercises.prompt: Let $U$ be a fair binary variable. Model A' has $X = U$ and $Y = X$; model B' has $X = U$ and $Y = U$. Calculate $P(Y{=}1 \mid do(X{=}0))$ in each. Can an unlimited observational sample choose between their answers?
exercises.solution: Model A' gives $0$, because $Y$ copies the set value of $X$. Model B' gives $1/2$, because $Y = U$ and $U$ stays fair when $X$ is set. Both models produce only the pairs $(0,0)$ and $(1,1)$, each with probability $1/2$, so their observational distributions are identical and no observational sample, however large, can separate them. (This toy also violates positivity, since $X = 0, Y = 1$ never occurs; the models of the first section show that non-identification does not need that.)

exercises.prompt: In a Markovian chain $X \to M \to Y$ with $P(M{=}1 \mid X{=}1) = 0.7$, $P(Y{=}1 \mid M{=}1) = 0.9$ and $P(Y{=}1 \mid M{=}0) = 0.2$, use the truncated factorization to find $P(Y{=}1 \mid do(X{=}1))$. Why does it equal $P(Y{=}1 \mid X{=}1)$ here?
exercises.solution: Truncation deletes $P(x)$: $P(m, y \mid do(x)) = P(m \mid x)P(y \mid m)$. Summing over $m$, $P(Y{=}1 \mid do(X{=}1)) = 0.7 \cdot 0.9 + 0.3 \cdot 0.2 = 0.63 + 0.06 = 0.69$. Since $X$ has no parents, the deleted factor carries no confounding, and $P(y \mid x) = \sum_m P(m \mid x)P(y \mid m)$ is the same sum: $(Y \perp\!\!\!\perp X)_{G_{\underline{X}}}$ holds, so Rule 2 applies directly.

exercises.prompt: For the joint distribution of the first section, show that without any assumption about hidden variables $P(Y{=}1 \mid do(X{=}1))$ can be any value in $[0.4, 0.9]$ and nothing outside it, and deduce the interval for the effect $P(Y{=}1 \mid do(X{=}1)) - P(Y{=}1 \mid do(X{=}0))$.
exercises.solution: Write $Y_1$ for the outcome a unit would have under $do(X{=}1)$, so $P(Y{=}1 \mid do(X{=}1)) = P(Y_1 = 1)$. Split by the observed $X$: $P(Y_1{=}1) = P(Y_1{=}1, X{=}1) + P(Y_1{=}1, X{=}0)$. For units with $X = 1$ the intervention changes nothing, so $Y_1 = Y$ and the first term is $P(Y{=}1, X{=}1) = 0.4$. The second term concerns units never seen treated; the data constrain it only to $[0, P(X{=}0)] = [0, 0.5]$, and any value in that range is achieved by assigning $Y_1$ to those units accordingly. Hence $[0.4, 0.9]$. In the same way $P(Y{=}1 \mid do(X{=}0)) \in [P(X{=}0, Y{=}1), P(X{=}0, Y{=}1) + P(X{=}1)] = [0.1, 0.6]$. The effect lies in $[0.4 - 0.6, 0.9 - 0.1] = [-0.2, 0.8]$, an interval of width $1$, which always contains $0$ for binary $Y$ without further assumptions.

exercises.prompt: Let a hidden coin $S$ with $P(S{=}1) = \lambda$ choose the mechanisms: if $S = 1$ the unit follows model A, if $S = 0$ it follows model B. Show that the joint $P(x, y)$ does not depend on $\lambda$ and that the effect is $0.6\lambda$. Which graph is this model compatible with?
exercises.solution: Conditioning on $S$, $P(x, y) = \lambda P_A(x, y) + (1 - \lambda)P_B(x, y) = P(x, y)$, since $P_A = P_B$. Under $do(X{=}x)$ the coin is untouched, so $P(Y{=}1 \mid do(x)) = \lambda P_A(Y{=}1 \mid do(x)) + (1 - \lambda)P_B(Y{=}1 \mid do(x))$, which gives $\lambda(0.8 - 0.2) + (1 - \lambda)(0.5 - 0.5) = 0.6\lambda$. The hidden pair $(S, U)$ points into both $X$ and $Y$, and $X$ points into $Y$, so the model fits the bow graph. Every effect in $[0, 0.6]$ is therefore compatible with the same data and graph.

exercises.prompt: Frontdoor graph: $X \to M \to Y$ with a hidden $U$ pointing into $X$ and $Y$ and no other arrows. Using only the three rules (state the graph and the separation for each use), derive $P(y \mid do(x)) = \sum_m P(m \mid x)\sum_{x'} P(y \mid m, x')P(x')$.
exercises.solution: (a) $P(m \mid do(x)) = P(m \mid x)$ by Rule 2: in $G_{\underline{X}}$ (delete $X \to M$) the only path from $X$ to $M$ is $X \leftarrow U \to Y \leftarrow M$, blocked at the collider $Y$. (b) $P(y \mid do(m)) = \sum_{x'} P(y \mid do(m), x')P(x' \mid do(m))$. Rule 3 gives $P(x' \mid do(m)) = P(x')$: in $G_{\overline{M}}$ (delete $X \to M$) the path $X \leftarrow U \to Y \leftarrow M$ is blocked at $Y$. Rule 2 gives $P(y \mid do(m), x') = P(y \mid m, x')$: in $G_{\underline{M}}$ (delete $M \to Y$) the only path $M \leftarrow X \leftarrow U \to Y$ is blocked by conditioning on the noncollider $X$. (c) $P(y \mid do(x)) = \sum_m P(y \mid do(x), m)P(m \mid do(x))$. Rule 2 gives $P(y \mid do(x), m) = P(y \mid do(x), do(m))$: in $G_{\overline{X}\underline{M}}$ (delete $U \to X$ and $M \to Y$) $M$ is connected only to $X$, and $X$ has no path to $Y$. Rule 3 gives $P(y \mid do(x), do(m)) = P(y \mid do(m))$: here $W$ is empty, so $Z(W) = \{X\}$ and the graph to check is $G_{\overline{M}\,\overline{X}}$ (delete $X \to M$ and $U \to X$), where $X$ has no edges at all. Substituting (a) and (b) into (c) gives the frontdoor formula.

check.question: Two causal models produce the same exact observational distribution but different values of $P(y \mid do(x))$. What can settle which value is right?
options: A larger observational sample of the same variables
Additional justified assumptions or informative interventions
check.explanation: Both models fit the exact distribution, so more data, narrower intervals and better-fitting regressions all leave the disagreement in place. Only information that the models treat differently, such as experimental data or a justified restriction that rules one out, can decide.

check.question: In a Markovian model with graph $Z \to X \to Y$ and $Z \to Y$, what is $P(z, y \mid do(x))$?
check.explanation: The truncated factorization deletes the factor $P(x \mid z)$ of the intervened variable and keeps the other factors with $x$ substituted. Using $P(z \mid x)$ would reintroduce the confounding by $Z$.

check.question: Which d-separation licenses rewriting $P(y \mid do(x), z)$ as $P(y \mid x, z)$?
options: $(Y \perp\!\!\!\perp X \mid Z)$ in $G_{\underline{X}}$, the graph without arrows out of $X$
$(Y \perp\!\!\!\perp X \mid Z)$ in $G_{\overline{X}}$, the graph without arrows into $X$
check.explanation: This is Rule 2, exchanging an action for an observation. Removing the arrows out of $X$ leaves only the backdoor paths; if $Z$ blocks all of them, seeing $X = x$ and setting $X = x$ give the same conditional distribution of $Y$.

check.question: In the graph $Z \to X \to Y$, $Z \to Y$ with all variables observed, which set satisfies the backdoor criterion for the effect of $X$ on $Y$?
check.explanation: The backdoor path $X \leftarrow Z \to Y$ is open without adjustment; conditioning on $Z$ blocks it, and $Z$ is not a descendant of $X$. So $\{Z\}$ is valid and gives $\sum_z P(y \mid x, z)P(z)$.

misconceptions.claim: "With enough data the causal effect will reveal itself."
misconceptions.correction: Data converge to the observational distribution. If two models share that distribution and disagree about the effect, as models A and B do, the limit of infinite data still leaves the effect undetermined. Sample size controls the estimation error, not the identification gap.

misconceptions.claim: "A model that predicts the data well gives the right causal answers."
misconceptions.correction: Models A and B predict every observational frequency perfectly. Predictive fit tests the observational distribution only; causal answers depend on the mechanism assumptions that fit cannot check.

misconceptions.claim: "Do-calculus lets you drop the do operator once you condition on enough variables."
misconceptions.correction: Each rule applies only when a specific d-separation holds in a specific mutilated graph. Conditioning on a collider or a descendant of $X$ can open paths and make the rewrite false.

lessons.connect: Identification of an effect from a known graph is the first half of the story. [L4-08](#lesson-l4-08) asks the mirror question, whether the graph itself is identified from data, and finds the same pattern: observationally equivalent graphs that only assumptions or interventions can separate. [L4-09](#lesson-l4-09) climbs to counterfactuals, where even interventional data can leave answers unidentified, and [L4-10](#lesson-l4-10) applies identification to transport between populations. The quantum causal models of Level 6 face the same split between what a causal structure implies and what statistics can reveal.
lessons.caution: This lesson treats nonparametric identification: no functional form is assumed beyond the graph. Parametric assumptions (linearity, an instrumental variable with a monotone effect, a known noise distribution) can identify more, and they are assumptions that need their own justification. The truncated factorization needs independent noises and positivity; with near-violations of positivity an identified estimand can still be estimated very poorly. The do-calculus is known to be complete for identifying $P(y \mid do(x))$ from the observational distribution in graphs with hidden variables, a result due to Shpitser and Pearl (2006) and to Huang and Valtorta (2006) [@huangvaltorta2006]. The simulations are illustrations, not empirical evidence about any treatment.

instructor.why: Students often meet causal inference as a list of estimators and adjustment recipes. Putting identification first, with a concrete pair of models that no data can separate, makes the role of assumptions unavoidable and gives the do-calculus a clear purpose [@pearlcausality; @hernan].
teaching_notes: Before showing model B, ask students to propose any model that reproduces the table $0.4, 0.1, 0.1, 0.4$ with zero effect. Most find a confounder story within minutes; the formal definition then reads as a summary of what they did.
Use the interactive to show that the gray no-assumption bounds always contain both the mixture's answers and $0$; ask what assumption would shrink the interval to a point.
In the do-calculus derivation, make students name the target, the action and $W$ before choosing the mutilated graph. Most errors come from checking the separation in the original graph.
Pair the error decomposition [](#eq-l4-07-split) with the figure: confidence intervals address only the first term.
instructor.assessment: The challenge exercise (frontdoor by the three rules) tests whether students can apply each rule with the correct graph. The stretch exercise on bounds tests whether they can reason about what data leave unconstrained. The check questions cover the core definitions.
instructor.extend: Show that the bow graph's effect becomes identified if an instrument $I \to X$ with a linear outcome model is assumed, and discuss which part of that is an assumption. For a full treatment of identification algorithms with hidden variables, see Pearl's *Causality*, chapter 3 [@pearlcausality], and Bareinboim's roadmap [@bareinboim].

further.note: Chapter 3 defines identifiability, proves the truncated factorization and presents the do-calculus.
Part I separates identification conditions (exchangeability, positivity, consistency) from estimation.
Chapter 6 treats interventions and adjustment in multivariate SCMs.

lessons.title: Causal discovery and its limits
lessons.objective: Explain what conditional independences can and cannot reveal about a causal graph: characterize Markov equivalence, run the PC algorithm, and recognize how faithfulness violations, test errors and modeling assumptions limit discovery.
lessons.big_idea: Under the Markov and faithfulness assumptions, perfect independence tests reveal a graph's skeleton and its v-structures and nothing more; every further arrow needs extra assumptions, interventions, or restrictions on the mechanisms.
outcomes: Decide whether two DAGs are Markov equivalent with the Verma-Pearl criterion, and list the members of a small equivalence class.
Run the PC algorithm by hand (skeleton search, collider orientation, Meek's rules) and state the assumptions under which it returns the correct pattern.
Construct a faithfulness violation by path cancellation and predict the wrong graph that PC then reports.
Explain what a continuous method such as NOTEARS adds (a smooth acyclicity constraint) and which assumptions it leaves in place.

key_terms.meaning: Every d-separation in the graph holds as a conditional independence in the distribution.
The converse: every conditional independence in the distribution comes from a d-separation in the graph, not from a numerical coincidence.
The undirected graph obtained by forgetting the direction of every edge.
An unshielded collider $a \to m \leftarrow c$ in which $a$ and $c$ are not adjacent.
The set of DAGs that imply exactly the same conditional independences.
A partially directed graph that represents an equivalence class: arrows shared by every member are directed, the rest are undirected.
No unmeasured variable is a common cause of two measured variables.

motivation: Three variables, thousands of records, and one clean finding: $X$ and $Z$ are dependent, but independent once $Y$ is known. A chain $X \to Y \to Z$ explains this. So does $Z \to Y \to X$, and so does the fork $X \leftarrow Y \to Z$. The three stories disagree about what happens if you intervene on $X$: in the first $Z$ moves, in the other two it does not. No test of independence, on any amount of data, can separate them, because all three graphs imply exactly the same independences.

Causal discovery algorithms, available in libraries such as causal-learn [@causallearn], promise graphs from data. This lesson measures what they can actually deliver. With perfect tests and the right assumptions they return an equivalence class, often with many arrows left undecided. When two causal paths happen to cancel, or a test misses a weak dependence, they return a wrong graph with no warning. And an optimizer that outputs a single DAG has solved its objective, which is not the same as finding the mechanism. As in [L4-07](#lesson-l4-07), the limits are limits of identification, not of sample size.

blocks.md: In [L4-02](#lesson-l4-02) you read independences off a graph: d-separation implies conditional independence under the Markov condition. Discovery runs the other way, from independences to a graph, and needs the converse too.

blocks.title: Markov condition and faithfulness
blocks.label: def-l4-08-faithful
blocks.md: Let $P$ be a distribution over the variables of a DAG $G$. $P$ is **Markov** to $G$ if every d-separation $(A \perp\!\!\!\perp B \mid S)_G$ implies $A \perp\!\!\!\perp B \mid S$ in $P$. $P$ is **faithful** to $G$ if the converse holds: every conditional independence $A \perp\!\!\!\perp B \mid S$ in $P$ implies the d-separation $(A \perp\!\!\!\perp B \mid S)_G$. A distribution that is both Markov and faithful to $G$ satisfies equation [](#eq-l4-08-faith) below.

blocks.latex: (A \perp\!\!\!\perp B \mid S)_G \iff A \perp\!\!\!\perp B \mid S \text{ in } P \quad \text{for all disjoint } A, B, S
blocks.label: eq-l4-08-faith

blocks.md: Under [](#eq-l4-08-faith) the independence model of $P$ is exactly the d-separation model of $G$. The question becomes: which graphs share a d-separation model?

blocks.alt: Three nodes X, Y, Z in a row. The arrows flip from chain to reverse chain to fork while the listed independences stay the same; then the collider X to Y from Z swaps them. Mini graphs group the first three into one class and the collider into its own.
blocks.caption: Flipping arrows on the skeleton $X - Y - Z$: three orientations imply the same independences; only the collider changes them.
blocks.describe: The skeleton $X - Y - Z$ is oriented as the chain $X \to Y \to Z$, and the implied statements appear: $X \not\perp\!\!\!\perp Z$ and $X \perp\!\!\!\perp Z \mid Y$. The arrows then flip to the reverse chain $X \leftarrow Y \leftarrow Z$ and to the fork $X \leftarrow Y \to Z$; each time the statements flash and a label says they are the same. When the arrows become the collider $X \to Y \leftarrow Z$, the statements change to $X \perp\!\!\!\perp Z$ and $X \not\perp\!\!\!\perp Z \mid Y$. Small copies of the three equivalent graphs appear in one box with the shared pattern $X - Y - Z$, the collider sits in a box of its own, and the closing line states the theorem: Markov equivalent if and only if same skeleton and same v-structures (Verma and Pearl).

blocks.title: Markov equivalence (Verma and Pearl)
blocks.label: thm-l4-08-vp
blocks.md: Two DAGs on the same variables imply the same d-separations, that is, they are Markov equivalent, if and only if they have the same skeleton and same v-structures [@pearlcausality; @spirtes; @peters].

*Only if.* (i) Adjacent nodes are d-separated by no set, since the edge is a path with no interior node. Nonadjacent nodes $a, b$ are d-separated by some set: if $b$ is not an ancestor of $a$ (relabel otherwise), then $a$ is a non-descendant of $b$ and the parents of $b$ d-separate $b$ from all its non-descendants. So adjacency means "no separating set", a property of the independence model, and equivalent DAGs have the same skeleton. (ii) Take an unshielded triple $a - m - c$. If $m$ is a noncollider (chain or fork), the path $a - m - c$ is open unless $m$ is conditioned on, so $m$ belongs to every separating set of $a$ and $c$. If $m$ is a collider $a \to m \leftarrow c$, label so that $c$ is not an ancestor of $a$; then the parents of $c$ separate $a$ and $c$, and $m$, a child of $c$, is not among them. So "$m$ lies in every separating set of $a, c$" holds exactly for noncolliders, and equivalent DAGs have the same v-structures.

*If* (sketch). One shows that whenever a path d-connects two nodes given $S$ in one DAG, some path d-connects them given $S$ in the other; the argument walks along the path and uses the shared skeleton and shared unshielded colliders to replace each segment. The theorem is due to Verma and Pearl (1990) and is stated, with references to the full proof, in Pearl's *Causality* and in Spirtes, Glymour and Scheines [@pearlcausality; @spirtes].

blocks.caption: The four DAGs on the skeleton $X - Y - Z$. Chain, reverse chain and fork (violet, dashed box) form one class with pattern $X - Y - Z$; the collider (red) is a class of one with pattern $X \to Y \leftarrow Z$. Every claim in the figure is checked by d-separation in the figure code.

blocks.explain: Check the Verma-Pearl theorem by brute force: enumerate every DAG on three and on four labeled nodes, group them once by skeleton and v-structures and once by their full lists of d-separations, and confirm that the two groupings coincide.

blocks.title: PC (Spirtes and Glymour)
blocks.label: alg-l4-08-pc
blocks.md:
Input: variables $V$ and a conditional-independence test. Output: a pattern.

1. **Skeleton.** Start from the complete undirected graph. For $\ell = 0, 1, 2, \dots$: for each adjacent pair $a, b$ and each set $S$ of $\ell$ current neighbors of $a$ other than $b$, if the test accepts $a \perp\!\!\!\perp b \mid S$, delete the edge and record $\mathrm{sep}(a, b) = S$. Stop when no node has more than $\ell$ other neighbors.
2. **Colliders.** For each unshielded triple $a - m - c$ with $m \notin \mathrm{sep}(a, c)$, orient $a \to m \leftarrow c$.
3. **Propagation (Meek's rules).** Repeat until nothing changes. Rule 1: if $r \to p - q$ and $r, q$ are not adjacent, orient $p \to q$ (otherwise a new collider would appear). Rule 2: if $p \to r \to q$ and $p - q$, orient $p \to q$ (otherwise a cycle). Rule 3: if $p - r \to q$, $p - s \to q$, $r, s$ nonadjacent and $p - q$, orient $p \to q$ [@meek1995; @spirtes].

blocks.alt: Five nodes V, W, X, Y, Z start fully connected. Edges turn red and vanish as separation statements are listed; then W to Y and X to Y become red arrows, Y to Z becomes a blue arrow, and V to W and V to X stay undirected.
blocks.caption: PC on data from $V \to W$, $V \to X$, $W \to Y$, $X \to Y$, $Y \to Z$, driven by a d-separation oracle: five deletions, one collider, one Meek step.
blocks.describe: The five nodes start with all ten edges. No pair is independent without conditioning, so nothing is removed at size 0. Then five edges are deleted one by one as their tests are written: $V \perp\!\!\!\perp Z \mid Y$, $W \perp\!\!\!\perp X \mid V$, $W \perp\!\!\!\perp Z \mid Y$, $X \perp\!\!\!\perp Z \mid Y$ and, with a two-element set, $V \perp\!\!\!\perp Y \mid W, X$. The skeleton $V - W$, $V - X$, $W - Y$, $X - Y$, $Y - Z$ remains. In the triple $W - Y - X$, $Y$ is not in $\mathrm{sep}(W, X) = \{V\}$, so the edges become red arrows $W \to Y \leftarrow X$. Meek rule 1 applies to $W \to Y - Z$ with $W$ and $Z$ not adjacent, giving the blue arrow $Y \to Z$. The edges $V - W$ and $V - X$ flash: they stay undirected, and the output is a pattern.

blocks.md: The run in the animation is the actual output of the algorithm on the true graph's d-separations. The key deletions are $W \perp\!\!\!\perp X \mid V$ (the fork at $V$ is blocked by conditioning on $V$) and $V \perp\!\!\!\perp Y \mid W, X$, which needs both mediating paths blocked at once. The undirected edges $V - W$ and $V - X$ are genuine ambiguity: orienting them as $V \to W, V \to X$ or $W \to V \to X$ or $X \to V \to W$ gives three DAGs with the same skeleton and the same single v-structure, while $W \to V \leftarrow X$ would add a v-structure and is excluded.

blocks.mermaid:
graph TD
