blocks.title: Conditional and average treatment effects
blocks.label: def-l4-10-cate
blocks.md: For a binary treatment $T$ with potential outcomes $Y(1), Y(0)$ and pre-treatment covariates $Z$, the **conditional average treatment effect** is $\tau(z) = E[Y(1) - Y(0) \mid Z = z]$ and the **average treatment effect** is $\mathrm{ATE} = E[\tau(Z)]$. Write $\mu_t(z) = E[Y \mid T = t, Z = z]$ for the outcome regressions and $e(z) = P(T = 1 \mid Z = z)$ for the propensity score.

blocks.title: Identification assumptions
blocks.label: asm-l4-10-ident
blocks.md: (i) **Consistency**: $Y = Y(T)$. (ii) **Conditional exchangeability**: $Y(t) \perp\!\!\!\perp T \mid Z$ for $t = 0, 1$; in graph terms, $Z$ satisfies the backdoor criterion. (iii) **Positivity**: $0 < e(z) < 1$ for every $z$ with positive probability [@hernan].

blocks.title: Two identification formulas
blocks.label: prop-l4-10-ident
blocks.md: Under the identification assumptions, $\tau(z) = \mu_1(z) - \mu_0(z)$, and the ATE equals both $E[\mu_1(Z) - \mu_0(Z)]$ and the weighting formula [](#eq-l4-10-ipw).

blocks.latex: \mathrm{ATE} = E\left[\frac{T\,Y}{e(Z)} - \frac{(1 - T)\,Y}{1 - e(Z)}\right]
blocks.label: eq-l4-10-ipw

blocks.md: By exchangeability and then consistency, $E[Y(t) \mid Z = z] = E[Y(t) \mid T = t, Z = z] = E[Y \mid T = t, Z = z] = \mu_t(z)$, which needs $P(T = t \mid Z = z) > 0$ (positivity). Subtract and average over $Z$. For the weighting formula, $E[TY/e(Z) \mid Z] = E[T\,Y(1) \mid Z]/e(Z) = e(Z)\,E[Y(1) \mid Z]/e(Z) = E[Y(1) \mid Z]$, using consistency, then exchangeability to factor $E[T\,Y(1) \mid Z] = E[T \mid Z]\,E[Y(1) \mid Z]$. The control term is the same with $1 - T$.

blocks.title: A flexible learner does not create identification
blocks.md: Gradient boosting, random forests, or neural networks can fit $\mu_t$ and $e$ well, and that matters for estimation. None of them can tell you whether $Z$ blocks every backdoor path. If an unmeasured confounder exists, a perfect fit of $\mu_1 - \mu_0$ converges to the wrong number.

The plug-in estimator averages $\hat\mu_1(Z_i) - \hat\mu_0(Z_i)$ and is only as good as the outcome model. The inverse probability weighted (IPW) estimator is the sample version of [](#eq-l4-10-ipw) and is only as good as the propensity model. The augmented IPW estimator of Robins, Rotnitzky and Zhao combines them [@robins1994]:

blocks.latex: \hat\tau_{\mathrm{AIPW}} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left[\hat\mu_1(Z_i) - \hat\mu_0(Z_i) + \frac{T_i\,(Y_i - \hat\mu_1(Z_i))}{\hat e(Z_i)} - \frac{(1 - T_i)(Y_i - \hat\mu_0(Z_i))}{1 - \hat e(Z_i)}\right]
blocks.label: eq-l4-10-aipw

blocks.title: Double robustness
blocks.label: prop-l4-10-dr
blocks.md: Suppose the identification assumptions hold, and let $m_1, m_0, \tilde e$ be fixed functions (the limits of the fitted models) with $0 < \tilde e < 1$. Let $\psi = m_1(Z) - m_0(Z) + T(Y - m_1(Z))/\tilde e(Z) - (1 - T)(Y - m_0(Z))/(1 - \tilde e(Z))$. If either $m_t = \mu_t$ for $t = 0, 1$, or $\tilde e = e$, then $E[\psi] = \mathrm{ATE}$.

Condition on $Z$. Since $E[T(Y - m_1(Z)) \mid Z] = e(Z)\,(\mu_1(Z) - m_1(Z))$, the treated part of $\psi$ has conditional mean $m_1 + e\,(\mu_1 - m_1)/\tilde e$. If $m_1 = \mu_1$ the correction vanishes and the mean is $\mu_1$. If $\tilde e = e$ the mean is $m_1 + \mu_1 - m_1 = \mu_1$. The control part is the same with $1 - e$ and $1 - \tilde e$. In both cases $E[\psi \mid Z] = \mu_1(Z) - \mu_0(Z)$, and averaging over $Z$ gives the ATE by the identification proposition.

blocks.caption: Simulated data with true ATE 2: $Z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1)$, $P(T = 1 \mid Z) = 1/(1 + e^{-1.5Z})$, $Y = 2T + Z + 0.5Z^3 + \text{noise}$. A wrong outcome model ignores $Z$; a wrong propensity model is a constant. Plug-in fails when the outcome model is wrong, IPW fails when the propensity model is wrong, and AIPW fails only when both are wrong.

blocks.explain: The simulation behind the figure. Each nuisance model is fitted either correctly or with $Z$ left out; the table shows which estimators survive which mistake. All three estimators collapse to the naive, confounded contrast when both models ignore $Z$.
blocks.source:
import numpy as np

def logistic_fit(Z, t, iters=25):
    # Newton's method for a logistic regression of t on the columns of Z
    b = np.zeros(Z.shape[1])
    for _ in range(iters):
        p = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-Z @ b))
        b += np.linalg.solve(Z.T @ (Z * (p * (1 - p))[:, None]), Z.T @ (t - p))
    return 1 / (1 + np.exp(-Z @ b))

def ols_predict(F, y, F_new):
    return F_new @ np.linalg.lstsq(F, y, rcond=None)[0]

rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
n = 20_000
z = rng.normal(0, 1, n)
t = (rng.random(n) < 1 / (1 + np.exp(-1.5 * z))).astype(float)   # confounded treatment
y = 2 * t + z + 0.5 * z ** 3 + rng.normal(0, 1, n)               # true ATE = 2

one = np.ones(n)
props = {'right': logistic_fit(np.column_stack([one, z]), t),     # correct propensity model
         'wrong': np.full(n, t.mean())}                           # ignores Z
outcomes = {}
for name, F in {'right': np.column_stack([one, z, z ** 3]), 'wrong': one[:, None]}.items():
    outcomes[name] = (ols_predict(F[t == 1], y[t == 1], F),       # fitted E[Y | T=1, Z]
                      ols_predict(F[t == 0], y[t == 0], F))       # fitted E[Y | T=0, Z]

print('naive contrast', round(y[t == 1].mean() - y[t == 0].mean(), 3))
for om in ('right', 'wrong'):
    for pm in ('right', 'wrong'):
        m1, m0 = outcomes[om]
        e = props[pm]
        plug = np.mean(m1 - m0)
        ipw = np.mean(t * y / e - (1 - t) * y / (1 - e))
        aipw = np.mean(m1 - m0 + t * (y - m1) / e - (1 - t) * (y - m0) / (1 - e))
        print(f'outcome {om:5s} propensity {pm:5s} | plug-in {plug:6.3f}  IPW {ipw:6.3f}  AIPW {aipw:6.3f}')

blocks.title: In practice
blocks.md: Real analyses fit $\hat\mu_t$ and $\hat e$ with flexible learners, usually on separate folds of the data from the ones used to average (cross-fitting [@chernozhukov2018]), and check for propensity scores near 0 or 1, where positivity is in doubt and the weights explode. Libraries such as DoWhy organize the steps of target, graph, identification, estimation, and refutation [@dowhy]. Double robustness protects against one wrong nuisance model, not against a wrong graph.

A study in a source population $\pi$ estimated effects; a decision is needed in a target population $\pi^*$. Write $P$ for the source and $P^*$ for the target. The question is which parts of the causal model are shared [@pearlbareinboim2014; @bareinboim].

blocks.title: Selection diagram
blocks.label: def-l4-10-selection
blocks.md: A **selection diagram** is the causal graph shared by $\pi$ and $\pi^*$, plus selection nodes $S$. An arrow $S \to V$ means the mechanism of $V$ (or the distribution of its background variable) may differ between the two populations. The absence of an arrow from $S$ into $V$ is an assumption: the mechanism of $V$ is the same in both.

blocks.mermaid:
graph TD
  S["S (population)"] --> Z
  Z --> X
  Z --> Y
  X --> Y
blocks.caption: The selection diagram of the running example. The two populations differ only in the distribution of the effect modifier $Z$ (say an age group); the mechanisms of treatment $X$ and outcome $Y$ are shared. An arrow from $S$ into $Y$ would break the transport formula.

blocks.title: Transport formula for covariate shift
blocks.label: thm-l4-10-transport
blocks.md: Suppose (a) in the selection diagram, $S$ points only into $Z$, and $Z$ separates $S$ from $Y$ once the arrows into $X$ are removed, that is $Y \perp\!\!\!\perp S \mid Z$ in that graph (this holds in the diagram above); (b) $Z$ is not affected by $X$; (c) $Z$ satisfies the backdoor criterion for $(X, Y)$ in the source; and (d) positivity: $P(x, z) > 0$ in the source for every $z$ with $P^*(z) > 0$. Then [](#eq-l4-10-transport) holds, and for effects $\mathrm{ATE}^* = \sum_z \tau(z)\,P^*(z)$ with $\tau$ estimated in the source [@pearlbareinboim2014; @bareinboim].

blocks.latex: P^*(y \mid do(x)) = \sum_z P(y \mid do(x), z)\,P^*(z) = \sum_z P(y \mid x, z)\,P^*(z)
blocks.label: eq-l4-10-transport

blocks.md: In the target, $P^*(y \mid do(x)) = \sum_z P^*(y \mid do(x), z)\,P^*(z \mid do(x))$. By (b), $Z$ is not a descendant of $X$, so $P^*(z \mid do(x)) = P^*(z)$. By (a), $Y \perp\!\!\!\perp S \mid Z$ in the graph with the arrows into $X$ removed, which is the graph of the action $do(x)$, so $P^*(y \mid do(x), z) = P(y \mid do(x), z)$: the stratum-specific causal law is shared. (Pointing only into $Z$ is not enough on its own: if a hidden variable affected both $Z$ and $Y$, conditioning on $Z$ would open the path $S \to Z \leftarrow L \to Y$.) By (c) and (d), $P(y \mid do(x), z) = P(y \mid x, z)$ is estimable from the source in every stratum the target needs.

blocks.alt: A selection diagram with S pointing into Z, two bars for stratum effects 1 and 3, and a row of ten dots that changes from five and five to eight and two; the average effect changes from 2 to 1.4. Then an arrow from S into Y appears and the formula is crossed out.
blocks.caption: Same stratum effects, new weights: $0.5(1) + 0.5(3) = 2$ in the source becomes $0.8(1) + 0.2(3) = 1.4$ in the target. An arrow from $S$ into $Y$ breaks the argument.
blocks.describe: The selection diagram shows $Z \to X$, $Z \to Y$, $X \to Y$ and a square node $S$ with an arrow into $Z$, labeled as marking where source and target differ. Bars show the stratum effects $\tau(z)$: 1 for $z = 0$ and 3 for $z = 1$. A row of ten dots shows the source mix, five of each stratum, with $\tau_{\text{source}} = 0.5(1) + 0.5(3) = 2$. The arrow from $S$ flashes, the dots recolor to eight and two (the target mix), and the formula transforms term by term into $\tau_{\text{target}} = 0.8(1) + 0.2(3) = 1.4$. Finally a red arrow from $S$ into $Y$ appears, the formula is crossed out, and a caption says that if $S$ points into $Y$, the stratum effects may differ too.

blocks.caption: Move the slider to change the share of stratum $z = 1$ in the target. The stratum effects stay at 1 and 3; the transported average effect moves along the line $1 + 2p$.
blocks.describe: The first panel compares the source mix (0.5 and 0.5, gray) with the target mix ($1 - p$ and $p$, violet) for the two strata, labeled with their effects 1 and 3. The second panel plots the transported ATE $1 + 2p$ against the target share $p$, with a dashed line at the source ATE 2 and a marker at the chosen $p$: 1.4 at $p = 0.2$, 2 at $p = 0.5$, 3 at $p = 1$.

blocks.explain: A source study with confounded treatment. Backdoor adjustment within strata recovers $\tau = (1, 3)$; reweighting by the target mix gives 1.4, which matches the target's true effect because the model satisfies the theorem's conditions. The last line breaks condition (a) by changing the mechanism of $Y$ in the target: the formula still says 1.4, but the truth is 2.4.
blocks.source:
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)

def population(n, p_z1):
    # Z: effect modifier and confounder; X: treatment; Y := X(1 + 2Z) + Z + noise
    z = rng.random(n) < p_z1
    x = rng.random(n) < np.where(z, 0.7, 0.3)      # treatment depends on Z (confounding)
    y = x * (1 + 2 * z) + z + rng.normal(0, 1, n)
    return z, x, y

def stratum_effects(z, x, y):
    # backdoor adjustment within each stratum of Z
    return np.array([y[(z == k) & x].mean() - y[(z == k) & ~x].mean() for k in (0, 1)])

z, x, y = population(200_000, p_z1=0.5)            # source study
tau = stratum_effects(z, x, y)
print('stratum effects in the source   ', tau.round(3))
print('naive treated-untreated contrast', round(y[x].mean() - y[~x].mean(), 3))
print('source ATE   0.5 tau0 + 0.5 tau1', round(0.5 * tau[0] + 0.5 * tau[1], 3))
w_target = np.array([0.8, 0.2])                     # P*(Z = z), measured in the target
print('transported  0.8 tau0 + 0.2 tau1', round(w_target @ tau, 3))

# compare with the target's true effect, known here because we wrote the model
zt = rng.random(200_000) < 0.2
print('true target ATE                 ', round(np.mean(1 + 2 * zt), 3))
# if the mechanism of Y also differs (S -> Y), the same formula is wrong
print('target ATE when S -> Y adds 1   ', round(np.mean(1 + 2 * zt + 1.0), 3), '(formula still says 1.4)')

blocks.title: When transport fails
blocks.md: If $S$ points into $Y$ (the outcome mechanism differs, for example because care differs between hospitals), the source data are compatible with any target effect, and transport needs target outcome data or further assumptions. The same holds if an unmeasured effect modifier is distributed differently, or if the target contains strata never seen in the source, where positivity fails and the formula would extrapolate.

A predictor can be accurate for the wrong reason. In the model [](#eq-l4-10-shift), $X_c$ is a cause of $Y$ and $X_s$ is an effect of $Y$ whose mechanism depends on the environment $e$. Training happens at $e = 1$.

blocks.latex: X_c \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1), \qquad Y := X_c + N_Y, \qquad X_s := e\,Y + N_s, \qquad N_Y \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 1),\ N_s \sim \mathcal{N}(0, 0.25)
blocks.label: eq-l4-10-shift

blocks.md: At $e = 1$, least squares on both features gives $\hat Y = 0.2X_c + 0.8X_s$ with mean squared error 0.2: given $X_c$, $Y$ has variance 1, and $X_s$ is a reading of $Y$ with noise variance 0.25, so the two are weighted 1 to 4 and the error variance is $1/(1 + 4) = 0.2$. The causal predictor $\hat Y = X_c$ has error 1. In a test environment with a new $e$, the error of the all-features predictor is $Y - \hat Y = (0.8 - 0.8e)X_c + (1 - 0.8e)N_Y - 0.8N_s$, so

By [](#eq-l4-10-mse) the error is 0.2 at $e = 1$, 1.8 at $e = 0$, and 5.96 at $e = -1$, while the causal predictor stays at 1 for every $e$. The two are equally good where $1.28e^2 - 2.88e + 0.8 = 0$, at $e \approx 0.32$ and $e \approx 1.93$.

blocks.alt: A graph X_c to Y to X_s with an environment node e pointing into X_s, and a plot of test error against e: a flat cyan line at 1 and an amber curve that is 0.2 at e = 1 and rises to 5.96 at e = -1.
blocks.caption: The all-features predictor wins in training (0.2 against 1) and loses badly once the environment changes the mechanism of $X_s$; the causal predictor's error does not move.
blocks.describe: The diagram shows $X_c \to Y \to X_s$ with a square environment node $e$ pointing into $X_s$, and the mechanism $X_s := e\,Y + N_s$. Two predictors are listed: causal, $\hat Y = X_c$, and all features, $\hat Y = 0.2X_c + 0.8X_s$. On axes of test MSE against $e$ from $-1$ to 2, a dashed line marks training $e = 1$, where the errors are 0.2 and 1. As $e$ sweeps from 1 to $-1$, a cyan dot traces a flat line at 1 and an amber dot traces a rising curve, ending at 5.96 against 1. The formula $\mathrm{MSE}(e) = 0.64(1-e)^2 + (1-0.8e)^2 + 0.16$ appears, and a red dot marks the crossing near $e = 0.32$. A closing line says the causal predictor is worse in training and stable everywhere.

blocks.caption: Move the slider to change the test environment $e$. Left: predictions against the true $Y$ for the causal predictor (cyan) and the all-features predictor (amber); points on the dotted diagonal are perfect. Right: test error of both predictors against $e$.
blocks.describe: The first panel plots predictions against the true $Y$ for 160 simulated units. The cyan cloud ($\hat Y = X_c$) never changes. The amber cloud ($0.2X_c + 0.8X_s$) hugs the diagonal at $e = 1$, flattens at $e = 0$, and tilts the wrong way at $e = -1$. The second panel plots the error curves: cyan flat at 1 and amber $0.64(1-e)^2 + (1-0.8e)^2 + 0.16$, with markers at the chosen $e$.

blocks.title: The causal conditional is invariant
blocks.label: prop-l4-10-invariance
blocks.md: Consider structural models indexed by an environment $e$ that share the mechanism $Y := f(\mathrm{pa}_Y, N_Y)$ and the law of $N_Y$, with $N_Y$ independent of $\mathrm{pa}_Y$ in every environment. Then the conditional law of $Y$ given $\mathrm{pa}_Y = p$ is the same in every environment, whatever the environments do to other mechanisms.

Given $\mathrm{pa}_Y = p$, $Y = f(p, N_Y)$, and because $N_Y$ is independent of $\mathrm{pa}_Y$, its conditional law given $\mathrm{pa}_Y = p$ is its unconditional law, which does not depend on $e$. So the law of $Y$ given $\mathrm{pa}_Y = p$ is the law of $f(p, N_Y)$ in every environment. Sets that include a child of $Y$, such as $\{X_c, X_s\}$ above, have no such guarantee.

blocks.title: Coverage of invariant causal prediction
blocks.label: thm-l4-10-icp
blocks.md: For each subset $S$ of predictors, let $H_{0,S}$ be the hypothesis that the conditional law of $Y$ given $X_S$ is the same in all observed environments, and test it at level $\alpha$. Let $\hat S$ be the intersection of all subsets whose hypothesis is not rejected (and $\hat S = \varnothing$ if all are rejected). If the parents $S^* = \mathrm{pa}_Y$ satisfy $H_{0,S^*}$, then $P(\hat S \subseteq S^*) \ge 1 - \alpha$ [@invariant].

If $H_{0,S^*}$ is not rejected, $S^*$ is one of the sets being intersected, so $\hat S \subseteq S^*$. The test of the true hypothesis $H_{0,S^*}$ rejects with probability at most $\alpha$. Hence $P(\hat S \subseteq S^*) \ge P(H_{0,S^*} \text{ not rejected}) \ge 1 - \alpha$. The guarantee is one-sided: $\hat S$ may be smaller than $S^*$, even empty, when the environments do not vary enough to reject the wrong sets.

blocks.explain: A small version of invariant causal prediction with two environments: the first has $\operatorname{sd}(X_c) = 1$ and $e = 1$, the second has $\operatorname{sd}(X_c) = 2$ and $e = -1$. For each subset, fit the regression separately in each environment and test whether the coefficients and the residual variances agree (normal approximations, Bonferroni correction). Only $\{X_c\}$ survives, so the estimate is $\{X_c\}$.
blocks.source:
import math
from itertools import combinations

rng = np.random.default_rng(11)

def environment(n, sd_c, e):
    xc = rng.normal(0, sd_c, n)                 # environments shift the cause X_c ...
    y = xc + rng.normal(0, 1, n)                # ... but never the mechanism of Y
    xs = e * y + rng.normal(0, 0.5, n)          # and change the mechanism of the effect X_s
    return np.column_stack([xc, xs]), y

def fit(F, y):
    b = np.linalg.lstsq(F, y, rcond=None)[0]
    r = y - F @ b
    s2 = r @ r / (len(y) - F.shape[1])
    return b, np.sqrt(np.diag(s2 * np.linalg.inv(F.T @ F))), s2

def p_two_sided(zscore):
    return math.erfc(abs(zscore) / math.sqrt(2))

envs = [environment(1000, 1.0, 1.0), environment(1000, 2.0, -1.0)]
names = ['X_c', 'X_s']
accepted = []
for k in range(3):
    for S in combinations(range(2), k):
        (b1, se1, v1), (b2, se2, v2) = [fit(np.column_stack([np.ones(len(yy))] + [X[:, j] for j in S]), yy)
                                        for X, yy in envs]
        ps = [p_two_sided((b1[i] - b2[i]) / math.hypot(se1[i], se2[i])) for i in range(len(b1))]
        ps.append(p_two_sided(math.log(v1 / v2) / math.sqrt(4 / 999)))   # equal residual variance
        p = min(1.0, len(ps) * min(ps))                                   # Bonferroni
        label = '{' + ', '.join(names[j] for j in S) + '}'
        print(label.ljust(12), 'p = %.3g' % p, 'accepted' if p > 0.05 else 'rejected')
        if p > 0.05:
            accepted.append(set(S))
S_hat = set.intersection(*accepted) if accepted else set()
print('ICP estimate of the causal parents:', {names[j] for j in S_hat})

blocks.title: What invariance does not show
blocks.md: Invariance is a consequence of causal structure under the stated assumptions, not a proof of it. Hidden confounding between a parent and $Y$, or an environment that changes the mechanism of $Y$ itself, breaks the guarantee. A causal predictor is also not always the most accurate: in the exercises it loses to the all-features predictor whenever the deployment environments stay close to training. Its virtue is stability under shifts that leave the mechanism of $Y$ alone [@invariant; @scholkopf; @peters].

Fairness criteria are formal versions of social goals, and different goals lead to different criteria. Statistical criteria compare groups: equal rates of positive predictions (demographic parity), equal error rates (equalized odds [@hardt2016]), or equal meaning of a score (calibration). When base rates differ between groups, calibration and equal error rates cannot both hold for an imperfect predictor [@kleinberg2016; @chouldechova2017]. Causal criteria ask instead how the protected attribute $A$ influences the prediction through the mechanisms of a model [@bareinboim]. One consequence is general: leaving $A$ out of the inputs does not by itself remove its influence, because $A$ can affect the features that remain.

blocks.title: Counterfactual fairness
blocks.label: def-l4-10-cf-fair
blocks.md: Fix a structural model with protected attribute $A$, features $X$, and background variables $U$, and a predictor $\hat Y = h(X, A)$. Write $\hat Y_{a'}$ for the prediction in the counterfactual world with $A$ set to $a'$. The predictor is **counterfactually fair** if for every $x$ and $a$ with $P(X = x, A = a) > 0$, every $a'$, and every $y$: $P(\hat Y_{a} = y \mid X = x, A = a) = P(\hat Y_{a'} = y \mid X = x, A = a)$. The condition is on the unit's evidence $X = x, A = a$, so it is computed by the three steps of [L4-09](#lesson-l4-09). The definition is due to Kusner, Loftus, Russell and Silva [@kusner2017].

blocks.title: Predictors of non-descendants are counterfactually fair
blocks.label: prop-l4-10-nondesc
blocks.md: If $\hat Y$ is a function only of $U$ and of variables that are not descendants of $A$ in the model, then $\hat Y$ is counterfactually fair [@kusner2017].

Setting $A$ to $a'$ changes only the mechanisms downstream of $A$. A variable that is not a descendant of $A$ is computed from $U$ by mechanisms that never read $A$, so its value in the counterfactual world equals its factual value for every $u$. Hence $\hat Y_{a}(u) = \hat Y_{a'}(u)$ for every $u$, and the two conditional distributions in the definition are equal.

The running example is as small as possible: one feature with $X := U + A$, where $U$ is independent of $A$. Consider $h_1 = X$, which does not take $A$ as input, and $h_2 = X - A$, which does. A unit with $A = 1$ and $X = 3$ has $u = 3 - 1 = 2$ by abduction. In the world with $A$ set to 0, $X = 2 + 0 = 2$. So $h_1$ gives 3 and 2: it is not counterfactually fair even though it never sees $A$. And $h_2 = X - A$ gives 2 and 2 for every unit, because in this model $h_2 = U$, a non-descendant of $A$.

blocks.alt: Two copies of a small graph, A and U pointing into X, share the node U. In the unit's own world A = 1 and X = 3; in the world with A set to 0, X = 2. A predictor equal to X gives 3 and 2; a predictor equal to X - A gives 2 and 2.
blocks.caption: One unit, two worlds, in the model $X := U + A$: the predictor that ignores $A$ changes when $A$ changes, and the predictor $h_2 = X - A$ does not.
blocks.describe: The model $X := U + A$, with $U$ independent of $A$, is written at the top. A shared node $U$ sits between two copies of the graph $A \to X \leftarrow U$. In the unit's own world, $A = 1$ and $X = 3$, and abduction writes $u = 3 - 1 = 2$ beside $U$. In the world with $A$ set to 0, the label $A := 0$ appears and $X = 2 + 0 = 2$. Below, $h_1 = X$ gives 3 versus 2, marked as changing and not counterfactually fair. Then $h_2 = X - A$ gives 2 versus 2, marked as the same in both worlds, in this model, and boxed. A closing line says the verdict depends on the model and on choosing to block the path from $A$ to $X$.

blocks.explain: The same check by computer: abduction for the unit, then each predictor in both worlds, then a population of units drawn from the model.
blocks.source:
# Counterfactual fairness in the model X := U + A, with U independent of A
def feature(u, a):
    return u + a

h1 = lambda x, a: x                             # does not take A as input
h2 = lambda x, a: x - a                         # uses A to undo its effect on X

a_obs, x_obs = 1, 3
u = x_obs - a_obs                               # abduction
for name, h in (('h1 = X    ', h1), ('h2 = X - A', h2)):
    own, other = h(feature(u, a_obs), a_obs), h(feature(u, 0), 0)
    print(name, '| own world', own, '| world with A set to 0', other)

# the same check for many units drawn from the model
rng = np.random.default_rng(5)
U = rng.normal(0, 1, 10_000)
A = rng.integers(0, 2, 10_000)
for name, h in (('h1', h1), ('h2', h2)):
    gap = np.abs(h(feature(U, 1), 1) - h(feature(U, 0), 0)).max()
    print(name, 'largest change when A is flipped:', round(gap, 6))
print('h2 recovers U for every unit:', np.allclose(h2(feature(U, A), A), U))

blocks.title: What this check does and does not establish
blocks.md: The verdict on $h_2$ is relative to the model. It assumes that $X := U + A$ is the right mechanism, with an effect of exactly 1 and no other path from $A$, and that $U$ is independent of $A$; neither can be fully checked from data. Treating the whole path $A \to X$ as one that the prediction should not follow is a value judgment; path-specific criteria allow some paths and block others. What it means to set a protected attribute to another value is itself debated, so the counterfactual world needs a careful definition in each application. Counterfactual fairness can conflict with statistical criteria and with accuracy, and a fair predictor does not by itself make the decisions built on it fair. These choices belong to the people affected and accountable, not to the algorithm.

worked_example.title: Transporting an effect across three strata
worked_example.problem: A trial in a source population estimated stratum effects $\tau = (0.5, 1.5, 4)$ for three age groups, whose shares in the source were $(0.2, 0.5, 0.3)$. A target population has shares $(0.5, 0.4, 0.1)$. The age groups are the only known difference between the populations. Estimate the target ATE and say what must be true for the estimate to be valid.
steps: Selection diagram: $S \to Z$ only, with $Z$ the age group, pre-treatment and unaffected by treatment. The trial randomized treatment, so $Z$ satisfies the backdoor criterion trivially, and each age group appears in the source with both arms (positivity).

Validity: the stratum effects must be the same in the target (no $S \to Y$ and no unmeasured effect modifier distributed differently). If the target also had a fourth age group absent from the source, its effect would be unidentified from these data.
worked_example.result: $\mathrm{ATE}^* = 1.25$ against a source ATE of $2.05$: the target has more people in the group with the smallest effect. The number is only as good as the assumption that the age groups carry all the relevant differences.

exercises.prompt: Conditional effects in two strata are 2 and $-1$. Target weights are 0.25 and 0.75. Calculate the transported average effect under the stability assumptions of the transport theorem. Does that number establish that a policy based on it is fair?
exercises.solution: $0.25(2) + 0.75(-1) = -0.25$. This is a target-population causal average under the assumptions. It does not establish fairness, which needs a stated criterion, a model of how the protected attribute acts, and further justification.

exercises.prompt: Four units have (treatment, outcome, propensity) equal to $(1, 4, 0.8)$, $(1, 2, 0.5)$, $(0, 1, 0.5)$, $(0, 3, 0.2)$. Compute the IPW estimate $\frac{1}{n}\sum_i [T_iY_i/e_i - (1 - T_i)Y_i/(1 - e_i)]$.
Show that the AIPW estimator [](#eq-l4-10-aipw) equals the IPW estimator when $\hat\mu_0 = \hat\mu_1 = 0$, and equals the plug-in estimator when every residual $Y_i - \hat\mu_{T_i}(Z_i)$ is zero.
exercises.solution: With $\hat\mu_t = 0$ the bracket is $T_iY_i/\hat e(Z_i) - (1 - T_i)Y_i/(1 - \hat e(Z_i))$, the IPW summand. If every residual is zero, then for a treated unit $Y_i - \hat\mu_1(Z_i) = 0$ and the term $(1 - T_i)(\dots)$ is zero, and for a control unit $Y_i - \hat\mu_0(Z_i) = 0$ and $T_i(\dots) = 0$; both correction terms vanish and the bracket is $\hat\mu_1(Z_i) - \hat\mu_0(Z_i)$, the plug-in summand.

exercises.prompt: In the shift model [](#eq-l4-10-shift), compute $\mathrm{MSE}(e)$ for the all-features predictor at $e = 0.5$, $e = 1.5$, and $e = 2$. If deployment environments are known to lie in $[0.5, 1.5]$, which predictor has the smaller worst-case error?
exercises.solution: From [](#eq-l4-10-mse): $\mathrm{MSE}(0.5) = 0.64(0.25) + 0.6^2 + 0.16 = 0.16 + 0.36 + 0.16 = 0.68$; $\mathrm{MSE}(1.5) = 0.64(0.25) + 0.2^2 + 0.16 = 0.36$; $\mathrm{MSE}(2) = 0.64 + 0.36 + 0.16 = 1.16$. The function is a convex quadratic in $e$, so on $[0.5, 1.5]$ its maximum is at an endpoint, $0.68 < 1$. The all-features predictor is better throughout that range; the causal predictor is preferable when the shift can be large or is unknown.

exercises.prompt: Take the model $X_1 := U + A$, $X_2 := U + N$ with $U$, $N$, $A$ independent, and the linear predictor $\hat Y = w_1X_1 + w_2X_2 + w_3A$. (a) For which weights is $\hat Y$ counterfactually fair? (b) Is the predictor $X_1$, which leaves out $A$, counterfactually fair? (c) Does $h = X_1 - A$ also satisfy demographic parity, $\hat Y \perp\!\!\!\perp A$, in this model?
exercises.solution: (a) Abduction fixes $u$ and $n$. Setting $A$ from $a$ to $a'$ changes $X_1$ by $a' - a$ and leaves $X_2$ unchanged, so $\hat Y_{a'} - \hat Y_{a} = (w_1 + w_3)(a' - a)$. The predictor is counterfactually fair exactly when $w_3 = -w_1$, for any $w_2$. (b) No: $w_1 = 1$, $w_3 = 0$, and the prediction changes by $a' - a$. (c) Yes: $X_1 - A = U$, which is independent of $A$. In this model the two criteria agree for $h$; in other models, for example if $U$ depended on $A$, they need not.

exercises.prompt: Show that when the selection diagram has an arrow $S \to Y$, the source distribution cannot determine $\mathrm{ATE}^*$: for the running transport example, construct a family of target models that all agree with the source data and with $P^*(z) = (0.8, 0.2)$ but have different target effects.
exercises.solution: Let the source model be $Y := X(1 + 2Z) + Z + N_Y$ and the target model $Y := X(1 + 2Z + \delta) + Z + N_Y$ for any real $\delta$, with the same mechanism for $X$ given $Z$ and $P^*(Z = 1) = 0.2$. The source data are generated by the first model whatever $\delta$ is, and the target covariate distribution is the same for all $\delta$. The target effect is $\mathrm{ATE}^* = 0.8(1 + \delta) + 0.2(3 + \delta) = 1.4 + \delta$, which takes every real value. So no function of the source distribution and $P^*(z)$ can equal $\mathrm{ATE}^*$ for all these models.

check.question: What must come before fitting a causal effect learner?
options: A guarantee that all populations share one effect
A decision to remove every demographic variable
A defined causal target and justified identification assumptions
check.explanation: A learner estimates quantities inside a causal analysis. The target and the identification assumptions decide whether its estimates answer the intended causal question.

check.question: Stratum effects are 1 and 3. The target population has stratum shares 0.8 and 0.2, and the selection diagram has an arrow from $S$ into the stratum variable only. What is the transported ATE?
check.explanation: With the selection node pointing only into $Z$, the stratum effects are shared, so $\mathrm{ATE}^* = 0.8(1) + 0.2(3) = 1.4$. The value 2 uses the source shares and 2.6 swaps the weights.

check.question: In the model $X := U + A$ with $U$ independent of $A$, is the predictor $h_1 = X$, which does not take $A$ as input, counterfactually fair?
options: It depends only on the accuracy of the predictor
Yes, because U is independent of A
No, because setting A to another value changes X and therefore the prediction
Yes, because the predictor never reads A
check.explanation: For a unit with $A = 1$, $X = 3$, abduction gives $u = 2$; with $A$ set to 0, $X = 2$, so the prediction moves from 3 to 2. Leaving $A$ out of the inputs does not block its effect through $X$.

check.question: In a graph where $Z$ satisfies the backdoor criterion for the effect of $X$ on $Y$, which expression equals $P(y \mid do(x))$?
check.explanation: Backdoor adjustment averages the stratum-specific outcome risks over the marginal distribution of $Z$. Weighting by $P(z \mid x)$ instead just rebuilds the observational $P(y \mid x)$. The transport formula has the same shape, with the target's $P^*(z)$.

misconceptions.claim: "A more accurate model gives a more causal answer."
misconceptions.correction: Accuracy measures how well a model fits the observed distribution. Without identification assumptions, a perfect fit of outcome regressions can converge to a confounded contrast, as the naive contrast of 4.37 against a true effect of 2 shows in the simulation.

misconceptions.claim: "Removing the protected attribute from the inputs makes a model fair."
misconceptions.correction: Other features can carry the attribute's influence. In the model $X := U + A$, the predictor $X$ never reads $A$ yet changes when $A$ changes; whether that is acceptable is a value judgment that must be made explicitly.

misconceptions.claim: "The causal predictor is always the most accurate one."
misconceptions.correction: In the training environment the causal predictor had error 1 against 0.2 for the predictor that used an effect of $Y$. Its advantage is stability when environments change mechanisms other than that of $Y$.

misconceptions.claim: "An effect estimated well in one population applies everywhere."
misconceptions.correction: Transport needs a selection diagram in which the populations differ only in measured covariates that block the selection nodes from $Y$, plus source data in every target stratum. A changed outcome mechanism defeats reweighting.

lessons.connect: The same discipline (define the target, state the assumptions, then estimate) carries into the rest of the course. Level 6 builds causal models for quantum systems, where the questions of intervention, invariance, and transport have to be asked again for quantum mechanisms, and Level 7 reads claims about quantum machine learning with the same accounting of assumptions used here.
lessons.caution: The simulations in this lesson are illustrations with known models; they show how the methods behave when their assumptions hold or fail, not that the assumptions hold in any real application. The transport theorem is stated for the simple case of covariate shift with a backdoor set; the general theory of transportability handles more complex selection diagrams and is not covered. The invariance demonstration uses normal approximations, two environments, and a Bonferroni correction; the published method has more careful tests and confidence statements. Counterfactual fairness is one criterion among several, it is relative to an assumed structural model, and the fairness example is deliberately abstract. Nothing here settles which fairness criterion is appropriate in a given setting.

instructor.why: Students arrive with machine learning habits (fit, validate, deploy) and need to see where causal assumptions enter that pipeline. The lesson connects the identification results of Level 4 to estimators used in practice, to transport across populations, to robustness under shift, and to fairness, while insisting that each claim names its assumptions [@hernan; @bareinboim; @invariant; @scholkopf].
teaching_notes: Start with the doubly robust figure: ask students to predict which estimator fails in each of the four settings before revealing the bars, then derive the proof of double robustness on the board.
Have students draw the selection diagram before computing any transported number; ask what would have to be true for an arrow into $Y$ to be absent.
In the shift example, emphasize that the all-features predictor is the better choice near training; the point is not that causal models always win, but what kind of shift each predictor tolerates.

Discuss counterfactual fairness neutrally: present the model, the computation, and then the list of assumptions and value choices, and let students argue about which choices a given application needs.
instructor.assessment: The stretch exercises check the estimator algebra and the shift computation; the challenge exercises test whether students can derive a fairness condition in a model and construct a non-transportability argument. The check questions cover the target-first principle, the transport formula, and the limits of removing an attribute.
instructor.extend: Implement cross-fitted AIPW with a flexible learner and compare its confidence interval with that of the plug-in estimator. Read the discussion of invariance and causal representation learning in Schölkopf and coauthors [@scholkopf], and the chapters on transportability and fairness in Bareinboim's roadmap [@bareinboim].

further.note: The original invariant causal prediction paper, with tests, confidence statements, and identifiability results.
Covers selection diagrams and transportability in general, and causal approaches to fairness.
A Python library that structures an analysis as model, identify, estimate, and refute.

unit.big_question: When can data that were only observed tell us what would happen if we acted, and what must we assume, state, and test before a causal claim is justified?
unit.summary: Students write structural causal models and compute interventions by replacing one mechanism. They read conditional independences off directed acyclic graphs with d-separation, sort variables into confounders, mediators, and colliders, and derive the backdoor and frontdoor formulas (full proofs for the core cases, cited sketches in general) that turn interventional questions into observational ones. They connect graphs to potential outcomes and randomized experiments, separate identification from estimation, and see why two models can fit the same data and disagree about an action. The unit closes with what data cannot reveal (Markov equivalence, faithfulness), counterfactuals by abduction, action, and prediction, and the extra assumptions needed for causal machine learning, transport between populations, and fairness claims.
unit.for_whom: Undergraduates who have finished Levels 2 and 3 of this course or an equivalent introduction to probability, expectation, linear algebra, and regression. The lessons suit a one-semester course or a study group; each has proofs for students who want them and runnable code for students who learn by computing.
unit.prerequisites: Conditional probability and Bayes' rule, expectation and variance, simple linear regression, and enough Python to run and modify a NumPy notebook.

time.pace: One lesson a week fits a semester with the project in the last three weeks; two lessons a week fits an intensive half-term. Each lesson splits into an intuition and animation sitting and a proofs, code, and exercises sitting.

session_flow: Warm up: predict the answer to the lesson's opening puzzle before any formula.
Watch the animations and read the definitions; restate each in your own words.
Work through the theorem and its proof, then the worked example by hand.
Run and modify the code; confirm the hand calculation numerically and use the interactive figure to test a prediction.
Solve the core and stretch exercises, then answer the check questions before opening the explanations.
Close by writing the assumptions each result needed and where they could fail.

outcomes.text: Write a structural causal model, compute an intervention by graph surgery, and compare it with conditioning.
Decide d-separation in a causal graph and state precisely what the soundness theorem does and does not guarantee.
Choose an adjustment set by graph roles and compute the bias caused by adjusting for a mediator or a collider.
Derive and apply the backdoor and frontdoor formulas, stating every graphical and positivity condition.
Define average treatment effects with potential outcomes and explain how randomization identifies them.
Separate identification from estimation, and show with two models that the same data can support different causal answers.
Answer a counterfactual question in an explicit structural model by abduction, action, and prediction.
State the additional assumptions behind causal machine learning, transport, and fairness claims, and audit a claim that omits them.

unit.evidence: Each lesson has three or four check questions (one reviews an earlier lesson), exercises at core, stretch, and challenge levels with complete solutions, and runnable code whose printed results must match the hand calculation. The project is a written causal analysis with code, judged with a four-part rubric.
materials: Python 3 with NumPy, SciPy, pandas, Matplotlib, Plotly, and networkx (the course notebooks run in Colab or Binder)
The course package qcai, whose science module contains the binary structural causal model used in the lessons
Paper and pencil for drawing graphs and checking paths by hand
Optional: the DoWhy or causal-learn libraries for the project

project.title: A causal analysis you can defend
project.summary: Over three sessions students state a causal question, draw and justify a graph, prove that the target effect is identified (or show that it is not), estimate it on simulated or public data, and write an analysis that keeps assumptions, identification, estimation, and limits apart.
questions: In a simulated hospital dataset generated from a structural model the student writes, what is the effect of a treatment on recovery, and which covariates must be adjusted for?

Using a public observational dataset described in a textbook (for example a job-training or smoking study), what effect can be identified under a stated graph, and how sensitive is the answer to one omitted confounder?
For a prediction model trained in one population, which causal assumptions would justify using it in a second population, and what would a fairness audit of it need to assume?
steps: State the causal question as a target quantity, such as the outcome distribution under an intervention or an average treatment effect, and say why prediction alone does not answer it.
Draw the causal graph, justify every arrow and every missing arrow in one sentence each, and list the testable independences it implies.
Prove identification with the backdoor or frontdoor criterion, or show by two models that the effect is not identified.
Estimate the effect with a standardization or regression estimator and report an uncertainty interval.
Test the graph's implied independences where data allow, and run one sensitivity analysis for an unmeasured confounder.
Write the analysis: question, graph, identification proof, estimate, checks, and the limits of the claim.

rubric.start: I described a relationship I am interested in.
rubric.got: I stated a precise interventional or counterfactual target.
rubric.explain: I can explain why that target differs from the corresponding conditional quantity in my data.

rubric.got: I justified each arrow and listed the independences the graph implies.
rubric.explain: I can say which conclusions would change if a specific arrow were added or removed.

rubric.start: I chose variables to adjust for.
rubric.got: I proved identification with a stated criterion, including positivity.
rubric.explain: I can show a second model that fits my data and gives a different answer when my assumptions fail.

rubric.got: I reported an estimate with uncertainty and at least one check of the graph.
rubric.explain: I can state what the estimate does not show and what new data or experiment would settle it.

udl: Every key idea appears three ways: a moving animation with a full text description, a formal statement with proof, and code whose output can be checked.
Students can show mastery by a proof, a computation, a simulation, or an annotated causal graph.
Each lesson has core, stretch, and challenge exercises, so the same lesson serves students who need consolidation and students who want depth.
Interactive figures let students test a prediction by changing one quantity at a time before they read the explanation.

readings.note: The reference text for structural causal models, the do-operator, d-separation, and identification.
Free textbook on causal inference from data, strong on confounding, selection bias, and potential outcomes.
Concise, mathematical treatment of SCMs, Markov properties, and causal discovery, free online.
Lecture notes with many small worked graphs; a gentle companion to every lesson.
Applied examples of graphs, adjustment, and identification strategies in social science data.
The source for faithfulness and constraint-based causal discovery.
A roadmap connecting causal inference with artificial intelligence, transport, and fairness.

unit.approach: The unit was planned backward from its outcomes [@ubd_whitepaper]. Each lesson moves from a concrete puzzle to an animation, then to a precise definition and theorem with proof, then to computation and practice, following first principles of instruction [@merrill2002], with retrieval and spaced review through check questions that revisit earlier lessons [@dunlosky2013]. Several 3Blue1Brown-style animations per lesson, made with Manim Community Edition [@manim_ce] and driven by the same numbers as the text, show what static notation hides: graph surgery, paths opening and closing, and selection creating correlation. Multiple representations follow Universal Design for Learning [@udl]. The content follows Pearl's structural account of causation [@pearlcausality; @pearl] together with the potential-outcomes treatment of Hernán and Robins [@hernan], the Markov and discovery theory of Spirtes, Glymour and Scheines and of Peters, Janzing and Schölkopf [@spirtes; @peters], and the causal AI roadmap of Bareinboim and colleagues [@bareinboim].
